abstract: Increasing attention has been paid to reinforcement learning algo(cid:173) rithms in recent years, partly due to successes in the theoretical analysis of their behavior in Markov environments. If the Markov assumption is removed, however, neither generally the algorithms nor the analyses continue to be usable. We propose and analyze a new learning algorithm to solve a certain class of non-Markov decision problems. Our algorithm applies to problems in which the environment is Markov, but the learner has restricted access to state information. The algorithm involves a Monte-Carlo pol(cid:173) icy evaluation combined with a policy improvement method that is similar to that of Markov decision problems and is guaranteed to converge to a local maximum. The algorithm operates in the space of stochastic policies, a space which can yield a policy that per(cid:173) forms considerably better than any deterministic policy. Although the space of stochastic policies is continuous-even for a discrete action space-our algorithm is computationally tractable. 346 Tommi Jaakkola, Satinder P. Singh, Michaell. Jordan

paragraphs: The paper addresses decision problems in which the environment is Markov but the learner cannot observe its complete state. Restricted observations mean the information available to the learner may not support the usual Markov assumptions. Consequently, algorithms and analyses built around fully accessible state information cannot generally be carried over unchanged.

The proposed algorithm combines Monte Carlo policy evaluation with a policy improvement procedure resembling that used in Markov decision problems. It searches over stochastic policies, which assign probabilities to actions rather than always selecting one fixed action for a given observation. In this setting, such policies can perform considerably better than any deterministic policy.

The authors analyze the method and guarantee convergence to a local maximum. That guarantee concerns a locally optimal policy, rather than necessarily the best policy in the entire search space. Although action probabilities create a continuous search space even when the action choices are discrete, the algorithm remains computationally tractable. The contribution is a learnable, analyzed approach for this class of restricted-observation problems.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces a tractable stochastic-policy learning algorithm with local convergence guarantees for a class of partially observable problems.

title: Reinforcement Learning Algorithm for Partially Observable Markov Decision Problems

abstract: In this study, an integrated neural network control architecture for nonlinear dynamic systems is presented. Most of the recent emphasis in the neural network control field has no error feedback as the control input, which rises the lack of adaptation problem. The integrated architecture in this paper combines feed forward control and error feedback adaptive control using neural networks. The paper reveals the different internal functionality of these two kinds of neural network controllers for certain input styles, e.g., state feedback and error feedback. With error feedback, neural network controllers learn the slopes or the gains with respect to the error feedback, producing an error driven adaptive control systems. The results demonstrate that the two kinds of control scheme can be combined to realize their individual advantages. Testing with disturbances added to the plant shows good tracking and adaptation with the integrated neural control architecture.

paragraphs: The paper presents a neural controller for nonlinear dynamic systems that combines feedforward control with adaptive control driven by error feedback. The motivation is that controllers without error as an input can lack a mechanism for adapting their behavior to the mismatch between the desired response and the system’s actual response.

The authors examine how neural controllers function internally when given different input styles, including system state and feedback error. With error feedback, the network learns slopes or gains that determine how strongly the controller reacts to an error. This makes adaptation directly responsive to the discrepancy the controller is trying to correct.

Combining the two control schemes is intended to retain their individual advantages within one architecture. Tests introduce disturbances into the controlled system and show good tracking and adaptation. These findings support the practical value of joining an anticipatory control pathway with an error-driven adaptive pathway: the integrated controller can pursue the desired behavior while adjusting its response when disturbances change what the system actually does.
summary.tldr: Combining feedforward neural control with error-driven adaptation produces good tracking when disturbances affect a nonlinear dynamic system.

title: An Integrated Architecture of Adaptive Neural Network Control for Dynamic Systems

abstract: Two dimensional image motion detection neural networks have been implemented using a general purpose analog neural computer. The neural circuits perform spatiotemporal feature extraction based on the cortical motion detection model of Adelson and Bergen. The neural computer provides the neurons, synapses and synaptic time-constants required to realize the model in VLSI hardware. Results show that visual motion estimation can be implemented with simple sum-and(cid:173) threshold neural hardware with temporal computational capabilities. The neural circuits compute general 20 visual motion in real-time.

paragraphs: The paper implements neural networks for detecting two-dimensional image motion on a general-purpose analog neural computer. The circuits follow the cortical motion-detection model of Adelson and Bergen. Their task is spatiotemporal feature extraction, meaning that they combine information about image structure with information about how it changes over time.

The neural computer supplies neurons, synapses, and synaptic time constants needed to realize the model in VLSI hardware. These time constants give the circuit temporal computational capabilities, which are essential when the relevant signal is motion. The implementation therefore maps both the connections and the time-dependent processing of the model into hardware.

The reported results show that simple sum-and-threshold neural circuitry with temporal capabilities can estimate visual motion. The circuits process general two-dimensional motion in real time. The contribution is a working hardware realization that connects a cortical computation model to the operations available on an analog neural computer, demonstrating that those operations suffice for the stated motion-processing task.
summary.tldr: An analog neural computer implements a cortical motion model and estimates two-dimensional visual motion in real time.

title: VLSI Implementation of Cortical Visual Motion Detection Using an Analog Neural Computer

abstract: We show the similarity between belief propagation and TAP, for decoding corrupted messages encoded by Sourlas's method. The latter is a special case of the Gallager error-correcting code, where the code word comprises products of J{ bits selected randomly from the original message. We examine the efficacy of solutions obtained by the two methods for various values of J{ and show that solutions for J{ 2': 3 may be sensitive to the choice of initial conditions in the case of unbiased patterns. Good approximations are obtained generally for J{ = 2 and for biased patterns in the case of J{ 2': 3, especially when Nishimori's temperature is being used.

paragraphs: The paper connects belief propagation and TAP in the task of decoding corrupted messages. It studies messages encoded by Sourlas's method, a special case of a Gallager error-correcting code. Encoded entries are products of K randomly selected message bits, making K a central feature of the decoding problem examined by the authors.

The authors show similarities between the two methods and compare the effectiveness of their solutions for different values of K. For unbiased patterns with K at least three, solutions may depend sensitively on the initial conditions. This means the starting point of the decoding procedure can matter in that setting; the abstract states this as a possibility rather than an unavoidable outcome.

Good approximations are generally obtained when K equals two and, for larger K, when the patterns are biased. Results are especially favorable when using Nishimori's temperature. These distinctions make the finding conditional on the encoding and pattern setting. The paper contributes both a relationship between two inference approaches and an account of circumstances associated with useful approximations or sensitivity to initialization.
summary.tldr: Belief propagation and TAP behave similarly in Sourlas decoding, with approximation quality and initialization sensitivity depending on encoding and pattern conditions.

title: The Belief in TAP

abstract: An important class of problems can be cast as inference in noisy(cid:173) OR Bayesian networks, where the binary state of each variable is a logical OR of noisy versions of the states of the variable's par(cid:173) ents. For example, in medical diagnosis, the presence of a symptom can be expressed as a noisy-OR of the diseases that may cause the symptom - on some occasions, a disease may fail to activate the symptom. Inference in richly-connected noisy-OR networks is in(cid:173) tractable, but approximate methods (e .g., variational techniques) are showing increasing promise as practical solutions. One prob(cid:173) lem with most approximations is that they tend to concentrate on a relatively small number of modes in the true posterior, ig(cid:173) noring other plausible configurations of the hidden variables. We introduce a new sequential variational method for bipartite noisy(cid:173) OR networks, that favors including all modes of the true posterior and models the posterior distribution as a tree. We compare this method with other approximations using an ensemble of networks with network statistics that are comparable to the QMR-DT med(cid:173) ical diagnostic network. paragraphs: Noisy-OR networks represent situations where several possible causes can activate an outcome, but each cause may sometimes fail to do so. The abstract uses diseases and symptoms as an example. In richly connected networks, exact inference is intractable, creating a need for approximations to the distribution over hidden causes.

The paper focuses on a particular weakness of many approximations: they concentrate on a few likely configurations and overlook other plausible explanations. It introduces a sequential variational method for bipartite noisy-OR networks that represents the posterior as a tree. The method favors including all posterior modes, addressing the breadth of explanations retained by the approximation.

The authors compare the method with other approximations on an ensemble of networks whose statistics resemble those of the QMR-DT medical diagnostic network. The central contribution is an inclusive approach to posterior approximation: the fitting procedure is designed to retain competing explanations rather than concentrate too narrowly. The stated aim of including modes is a property the method favors, rather than a guarantee that every explanation is recovered.
summary.tldr: Sequential tree-based variational inference is designed to preserve competing explanations in bipartite noisy-OR networks.

title: Sequentially Fitting ``Inclusive'' Trees for Inference in Noisy-OR Networks

abstract: The standard representation of text documents as bags of words suffers from well known limitations, mostly due to its inability to exploit semantic similarity between terms. Attempts to incorpo(cid:173) rate some notion of term similarity include latent semantic index(cid:173) ing [8], the use of semantic networks [9], and probabilistic methods [5]. In this paper we propose two methods for inferring such sim(cid:173) ilarity from a corpus. The first one defines word-similarity based on document-similarity and viceversa, giving rise to a system of equations whose equilibrium point we use to obtain a semantic similarity measure. The second method models semantic relations by means of a diffusion process on a graph defined by lexicon and co-occurrence information. Both approaches produce valid kernel functions parametrised by a real number. The paper shows how the alignment measure can be used to successfully perform model selection over this parameter. Combined with the use of support vector machines we obtain positive results.

paragraphs: Bag-of-words representations describe documents through their terms but do not directly capture similarity in meaning between different terms. This paper proposes two ways to infer semantic similarity from a corpus. Both methods produce kernel functions, making the resulting similarities usable in kernel-based learning methods such as support vector machines.

The first method makes word similarity and document similarity depend on each other. Similar documents help establish relationships between words, while related words help establish relationships between documents. The authors express this mutual dependence as a system of equations and use its equilibrium to define similarity. The second method uses diffusion on a graph built from lexicon and co-occurrence information.

Each approach yields a family of valid kernels controlled by a real-valued parameter. The paper shows that an alignment measure can successfully guide selection of this parameter. Combined with support vector machines, the approaches produce positive results. Their shared contribution is to turn corpus-derived semantic relationships into a tunable similarity measure that a classifier can use.
summary.tldr: Two corpus-based methods learn semantic similarity kernels through mutual word-document relationships or graph diffusion, with positive SVM results.

title: Learning Semantic Similarity

abstract: We present a framework for sparse Gaussian process (GP) methods which uses forward selection with criteria based on information- theoretic principles, previously suggested for active learning. Our goal is not only to learn d{sparse predictors (which can be evalu- ated in O(d) rather than O(n), d (cid:28) n, n the number of training points), but also to perform training under strong restrictions on time and memory requirements. The scaling of our method is at most O(n (cid:1) d2), and in large real-world classi(cid:12)cation experiments we show that it can match prediction performance of the popular support vector machine (SVM), yet can be signi(cid:12)cantly faster in training. In contrast to the SVM, our approximation produces esti- mates of predictive probabilities (‘error bars’), allows for Bayesian model selection and is less complex in implementation.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a sparse Gaussian-process framework designed to reduce both prediction cost and the resources needed for training. It uses forward selection, choosing a compact set through information-theoretic criteria previously suggested for active learning. The goal is to retain useful predictive information while working under tight time and memory constraints.

With n training points and a sparse representation of size d, where d is much smaller than n, predictions require O(d) work instead of O(n). The method's scaling is at most O(n d²). These properties address two distinct needs: making the trained predictor economical to evaluate and keeping construction of that predictor manageable.

In large real-world classification experiments, the method can match support vector machine prediction performance while training significantly faster. The authors also emphasize that their approximation produces predictive probability estimates, supports Bayesian model selection, and has a less complex implementation than the SVM. The reported result is a combination of competitive classification, potentially substantial training savings, and probabilistic outputs, rather than a universal speed or accuracy advantage.
summary.tldr: Information-based forward selection yields sparse Gaussian-process predictors that can match SVM accuracy while training faster and retaining probabilistic predictions.

title: Fast Sparse Gaussian Process Methods: The Informative Vector Machine

abstract: Face detection is a canonical example of a rare event detection prob- lem, in which target patterns occur with much lower frequency than non- targets. Out of millions of face-sized windows in an input image, for ex- ample, only a few will typically contain a face. Viola and Jones recently proposed a cascade architecture for face detection which successfully ad- dresses the rare event nature of the task. A central part of their method is a feature selection algorithm based on AdaBoost. We present a novel cascade learning algorithm based on forward feature selection which is two orders of magnitude faster than the Viola-Jones approach and yields classiﬁers of equivalent quality. This faster method could be used for more demanding classiﬁcation tasks, such as on-line learning.

paragraphs: Face detection illustrates a severe imbalance between targets and nontargets. An image can contain millions of candidate windows of the right size, while only a few contain faces. The paper builds on the cascade architecture used by Viola and Jones, which addresses this rare-event setting through a sequence of classification stages.

The contribution is a new way to learn the cascade using forward feature selection. Feature selection is a central component of the earlier approach, where it is based on AdaBoost. By changing this learning component, the authors target the work needed to construct the detector while retaining classifiers of equivalent quality.

The paper reports that its cascade-learning method is two orders of magnitude faster than the Viola–Jones approach. This is a claim about learning the classifier, rather than a stated speedup in running the finished detector. The authors suggest that faster learning could make more demanding uses, such as online learning, feasible. That application remains a proposed possibility in the abstract.
summary.tldr: Forward feature selection learns rare-event detection cascades two orders of magnitude faster than the Viola–Jones approach while yielding equivalent classifier quality.

title: Learning a Rare Event Detection Cascade by Direct Feature Selection

abstract: We consider situations where training data is abundant and computing resources are comparatively scarce. We argue that suitably designed online learning algorithms asymptotically outperform any batch learning algorithm. Both theoretical and experimental evidences are presented.
originalAbstract: We consider situations where training data is abundant and computing resources are comparatively scarce. We argue that suitably designed online learning algorithms asymptotically outperform any batch learning algorithm. Both theoretical and experimental evidences are presented.
title: Large Scale Online Learning

abstract: On-line handwriting recognition is unusual among sequence labelling tasks in that the underlying generator of the observed data, i.e. the movement of the pen, is recorded directly. However, the raw data can be difficult to interpret because each letter is spread over many pen locations. As a consequence, sophisticated pre-processing is required to obtain inputs suitable for conventional sequence labelling algorithms, such as HMMs. In this paper we describe a system capable of directly transcribing raw on-line handwriting data. The system consists of a recurrent neural network trained for sequence labelling, combined with a probabilistic language model. In experiments on an unconstrained on-line database, we record excellent results using either raw or pre-processed data, well outperforming a benchmark HMM in both cases.

paragraphs: Online handwriting recognition records the movement of the pen directly. Even with that information, recognizing letters is difficult because a single letter extends across many recorded pen positions. Conventional sequence-labeling approaches such as hidden Markov models therefore require sophisticated preprocessing to turn the raw trajectory into suitable inputs.

This paper presents a system that can transcribe the raw handwriting sequence directly. It combines a recurrent neural network trained for sequence labeling with a probabilistic language model. The network handles the recorded sequence, while the language model contributes information about plausible text sequences to the overall recognition system.

Experiments on an unconstrained online handwriting database report strong results with both raw and preprocessed input. In each case, the system substantially outperforms the benchmark hidden Markov model. The raw-input result is particularly relevant to the paper’s motivation: the proposed combination can operate directly on pen data despite each character spanning multiple observations. The preprocessed-input result shows that its reported advantage also holds when preprocessing is supplied.
summary.tldr: A recurrent network combined with a language model directly transcribes pen trajectories and outperforms a benchmark HMM on raw and preprocessed handwriting.

title: Unconstrained On-line Handwriting Recognition with Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: We extend the Bayesian skill rating system TrueSkill to infer entire time series of skills of players by smoothing through time instead of (cid:12)ltering. The skill of each participating player, say, every year is represented by a latent skill variable which is a(cid:11)ected by the relevant game outcomes that year, and coupled with the skill variables of the previous and subsequent year. Inference in the resulting factor graph is carried out by approximate message passing (EP) along the time series of skills. As before the system tracks the uncertainty about player skills, explicitly models draws, can deal with any number of competing entities and can infer individual skills from team results. We extend the system to estimate player-speci(cid:12)c draw mar- gins. Based on these models we present an analysis of the skill curves of important players in the history of chess over the past 150 years. Results include plots of players’ lifetime skill development as well as the ability to compare the skills of di(cid:11)erent players across time. Our results indicate that a) the overall playing strength has increased over the past 150 years, and b) that modelling a player’s ability to force a draw provides signi(cid:12)cantly better predictive power.

paragraphs: TrueSkill Through Time extends Bayesian skill ratings from sequential updates to estimates of entire skill histories. Each player's skill at a given time is linked to relevant game outcomes and to skill variables at neighboring times. Smoothing allows later observations to inform earlier skill estimates, producing a connected account of development over time.

The model uses approximate message passing in a factor graph and retains uncertainty estimates, explicit treatment of draws, support for multiple competitors, and inference of individual skills from team outcomes. It also introduces player-specific draw margins, allowing the model to represent differences between players in their tendency or ability to produce draws.

Applied to 150 years of chess history, the approach produces lifetime skill curves and comparisons between players across time. The results indicate an increase in overall playing strength over that period. They also show significantly better predictive power when the model accounts for a player's ability to force a draw, supporting that addition to the skill representation.
summary.tldr: Temporal smoothing reconstructs chess players' skill histories, while player-specific draw modeling significantly improves predictive power.

title: TrueSkill Through Time: Revisiting the History of Chess

abstract: Multiple-Instance learning has been long known as a hard non-convex problem. In this work, we propose an approach that recasts it as a convex likelihood ratio estimation problem. Firstly, the constraint in multiple-instance learning is reformulated into a convex constraint on the likelihood ratio. Then we show that a joint estimation of a likelihood ratio function and the likelihood on training instances can be learned convexly. Theoretically, we prove a quantitative relationship between the risk estimated under the 0-1 classification loss, and under a loss function for likelihood ratio estimation. It is shown that our likelihood ratio estimation is generally a good surrogate for the 0-1 loss, and separates positive and negative instances well. However with the joint estimation it tends to underestimate the likelihood of an example to be positive. We propose to use these likelihood ratio estimates as features, and learn a linear combination on them to classify the bags. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show the superiority of the approach.

paragraphs: Multiple-instance learning involves classifying collections of instances, called bags, while reasoning about the instances within them. Its constraints have traditionally led to difficult nonconvex optimization problems. This paper changes the quantity being learned: it expresses the multiple-instance constraint as a convex restriction on a likelihood ratio, making a different optimization route available.

The authors show that a likelihood-ratio function and likelihoods on training instances can be estimated jointly through convex learning. They also prove a quantitative connection between the loss used for ratio estimation and classification error measured with zero-one loss. This establishes a theoretical reason to use the ratio-estimation objective as a surrogate for classification, alongside its ability to separate positive and negative instances.

The joint estimation nevertheless tends to underestimate how likely an example is to be positive. The proposed classification procedure uses the estimated ratios as features and learns a linear combination for predicting bag labels. Synthetic and real-data experiments report superior performance for the approach, supporting the usefulness of this convex reformulation and subsequent classification step.
summary.tldr: The paper reformulates multiple-instance learning through convex likelihood-ratio estimation and uses the estimates as features for bag classification.

title: Convex Multiple-Instance Learning by Estimating Likelihood Ratio

abstract: We present a Bayesian nonparametric model for genetic sequence data in which a set of genetic sequences is modelled using a Markov model of partitions. The partitions at consecutive locations in the genome are related by their clusters first splitting and then merging. Our model can be thought of as a discrete time analogue of continuous time fragmentation-coagulation processes [Teh et al 2011], preserving the important properties of projectivity, exchangeability and reversibility, while being more scalable. We apply this model to the problem of genotype imputation, showing improved computational efficiency while maintaining the same accuracies as in [Teh et al 2011].

The partitions at consecutive locations in the genome are related by their clusters first splitting and then merging. Our model can be thought of as a discrete time analogue of continuous time fragmentation-coagulation processes [Teh et al 2011], preserving the important properties of projectivity, exchangeability and reversibility, while being more scalable. We apply this model to the problem of genotype imputation, showing improved computational efficiency while maintaining the same accuracies as in [Teh et al 2011].

paragraphs: This paper presents a Bayesian nonparametric model for collections of genetic sequences. It describes the sequences through partitions that change along the genome. At each location, a partition groups sequences into clusters, and a Markov model connects the grouping at one location to the next.

The transition works through two stages: existing clusters split, and the resulting clusters then merge. This creates a discrete-time counterpart to a previously developed continuous-time fragmentation–coagulation process. The construction preserves projectivity, exchangeability, and reversibility while improving scalability. These are structural properties of the probabilistic model that the authors retain as they change how its transitions are represented.

The authors apply the model to genotype imputation, the task of filling in missing genetic data. They report better computational efficiency while maintaining the accuracy of the earlier continuous-time approach. The finding therefore supports a computational advantage for the discrete formulation in the studied application, with the model's important probabilistic properties preserved and no reported loss in imputation accuracy.
summary.tldr: A discrete split-and-merge model improves genetic imputation efficiency while preserving the earlier model's accuracy and key probabilistic properties.

title: Scalable imputation of genetic data with a discrete fragmentation-coagulation process

abstract: We describe an approach to speed-up inference with latent variable PCFGs, which have been shown to be highly effective for natural language parsing. Our approach is based on a tensor formulation recently introduced for spectral estimation of latent-variable PCFGs coupled with a tensor decomposition algorithm well-known in the multilinear algebra literature. We also describe an error bound for this approximation, which bounds the difference between the probabilities calculated by the algorithm and the true probabilities that the approximated model gives. Empirical evaluation on real-world natural language parsing data demonstrates a significant speed-up at minimal cost for parsing performance.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the computational cost of inference in latent-variable probabilistic context-free grammars, a model family used for natural-language parsing. Its objective is to make parsing faster while preserving the useful predictive behavior of these grammars. The contribution centers on how inference is computed within the model.

The authors combine a tensor formulation developed for spectral estimation of these grammars with an established tensor decomposition algorithm from multilinear algebra. This supplies an approximation used to accelerate inference. They also derive an error bound comparing the probabilities calculated by the algorithm with the true probabilities supplied by the model being approximated.

Evaluation on real-world parsing data reports a significant speed increase with minimal loss in parsing performance. The theoretical bound and empirical result address different aspects of the approximation: one controls discrepancies in computed probabilities, while the other measures its practical effect on parsing. Together, they support tensor decomposition as a useful computational approach for inference in this grammar family.
summary.tldr: Tensor decomposition accelerates latent-variable grammar inference with a probability error bound and minimal reported parsing-performance loss.

title: Tensor Decomposition for Fast Parsing with Latent-Variable PCFGs

abstract: This paper proposes an efficient online learning algorithm to track the smoothing functions of Additive Models. The key idea is to combine the linear representation of Additive Models with a Recursive Least Squares (RLS) filter. In order to quickly track changes in the model and put more weight on recent data, the RLS filter uses a forgetting factor which exponentially weights down observations by the order of their arrival. The tracking behaviour is further enhanced by using an adaptive forgetting factor which is updated based on the gradient of the a priori errors. Using results from Lyapunov stability theory, upper bounds for the learning rate are analyzed. The proposed algorithm is applied to 5 years of electricity load data provided by the French utility company Electricite de France (EDF). Compared to state-of-the-art methods, it achieves a superior performance in terms of model tracking and prediction accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper develops an online method for updating the smoothing functions in an additive model as observations arrive. The objective is to follow changing relationships over time, a useful requirement for electricity demand forecasting. The approach combines a linear representation of the additive model with a Recursive Least Squares filter.

The filter discounts older observations exponentially through a forgetting factor, giving recent data greater influence. The authors then make this factor adaptive: it changes using the gradient of prediction errors computed before updating the model. This adds a mechanism for adjusting how strongly past observations influence current learning. The paper also uses Lyapunov stability theory to analyze upper bounds on the learning rate.

The method is evaluated using five years of electricity load observations from EDF. In that application, the authors report better model tracking and prediction accuracy than the compared state-of-the-art methods. The findings support adaptive forgetting as a practical way to keep an additive forecasting model responsive to changing data.
summary.tldr: An online additive-model learner adapts its forgetting rate to track changing electricity demand and improve forecasting in the reported evaluation.

title: Adaptive Learning of Smoothing Functions: Application to Electricity Load Forecasting

abstract: In the conventional approaches for supervised parametric learning, relations between data and target variables are provided through training sets consisting of pairs of corresponded data and target variables. In this work, we describe a new learning scheme for parametric learning, in which the target variables $\y$ can be modeled with a prior model $p(\y)$ and the relations between data and target variables are estimated through $p(\y)$ and a set of uncorresponded data $\x$ in training. We term this method as learning with target priors (LTP). Specifically, LTP learning seeks parameter $\t$ that maximizes the log likelihood of $f_\t(\x)$ on a uncorresponded training set with regards to $p(\y)$. Compared to the conventional (semi)supervised learning approach, LTP can make efficient use of prior knowledge of the target variables in the form of probabilistic distributions, and thus removes/reduces the reliance on training data in learning. Compared to the Bayesian approach, the learned parametric regressor in LTP can be more efficiently implemented and deployed in tasks where running efficiency is critical, such as on-line BCI signal decoding. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach on parametric regression tasks for BCI signal decoding and pose estimation from video.

paragraphs: Conventional supervised regression learns from inputs paired with their target outputs. This paper investigates a different source of training information: a probability model describing the target variables, together with inputs that lack corresponding targets. The proposed scheme, learning with target priors, uses this distributional knowledge to estimate the relationship between inputs and outputs.

The method chooses the parameters of a regressor so that its predictions on the unpaired training inputs have high likelihood under the target prior. This makes prior knowledge about plausible outputs directly influence learning. Its usefulness depends on having a model of the targets that can supply information otherwise obtained from paired examples.

The authors argue that this approach can reduce or remove reliance on conventional training data and can produce a regressor suited to efficient deployment. They demonstrate effectiveness on brain-computer interface signal decoding and pose estimation from video. The efficiency claim is especially relevant to online decoding, where the learned mapping must be applied quickly, while the central learning contribution is the use of target distributions as supervision.
summary.tldr: Learning with target priors trains a parametric regressor from unpaired inputs by making its outputs likely under a known target distribution.

title: Learning with Target Prior

abstract: In visual recognition problems, the common data distribution mismatches between training and testing make domain adaptation essential. However, image data is difficult to manually divide into the discrete domains required by adaptation algorithms, and the standard practice of equating datasets with domains is a weak proxy for all the real conditions that alter the statistics in complex ways (lighting, pose, background, resolution, etc.) We propose an approach to automatically discover latent domains in image or video datasets. Our formulation imposes two key properties on domains: maximum distinctiveness and maximum learnability. By maximum distinctiveness, we require the underlying distributions of the identified domains to be different from each other; by maximum learnability, we ensure that a strong discriminative model can be learned from the domain. We devise a nonparametric representation and efficient optimization procedure for distinctiveness, which, when coupled with our learnability constraint, can successfully discover domains among both training and test data. We extensively evaluate our approach on object recognition and human activity recognition tasks.

paragraphs: Visual training and test data often differ because of lighting, pose, backgrounds, resolution, and other conditions. Domain adaptation addresses these mismatches, but it commonly assumes that data has already been divided into domains. Treating each dataset as one domain can miss the distributional differences within and across collections.

The paper proposes discovering latent domains automatically in image and video data. Its formulation combines distinctiveness with learnability. Identified groups should have different underlying distributions, while each group should also support learning a strong discriminative model. This makes the grouping task sensitive to both distributional separation and its usefulness for recognition.

The authors introduce a nonparametric representation and an efficient optimization procedure for distinctiveness, coupled with the learnability constraint. The approach can discover domains among training and test data and is extensively evaluated on object and human activity recognition. Its contribution is a way to construct the domains adaptation methods need, using the visual data's structure instead of relying solely on dataset boundaries.
summary.tldr: Automatically discovering visually distinct yet learnable domains provides a more meaningful basis for adaptation than dataset boundaries alone.

title: Reshaping Visual Datasets for Domain Adaptation

abstract: Most standard algorithms for prediction with expert advice depend on a parameter called the learning rate. This learning rate needs to be large enough to fit the data well, but small enough to prevent overfitting. For the exponential weights algorithm, a sequence of prior work has established theoretical guarantees for higher and higher data-dependent tunings of the learning rate, which allow for increasingly aggressive learning. But in practice such theoretical tunings often still perform worse (as measured by their regret) than ad hoc tuning with an even higher learning rate. To close the gap between theory and practice we introduce an approach to learn the learning rate. Up to a factor that is at most (poly)logarithmic in the number of experts and the inverse of the learning rate, our method performs as well as if we would know the empirically best learning rate from a large range that includes both conservative small values and values that are much higher than those for which formal guarantees were previously available. Our method employs a grid of learning rates, yet runs in linear time regardless of the size of the grid.

paragraphs: Algorithms for prediction with expert advice use a learning rate to control how aggressively they respond to observed performance. Existing theoretical choices for exponential weights can be more conservative than choices that work well empirically. This paper addresses that gap by learning the learning rate over a broad range of possible values.

The method competes with the empirically best learning rate in that range, including both small values and values much larger than those covered by earlier formal guarantees. Its performance matches that reference up to a factor that is at most polylogarithmic in the number of experts and the inverse learning rate. The claim is approximate competitiveness, rather than exact equality.

Although the approach uses a grid of learning rates, it runs in linear time regardless of the grid's size. This makes considering many candidate rates computationally attractive. The contribution combines adaptation to empirical performance with a theoretical guarantee, extending the range of aggressive learning behavior that can be supported by analysis.
summary.tldr: The method learns a learning rate that competes with the empirically best choice across a broad grid while retaining linear runtime.

title: Learning the Learning Rate for Prediction with Expert Advice

abstract: The persistent and graded activity often observed in cortical circuits is sometimes seen as a signature of autoassociative retrieval of memories stored earlier in synaptic efficacies. However, despite decades of theoretical work on the subject, the mechanisms that support the storage and retrieval of memories remain unclear. Previous proposals concerning the dynamics of memory networks have fallen short of incorporating some key physiological constraints in a unified way. Specifically, some models violate Dale's law (i.e. allow neurons to be both excitatory and inhibitory), while some others restrict the representation of memories to a binary format, or induce recall states in which some neurons fire at rates close to saturation. We propose a novel control-theoretic framework to build functioning attractor networks that satisfy a set of relevant physiological constraints. We directly optimize networks of excitatory and inhibitory neurons to force sets of arbitrary analog patterns to become stable fixed points of the dynamics. The resulting networks operate in the balanced regime, are robust to corruptions of the memory cue as well as to ongoing noise, and incidentally explain the reduction of trial-to-trial variability following stimulus onset that is ubiquitously observed in sensory and motor cortices. Our results constitute a step forward in our understanding of the neural substrate of memory.

paragraphs: Persistent neural activity can be interpreted as a network recalling a pattern stored in its connections. Building models of this process is difficult when physiological constraints matter. Earlier proposals sometimes let individual neurons act as both excitatory and inhibitory, restrict memories to binary patterns, or produce recall with firing rates near saturation.

The paper develops a control-theoretic framework for constructing attractor networks under relevant physiological constraints. It directly optimizes networks containing excitatory and inhibitory neurons so that specified analog activity patterns become stable fixed points. In plain language, the network is designed to maintain graded patterns of activity, with stability supporting their recovery after disturbances.

The resulting networks operate in a balanced regime and withstand both corrupted memory cues and continuing noise. They also account for a reduction in variability across repeated trials after a stimulus begins, an observation associated with sensory and motor cortices. Together, these results provide a model connecting stable analog memory with physiological requirements, contributing to understanding memory mechanisms without establishing that this construction is the brain's actual implementation.
summary.tldr: A control-theoretic construction produces balanced excitatory–inhibitory networks that stably store analog memories and tolerate noise.

title: Analog Memories in a Balanced Rate-Based Network of E-I Neurons

abstract: We propose a novel sampling framework for inference in probabilistic models: an active learning approach that converges more quickly (in wall-clock time) than Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) benchmarks. The central challenge in probabilistic inference is numerical integration, to average over ensembles of models or unknown (hyper-)parameters (for example to compute marginal likelihood or a partition function). MCMC has provided approaches to numerical integration that deliver state-of-the-art inference, but can suffer from sample inefficiency and poor convergence diagnostics. Bayesian quadrature techniques offer a model-based solution to such problems, but their uptake has been hindered by prohibitive computation costs. We introduce a warped model for probabilistic integrands (likelihoods) that are known to be non-negative, permitting a cheap active learning scheme to optimally select sample locations. Our algorithm is demonstrated to offer faster convergence (in seconds) relative to simple Monte Carlo and annealed importance sampling on both synthetic and real-world examples.

MCMC has provided approaches to numerical integration that deliver state-of-the-art inference, but can suffer from sample inefficiency and poor convergence diagnostics. Bayesian quadrature techniques offer a model-based solution to such problems, but their uptake has been hindered by prohibitive computation costs. We introduce a warped model for probabilistic integrands (likelihoods) that are known to be non-negative, permitting a cheap active learning scheme to optimally select sample locations. Our algorithm is demonstrated to offer faster convergence (in seconds) relative to simple Monte Carlo and annealed importance sampling on both synthetic and real-world examples.

paragraphs: Probabilistic inference often requires numerical integration to average over unknown models or parameters. Monte Carlo methods provide a powerful approach, but can use samples inefficiently and make convergence difficult to assess. Bayesian quadrature instead models the function being integrated, although the computational expense of doing so has limited its use.

The paper introduces a warped model for integrands, such as likelihoods, that are known to be non-negative. Using that property enables a cheap active-learning scheme for choosing sample locations optimally within the proposed framework. Sample selection is therefore guided by a model of the integration problem, with computational cost explicitly addressed in the design.

The method demonstrates faster convergence measured in seconds than simple Monte Carlo and annealed importance sampling on synthetic and real-world examples. Measuring elapsed time matters because more informative samples alone would not ensure faster inference if selecting them were too expensive. The reported results support the combination of model-guided sampling and inexpensive selection as a practical way to accelerate the integration tasks tested.
summary.tldr: A non-negativity-aware Bayesian quadrature model selects informative samples cheaply and converges faster in elapsed time than tested Monte Carlo alternatives.

title: Sampling for Inference in Probabilistic Models with Fast Bayesian Quadrature

abstract: We suggest a new loss for learning deep embeddings. The key characteristics of the new loss is the absence of tunable parameters and very good results obtained across a range of datasets and problems. The loss is computed by estimating two distribution of similarities for positive (matching) and negative (non-matching) point pairs, and then computing the probability of a positive pair to have a lower similarity score than a negative pair based on these probability estimates. We show that these operations can be performed in a simple and piecewise-differentiable manner using 1D histograms with soft assignment operations. This makes the proposed loss suitable for learning deep embeddings using stochastic optimization. The experiments reveal favourable results compared to recently proposed loss functions.

The key characteristics of the new loss is the absence of tunable parameters and very good results obtained across a range of datasets and problems. The loss is computed by estimating two distribution of similarities for positive (matching) and negative (non-matching) point pairs, and then computing the probability of a positive pair to have a lower similarity score than a negative pair based on these probability estimates. We show that these operations can be performed in a simple and piecewise-differentiable manner using 1D histograms with soft assignment operations. This makes the proposed loss suitable for learning deep embeddings using stochastic optimization. The experiments reveal favourable results compared to recently proposed loss functions.

paragraphs: A useful embedding should assign greater similarity to matching examples than to non-matching examples. This paper turns that ordering goal into a training loss by comparing two distributions: similarity scores for positive pairs and similarity scores for negative pairs. The objective measures how often their ordering goes the wrong way.

Specifically, the loss estimates the probability that a positive pair receives a lower similarity than a negative pair. The authors compute this through one-dimensional histograms with soft assignments. These operations are simple and piecewise differentiable, allowing the loss to be used in stochastic optimization when training a deep embedding network.

The loss itself has no tunable parameters, reducing the need to select settings for the training criterion. Experiments across multiple datasets and problems show favorable results compared with recently proposed losses. The contribution is a distribution-based way to express the desired separation between matching and non-matching pairs, together with a histogram construction that makes that objective usable in neural-network training.
summary.tldr: Histogram loss trains embeddings by estimating how often non-matching pairs appear more similar than matching pairs.

title: Learning Deep Embeddings with Histogram Loss

abstract: Nowadays, the number of layers and of neurons in each layer of a deep network are typically set manually. While very deep and wide networks have proven effective in general, they come at a high memory and computation cost, thus making them impractical for constrained platforms. These networks, however, are known to have many redundant parameters, and could thus, in principle, be replaced by more compact architectures. In this paper, we introduce an approach to automatically determining the number of neurons in each layer of a deep network during learning. To this end, we propose to make use of a group sparsity regularizer on the parameters of the network, where each group is defined to act on a single neuron. Starting from an overcomplete network, we show that our approach can reduce the number of parameters by up to 80\% while retaining or even improving the network accuracy.

paragraphs: Deep networks often have their layer widths chosen manually. Wide architectures can perform well, but their memory and computation requirements make them difficult to use on constrained platforms. This paper starts from the observation that many network parameters are redundant and asks whether the number of neurons in each layer can instead be determined during learning.

The proposed method applies a group-sparsity regularizer to network parameters, with each group associated with a single neuron. This organizes the pressure toward compactness around whole neurons, making the regularizer relevant to layer width. Training begins with an overcomplete network, allowing the learning procedure to identify a smaller architecture within that starting model.

The authors show parameter reductions of up to 80% while retaining or even improving accuracy. This is a reported attainable reduction, rather than a guarantee for every network. The result supports learning layer widths through neuron-level sparsity as a practical way to obtain compact models without necessarily sacrificing predictive quality.
summary.tldr: Neuron-level group sparsity learns layer widths during training, reducing parameters by up to 80% while retaining or improving accuracy.

title: Learning the Number of Neurons in Deep Networks

abstract: This paper introduces the QMDP-net, a neural network architecture for planning under partial observability. The QMDP-net combines the strengths of model-free learning and model-based planning. It is a recurrent policy network, but it represents a policy for a parameterized set of tasks by connecting a model with a planning algorithm that solves the model, thus embedding the solution structure of planning in a network learning architecture. The QMDP-net is fully differentiable and allows for end-to-end training. We train a QMDP-net on different tasks so that it can generalize to new ones in the parameterized task set and “transfer” to other similar tasks beyond the set. In preliminary experiments, QMDP-net showed strong performance on several robotic tasks in simulation. Interestingly, while QMDP-net encodes the QMDP algorithm, it sometimes outperforms the QMDP algorithm in the experiments, as a result of end-to-end learning.

paragraphs: Planning under partial observability means choosing actions without directly observing the full state of the environment. QMDP-net addresses this problem through a recurrent policy network that connects a model to a planning algorithm. The network therefore incorporates the structure of a planning solution into a trainable architecture.

The architecture is fully differentiable, allowing the combined system to be trained end to end. It represents policies for a parameterized collection of tasks, and training across different tasks is intended to support generalization to new members of that collection. The authors also investigate transfer to similar tasks outside it, combining model-based planning structure with learning across tasks.

Preliminary experiments on several simulated robotic tasks show strong performance. Although the network encodes the QMDP algorithm, it sometimes outperforms that algorithm in the reported experiments, which the authors attribute to end-to-end learning. The result illustrates how training a system containing a planning procedure can improve its behavior beyond that of the encoded procedure used on its own.
summary.tldr: QMDP-net embeds differentiable planning in a recurrent policy network and shows promising task generalization and performance in preliminary robotic simulations.

title: QMDP-Net: Deep Learning for Planning under Partial Observability

abstract: Although gradient descent (GD) almost always escapes saddle points asymptotically [Lee et al., 2016], this paper shows that even with fairly natural random initialization schemes and non-pathological functions, GD can be significantly slowed down by saddle points, taking exponential time to escape. On the other hand, gradient descent with perturbations [Ge et al., 2015, Jin et al., 2017] is not slowed down by saddle points—it can find an approximate local minimizer in polynomial time. This result implies that GD is inherently slower than perturbed GD, and justifies the importance of adding perturbations for efficient non-convex optimization. While our focus is theoretical, we also present experiments that illustrate our theoretical findings.

On the other hand, gradient descent with perturbations [Ge et al., 2015, Jin et al., 2017] is not slowed down by saddle points—it can find an approximate local minimizer in polynomial time. This result implies that GD is inherently slower than perturbed GD, and justifies the importance of adding perturbations for efficient non-convex optimization. While our focus is theoretical, we also present experiments that illustrate our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Eventually escaping a saddle point does not establish that an optimization method will escape quickly. This paper makes that distinction concrete for gradient descent. Although gradient descent almost always escapes saddles asymptotically, the authors show that saddle points can still delay its progress for an exponentially long time.

The result holds even with fairly natural random initialization schemes and functions described as non-pathological. Thus, the slowdown cannot simply be dismissed as requiring an obviously artificial starting point or a severely irregular objective. The claim establishes a possible computational obstacle for gradient descent, rather than saying that every problem or every saddle causes exponential delay.

The paper contrasts this behavior with perturbed gradient descent, which can reach an approximate local minimizer in polynomial time in the theoretical comparison. This provides a reason to introduce perturbations when efficient nonconvex optimization matters. Experiments illustrate the theoretical findings, while the main contribution is the separation between an eventual-escape guarantee and a useful bound on the time required.
summary.tldr: Gradient descent can take exponential time to escape saddles, establishing a theoretical efficiency advantage for perturbations in the analyzed comparison.

title: Gradient Descent Can Take Exponential Time to Escape Saddle Points

abstract: We present SNIPER, an algorithm for performing efficient multi-scale training in instance level visual recognition tasks. Instead of processing every pixel in an image pyramid, SNIPER processes context regions around ground-truth instances (referred to as chips) at the appropriate scale. For background sampling, these context-regions are generated using proposals extracted from a region proposal network trained with a short learning schedule. Hence, the number of chips generated per image during training adaptively changes based on the scene complexity. SNIPER only processes 30% more pixels compared to the commonly used single scale training at 800x1333 pixels on the COCO dataset. But, it also observes samples from extreme resolutions of the image pyramid, like 1400x2000 pixels. As SNIPER operates on resampled low resolution chips (512x512 pixels), it can have a batch size as large as 20 on a single GPU even with a ResNet-101 backbone. Therefore it can benefit from batch-normalization during training without the need for synchronizing batch-normalization statistics across GPUs. SNIPER brings training of instance level recognition tasks like object detection closer to the protocol for image classification and suggests that the commonly accepted guideline that it is important to train on high resolution images for instance level visual recognition tasks might not be correct. Our implementation based on Faster-RCNN with a ResNet-101 backbone obtains an mAP of 47.6% on the COCO dataset for bounding box detection and can process 5 images per second during inference with a single GPU. Code is available at https://github.com/MahyarNajibi/SNIPER/ .

Hence, the number of chips generated per image during training adaptively changes based on the scene complexity. SNIPER only processes 30% more pixels compared to the commonly used single scale training at 800x1333 pixels on the COCO dataset. But, it also observes samples from extreme resolutions of the image pyramid, like 1400x2000 pixels. As SNIPER operates on resampled low resolution chips (512x512 pixels), it can have a batch size as large as 20 on a single GPU even with a ResNet-101 backbone. Therefore it can benefit from batch-normalization during training without the need for synchronizing batch-normalization statistics across GPUs. SNIPER brings training of instance level recognition tasks like object detection closer to the protocol for image classification and suggests that the commonly accepted guideline that it is important to train on high resolution images for instance level visual recognition tasks might not be correct. Our implementation based on Faster-RCNN with a ResNet-101 backbone obtains an mAP of 47.6% on the COCO dataset for bounding box detection and can process 5 images per second during inference with a single GPU. Code is available at https://github.com/MahyarNajibi/SNIPER/ .

paragraphs: SNIPER makes multi-scale object-recognition training more efficient by processing selected image regions called chips. These regions surround labeled objects at appropriate scales, avoiding the cost of processing every pixel at every image-pyramid resolution. Background regions come from proposals produced by a briefly trained region proposal network, so the number of chips adapts to scene complexity.

On COCO, this approach processes only 30% more pixels than single-scale training at 800×1333 while still seeing samples from resolutions as large as 1400×2000. Resampling the chips to 512×512 permits batches as large as 20 on one GPU with ResNet-101. That makes batch normalization usable without synchronizing its statistics across GPUs.

A Faster-RCNN implementation with ResNet-101 achieves 47.6% bounding-box mAP on COCO and processes five images per second during single-GPU inference. The findings suggest that training on full high-resolution images may not be essential for strong instance-level recognition. The approach preserves exposure to multiple object scales while concentrating computation on smaller regions.
summary.tldr: SNIPER trains on selected, resampled image chips to obtain multi-scale object-recognition benefits with substantially less pixel processing.

title: SNIPER: Efficient Multi-Scale Training

abstract: We investigate 1) the rate at which refined properties of the empirical risk---in particular, gradients---converge to their population counterparts in standard non-convex learning tasks, and 2) the consequences of this convergence for optimization. Our analysis follows the tradition of norm-based capacity control. We propose vector-valued Rademacher complexities as a simple, composable, and user-friendly tool to derive dimension-free uniform convergence bounds for gradients in non-convex learning problems. As an application of our techniques, we give a new analysis of batch gradient descent methods for non-convex generalized linear models and non-convex robust regression, showing how to use any algorithm that finds approximate stationary points to obtain optimal sample complexity, even when dimension is high or possibly infinite and multiple passes over the dataset are allowed. Moving to non-smooth models we show----in contrast to the smooth case---that even for a single ReLU it is not possible to obtain dimension-independent convergence rates for gradients in the worst case. On the positive side, it is still possible to obtain dimension-independent rates under a new type of distributional assumption.

paragraphs: Training uses gradients computed from a finite dataset, while the underlying learning objective concerns the full population. This paper studies how closely those gradients agree throughout nonconvex learning problems and what that agreement implies for optimization. It develops vector-valued Rademacher complexities as a composable tool for deriving uniform gradient bounds using norm-based capacity control.

For the smooth problems analyzed, the bounds can avoid explicit dependence on dimension. Applications include nonconvex generalized linear models and robust regression. The analysis shows how algorithms that find approximate stationary points can attain optimal sample complexity, even in high or potentially infinite dimension and when the dataset is reused for multiple passes.

The paper also identifies a sharp complication for nonsmooth models. Even a single ReLU cannot have dimension-independent gradient convergence rates in the worst case. A new distributional assumption restores dimension-independent rates. The results therefore explain both when gradient-based reasoning can support strong learning guarantees and why nonsmoothness requires additional care about the data distribution.
summary.tldr: Uniform gradient bounds yield dimension-free learning guarantees for analyzed smooth problems, while ReLU models require additional distributional assumptions.

title: Uniform Convergence of Gradients for Non-Convex Learning and Optimization

abstract: Understanding, reasoning, and manipulating semantic concepts of images have been a fundamental research problem for decades. Previous work mainly focused on direct manipulation of natural image manifold through color strokes, key-points, textures, and holes-to-fill. In this work, we present a novel hierarchical framework for semantic image manipulation. Key to our hierarchical framework is that we employ structured semantic layout as our intermediate representations for manipulation. Initialized with coarse-level bounding boxes, our layout generator first creates pixel-wise semantic layout capturing the object shape, object-object interactions, and object-scene relations. Then our image generator fills in the pixel-level textures guided by the semantic layout. Such framework allows a user to manipulate images at object-level by adding, removing, and moving one bounding box at a time. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the advantages of the hierarchical manipulation framework over existing image generation and context hole-filing models, both qualitatively and quantitatively. Benefits of the hierarchical framework are further demonstrated in applications such as semantic object manipulation, interactive image editing, and data-driven image manipulation.

paragraphs: Object-level image editing requires connecting a simple user instruction with detailed changes to the image. This paper introduces a hierarchical framework that uses a structured semantic layout as an intermediate representation. Users begin with coarse bounding boxes, which provide controls for adding, removing, or moving objects.

A layout generator translates those boxes into a pixel-level semantic arrangement. The layout captures object shapes, relationships between objects, and relationships between objects and the surrounding scene. An image generator then uses this layout to fill in textures. Separating these stages gives the image generator an explicit spatial and semantic structure to follow.

The resulting editing process allows a user to change one bounding box at a time while the framework generates the corresponding detailed image. Qualitative and quantitative experiments report advantages over existing image-generation and context-hole-filling models. Applications include semantic object manipulation, interactive editing, and data-driven manipulation. The contribution is a structured route from coarse object controls to detailed visual changes, with the intermediate layout connecting user intent to image synthesis.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical generator turns editable object bounding boxes into semantic layouts and then textured images.

title: Learning Hierarchical Semantic Image Manipulation through Structured Representations

abstract: Gaussian Processes (GPs) are a generic modelling tool for supervised learning. While they have been successfully applied on large datasets, their use in safety-critical applications is hindered by the lack of good performance guarantees. To this end, we propose a method to learn GPs and their sparse approximations by directly optimizing a PAC-Bayesian bound on their generalization performance, instead of maximizing the marginal likelihood. Besides its theoretical appeal, we find in our evaluation that our learning method is robust and yields significantly better generalization guarantees than other common GP approaches on several regression benchmark datasets.

While they have been successfully applied on large datasets, their use in safety-critical applications is hindered by the lack of good performance guarantees. To this end, we propose a method to learn GPs and their sparse approximations by directly optimizing a PAC-Bayesian bound on their generalization performance, instead of maximizing the marginal likelihood. Besides its theoretical appeal, we find in our evaluation that our learning method is robust and yields significantly better generalization guarantees than other common GP approaches on several regression benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: This paper changes the objective used to learn Gaussian process models. Although these models are broadly useful for supervised learning, the authors identify weak performance guarantees as an obstacle to safety-critical use. Their approach makes a bound on generalization performance the quantity optimized during learning, directly connecting training to a theoretical performance guarantee.

The method minimizes a PAC-Bayesian generalization bound rather than maximizing marginal likelihood. It applies both to Gaussian processes and to sparse approximations of them. This is significant because the proposed training principle extends to approximations used when working with larger datasets, rather than being confined to the full model.

On several regression benchmarks, the authors find that the method is robust and provides significantly better generalization guarantees than common Gaussian process approaches. The stated improvement is in the guarantees obtained through evaluation, not a claim that every predictive metric improves in every application. The work shows how a guarantee-oriented objective can serve as a practical learning criterion for probabilistic regression.
summary.tldr: Training Gaussian processes by minimizing PAC-Bayesian bounds yields stronger generalization guarantees on several regression benchmarks.

title: Learning Gaussian Processes by Minimizing PAC-Bayesian Generalization Bounds

abstract: Time series constitute a challenging data type for machine learning algorithms, due to their highly variable lengths and sparse labeling in practice. In this paper, we tackle this challenge by proposing an unsupervised method to learn universal embeddings of time series. Unlike previous works, it is scalable with respect to their length and we demonstrate the quality, transferability and practicability of the learned representations with thorough experiments and comparisons. To this end, we combine an encoder based on causal dilated convolutions with a novel triplet loss employing time-based negative sampling, obtaining general-purpose representations for variable length and multivariate time series.

paragraphs: Time series can differ greatly in length, and useful labels are often scarce. This paper proposes an unsupervised method for learning general-purpose representations of such data. The aim is to produce embeddings for variable-length sequences with multiple measurements over time, while keeping the method scalable as sequences become longer.

The method combines an encoder built from causal dilated convolutions with a new triplet loss using time-based negative sampling. The encoder supplies the representation, while the training objective organizes learning through comparisons between examples. Together, these components provide a way to learn useful sequence descriptions without requiring labels for the training data.

The authors evaluate the representations through experiments and comparisons addressing their quality, transferability, and practical usefulness. These findings support the proposed embeddings as reusable descriptions of time series rather than representations tied only to a single labeled task. The central contribution brings unsupervised learning, variable-length multivariate inputs, and scalability with sequence length into one representation-learning approach.
summary.tldr: Causal dilated convolutions and a time-based triplet objective learn scalable, transferable representations of unlabeled multivariate time series.

title: Unsupervised Scalable Representation Learning for Multivariate Time Series

abstract: Despite many years of research into latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA), applying LDA to collections of non-categorical items is still challenging for practitioners. Yet many problems with much richer data share a similar structure and could benefit from the vast literature on LDA. We propose logistic LDA, a novel discriminative variant of latent Dirichlet allocation which is easy to apply to arbitrary inputs. In particular, our model can easily be applied to groups of images, arbitrary text embeddings, or integrate deep neural networks. Although it is a discriminative model, we show that logistic LDA can learn from unlabeled data in an unsupervised manner by exploiting the group structure present in the data. In contrast to other recent topic models designed to handle arbitrary inputs, our model does not sacrifice the interpretability and principled motivation of LDA.
