paragraphs: Latent Dirichlet allocation provides a way to discover interpretable topics in grouped data, but applying it to items beyond categorical observations remains challenging. Many richer datasets have a similar grouping structure. This paper introduces logistic LDA to make that topic-modeling approach easier to apply when the individual items take more general forms.

Logistic LDA is a discriminative variant that can handle groups of images, text embeddings, and models incorporating deep neural networks. Its central contribution is to accommodate these inputs while retaining the interpretability and principled motivation associated with LDA. The structure of the data remains central even as the representation of each item becomes more flexible.

Although the model is discriminative, the authors show that it can learn without labels by exploiting how items are grouped. This matters because richer input formats do not have to come with supervised topic assignments. The paper offers a route for bringing interpretable topic modeling to grouped observations that are awkward to represent as conventional categorical inputs.
summary.tldr: Logistic LDA uses group structure to learn interpretable topics from unlabeled, general-purpose inputs such as images and text embeddings.

title: Discriminative Topic Modeling with Logistic LDA

abstract: Explanation methods aim to make neural networks more trustworthy and interpretable. In this paper, we demonstrate a property of explanation methods which is disconcerting for both of these purposes. Namely, we show that explanations can be manipulated arbitrarily by applying visually hardly perceptible perturbations to the input that keep the network's output approximately constant. We establish theoretically that this phenomenon can be related to certain geometrical properties of neural networks. This allows us to derive an upper bound on the susceptibility of explanations to manipulations. Based on this result, we propose effective mechanisms to enhance the robustness of explanations.
originalAbstract: Explanation methods aim to make neural networks more trustworthy and interpretable. In this paper, we demonstrate a property of explanation methods which is disconcerting for both of these purposes. Namely, we show that explanations can be manipulated arbitrarily by applying visually hardly perceptible perturbations to the input that keep the network's output approximately constant. We establish theoretically that this phenomenon can be related to certain geometrical properties of neural networks. This allows us to derive an upper bound on the susceptibility of explanations to manipulations. Based on this result, we propose effective mechanisms to enhance the robustness of explanations.

paragraphs: An explanation method is intended to make a neural network's prediction easier to understand and assess. This paper demonstrates that the explanation itself can be a target of manipulation. Visually barely noticeable changes to an input can arbitrarily alter its explanation while leaving the network's output approximately unchanged.

The distinction between the prediction and its explanation is central. An observer could see essentially the same input and receive essentially the same prediction, yet be shown a substantially different account of that prediction. The demonstrated vulnerability therefore concerns the reliability of explanations as evidence about model behavior, even when the prediction appears stable.

The authors connect this phenomenon theoretically to geometric properties of neural networks. That connection lets them derive an upper bound on how susceptible explanations are to manipulation and propose mechanisms that improve their robustness. The contribution combines a demonstration of vulnerability with an analytical account and a route toward mitigation. The stated improvement is enhanced robustness, rather than a claim that explanations become immune to manipulation.
summary.tldr: Nearly imperceptible input changes can manipulate explanations while preserving predictions, and a geometric analysis motivates ways to improve explanation robustness.

title: Explanations can be manipulated and geometry is to blame

abstract: Recently, neural network based approaches have achieved significant progress for solving large, complex, graph-structured problems. Nevertheless, the advantages of multi-scale information and deep architectures have not been sufficiently exploited. In this paper, we first analyze key factors constraining the expressive power of existing Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), including the activation function and shallow learning mechanisms. Then, we generalize spectral graph convolution and deep GCN in block Krylov subspace forms, upon which we devise two architectures, both scalable in depth however making use of multi-scale information differently. On several node classification tasks, the proposed architectures achieve state-of-the-art performance.
originalAbstract: Recently, neural network based approaches have achieved significant progress for solving large, complex, graph-structured problems. Nevertheless, the advantages of multi-scale information and deep architectures have not been sufficiently exploited. In this paper, we first analyze key factors constraining the expressive power of existing Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), including the activation function and shallow learning mechanisms. Then, we generalize spectral graph convolution and deep GCN in block Krylov subspace forms, upon which we devise two architectures, both scalable in depth however making use of multi-scale information differently. On several node classification tasks, the proposed architectures achieve state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Graph convolutional networks learn from graph-structured data, but the paper argues that existing approaches do not fully exploit either depth or information at multiple scales. It begins by examining constraints on their expressive power. The analysis specifically identifies activation functions and shallow learning mechanisms as factors that can restrict what these networks represent.

The authors then generalize spectral graph convolution and deep graph convolutional networks using block Krylov subspace formulations. This mathematical framework provides the basis for two architectures. Both can scale in depth, but they incorporate information from multiple graph scales differently. The design therefore addresses the representation of graph information alongside the organization of deeper networks.

On several node classification tasks, the proposed architectures achieve reported state-of-the-art performance. These results support the usefulness of the framework for the evaluated tasks. The broader contribution is a connection between an analysis of representational constraints and concrete network designs: identifying what limits existing models leads to architectures that make fuller use of depth and multiple scales of graph information.
summary.tldr: Two graph convolutional architectures use a block Krylov framework to exploit depth and multiple graph scales, achieving strong node classification results.

title: Break the Ceiling: Stronger Multi-scale Deep Graph Convolutional Networks

abstract: Smart portable applications increasingly rely on edge computing due to privacy and latency concerns. But guaranteeing always-on functionality comes with two major challenges: heavily resource-constrained hardware; and dynamic application conditions. Probabilistic models present an ideal solution to these challenges: they are robust to missing data, allow for joint predictions and have small data needs. In addition, ongoing efforts in field of tractable learning have resulted in probabilistic models with strict inference efficiency guarantees. However, the current notions of tractability are often limited to model complexity, disregarding the hardware's specifications and constraints. We propose a novel resource-aware cost metric that takes into consideration the hardware's properties in determining whether the inference task can be efficiently deployed. We use this metric to evaluate the performance versus resource trade-off relevant to the application of interest, and we propose a strategy that selects the device-settings that can optimally meet users' requirements. We showcase our framework on a mobile activity recognition scenario, and on a variety of benchmark datasets representative of the field of tractable learning and of the applications of interest.

paragraphs: An inference algorithm can be efficient in terms of model complexity yet still be unsuitable for a particular portable device. This paper examines that gap for probabilistic models used in edge computing. Always-on applications must accommodate limited hardware resources and changing conditions, so deployment feasibility depends on more than an abstract count of model operations.

The authors introduce a resource-aware cost metric that incorporates hardware properties when assessing inference efficiency. They use it to examine the trade-off between application performance and resource use, then propose a strategy for selecting device settings that optimally meet user requirements. This makes hardware characteristics part of the decision about how a model should operate.

The framework is demonstrated through mobile activity recognition and benchmark datasets representing tractable learning and relevant applications. Probabilistic models motivate the work because they can handle missing data, support joint predictions, and have modest data requirements. The contribution is a way to evaluate and configure these models against deployment constraints, extending tractability from a property of the model toward a relationship between the inference task and its hardware.
summary.tldr: A hardware-aware cost metric helps assess probabilistic inference and select device settings around application performance and resource requirements.

title: Towards Hardware-Aware Tractable Learning of Probabilistic Models

abstract: Variational Bayes (VB) is a scalable alternative to Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) for Bayesian posterior inference. Though popular, VB comes with few theoretical guarantees, most of which focus on well-specified models. However, models are rarely well-specified in practice. In this work, we study VB under model misspecification. We prove the VB posterior is asymptotically normal and centers at the value that minimizes the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence to the true data-generating distribution. Moreover, the VB posterior mean centers at the same value and is also asymptotically normal. These results generalize the variational Bernstein--von Mises theorem [29] to misspecified models. As a consequence of these results, we find that the model misspecification error dominates the variational approximation error in VB posterior predictive distributions. It explains the widely observed phenomenon that VB achieves comparable predictive accuracy with MCMC even though VB uses an approximating family. As illustrations, we study VB under three forms of model misspecification, ranging from model over-/under-dispersion to latent dimensionality misspecification. We conduct two simulation studies that demonstrate the theoretical results.

paragraphs: Variational Bayes offers scalable posterior inference by using an approximating family of distributions. Much of its theoretical support assumes that the statistical model is correctly specified. This paper examines the more realistic possibility that the chosen model cannot exactly represent the true process generating the data.

The authors establish asymptotic normality of the variational posterior and its centering at the model value closest to the true distribution in Kullback-Leibler divergence. The posterior mean also centers at that value and is asymptotically normal. These results extend the variational Bernstein–von Mises theorem to misspecified models, explaining the limiting behavior of inference when the model itself is imperfect.

A consequence is that model misspecification error dominates variational approximation error in the posterior predictive distributions covered by the analysis. This helps explain why variational Bayes can predict comparably to MCMC despite its approximation. The paper illustrates three forms of misspecification, including incorrect dispersion and latent dimensionality, and provides two simulation studies. The asymptotic results do not assert identical finite-sample behavior for all models.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes variational Bayes under misspecified models and explains how model error can dominate predictive approximation error.

title: Variational Bayes under Model Misspecification

abstract: A recent line of research has highlighted the existence of a ``double descent'' phenomenon in deep learning, whereby increasing the number of training examples N causes the generalization error of neural networks to peak when N is of the same order as the number of parameters P. In earlier works, a similar phenomenon was shown to exist in simpler models such as linear regression, where the peak instead occurs when N is equal to the input dimension D. Since both peaks coincide with the interpolation threshold, they are often conflated in the litterature. In this paper, we show that despite their apparent similarity, these two scenarios are inherently different. In fact, both peaks can co-exist when neural networks are applied to noisy regression tasks. The relative size of the peaks is then governed by the degree of nonlinearity of the activation function. Building on recent developments in the analysis of random feature models, we provide a theoretical ground for this sample-wise triple descent. As shown previously, the nonlinear peak at N=P is a true divergence caused by the extreme sensitivity of the output function to both the noise corrupting the labels and the initialization of the random features (or the weights in neural networks). This peak survives in the absence of noise, but can be suppressed by regularization. In contrast, the linear peak at N=D is solely due to overfitting the noise in the labels, and forms earlier during training. We show that this peak is implicitly regularized by the nonlinearity, which is why it only becomes salient at high noise and is weakly affected by explicit regularization. Throughout the paper, we compare the analytical results obtained in the random feature model with the outcomes of numerical experiments involving realistic neural networks.

paragraphs: Increasing the number of training examples can sometimes make prediction error rise before it falls again. This paper separates two peaks often treated as the same phenomenon: one when sample count N matches parameter count P, and another when N matches input dimension D. Both can occur in noisy neural-network regression, producing sample-wise triple descent.

Using random-feature theory and comparisons with neural-network experiments, the authors identify different causes. The nonlinear peak at N=P reflects extreme sensitivity to label noise and feature or weight initialization. It can remain without label noise and can be suppressed by explicit regularization. The linear peak at N=D arises entirely from fitting noise in the labels and develops earlier during training.

Activation nonlinearity controls the relative prominence of the peaks. It implicitly regularizes the linear peak, which becomes prominent mainly at high noise and responds weakly to explicit regularization. These distinctions explain why apparently similar error curves can react differently to noise and regularization. The theoretical analysis supplies a mechanism for two separate overfitting effects to coexist in the same learning problem.
summary.tldr: Two distinct overfitting mechanisms can create separate error peaks at sample counts matching input dimension and parameter count, producing triple descent.

title: Triple descent and the two kinds of overfitting: where & why do they appear?

abstract: Generalizable, transferrable, and robust representation learning on graph-structured data remains a challenge for current graph neural networks (GNNs). Unlike what has been developed for convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for image data, self-supervised learning and pre-training are less explored for GNNs. In this paper, we propose a graph contrastive learning (GraphCL) framework for learning unsupervised representations of graph data. We first design four types of graph augmentations to incorporate various priors. We then systematically study the impact of various combinations of graph augmentations on multiple datasets, in four different settings: semi-supervised, unsupervised, and transfer learning as well as adversarial attacks. The results show that, even without tuning augmentation extents nor using sophisticated GNN architectures, our GraphCL framework can produce graph representations of similar or better generalizability, transferrability, and robustness compared to state-of-the-art methods. We also investigate the impact of parameterized graph augmentation extents and patterns, and observe further performance gains in preliminary experiments. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Shen-Lab/GraphCL.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks need representations that transfer between tasks, generalize beyond training data, and withstand disturbances. This paper develops GraphCL, a framework for learning graph representations without labels. It brings contrastive learning and graph augmentation into a setting where self-supervised training and pretraining were less explored than they were for image models.

The authors design four kinds of graph augmentation to incorporate different prior assumptions. They systematically examine combinations of these transformations across multiple datasets. Their evaluation covers semi-supervised learning, unsupervised learning, transfer learning, and adversarial attacks, allowing them to study several distinct aspects of representation quality.

GraphCL achieves similar or better generalization, transfer, and robustness than state-of-the-art methods in the reported evaluations, even without tuning augmentation strength or using elaborate graph neural architectures. Preliminary experiments that parameterize augmentation strengths and patterns show additional gains. These results make augmentation design a central part of the contribution: useful graph representations can emerge from how training examples are transformed and compared, alongside the choice of network architecture.
summary.tldr: GraphCL uses graph augmentations for unsupervised contrastive learning, producing competitive generalization, transfer, and robustness across several evaluation settings.

title: Graph Contrastive Learning with Augmentations

abstract: Synthesizing larger texture images from a smaller exemplar is an important task in graphics and vision. The conventional CNNs, recently adopted for synthesis, require to train and test on the same set of images and fail to generalize to unseen images. This is mainly because those CNNs fully rely on convolutional and upsampling layers that operate locally and not suitable for a task as global as texture synthesis. In this work, inspired by the repetitive nature of texture patterns, we find that texture synthesis can be viewed as (local) \textit{upsampling} in the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) domain. However, FFT of natural images exhibits high dynamic range and lacks local correlations. Therefore, to train CNNs we design a framework to perform FFT upsampling in feature space using deformable convolutions. Such design allows our framework to generalize to unseen images, and synthesize textures in a single pass. Extensive evaluations confirm that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance both quantitatively and qualitatively.

abstract: Given a discrete probability measure supported on $N$ atoms and a set of $n$ real-valued functions, there exists a probability measure that is supported on a subset of $n+1$ of the original $N$ atoms and has the same mean when integrated against each of the $n$ functions. If $ N \gg n$ this results in a huge reduction of complexity. We give a simple geometric characterization of barycenters via negative cones and derive a randomized algorithm that computes this new measure by ``greedy geometric sampling''. We then study its properties, and benchmark it on synthetic and real-world data to show that it can be very beneficial in the $N\gg n$ regime. A Python implementation is available at \url{https://github.com/FraCose/Recombination_Random_Algos}.

paragraphs: A discrete probability distribution assigns weights to a collection of points, called atoms. Sometimes the quantities that matter are only the averages of a specified set of functions over those points. The paper considers how to shrink the distribution while preserving all of those selected averages exactly.

For a distribution on N atoms and n real-valued functions, a replacement distribution exists on at most n+1 of the original atoms with the same function averages. The task is to compute such a replacement. The authors give a geometric description of weighted centers using negative cones, then build a randomized algorithm called greedy geometric sampling around that description.

The authors study the algorithm's properties and benchmark it on synthetic and real data. They report particular benefits when the original number of atoms is much larger than the number of functions. The compression preserves the specified averages; it does not claim to preserve every property of the original distribution. Its value is reducing the representation needed for those selected quantities.
summary.tldr: A randomized geometric algorithm compresses a discrete distribution while exactly preserving the averages of a specified set of functions.

title: A Randomized Algorithm to Reduce the Support of Discrete Measures

abstract: We introduce a new and completely online contextual bandit algorithm called Gated Linear Contextual Bandits (GLCB). This algorithm is based on Gated Linear Networks (GLNs), a recently introduced deep learning architecture with properties well-suited to the online setting. Leveraging data-dependent gating properties of the GLN we are able to estimate prediction uncertainty with effectively zero algorithmic overhead. We empirically evaluate GLCB compared to 9 state-of-the-art algorithms that leverage deep neural networks, on a standard benchmark suite of discrete and continuous contextual bandit problems. GLCB obtains mean first-place despite being the only online method, and we further support these results with a theoretical study of its convergence properties.

paragraphs: The paper introduces Gated Linear Contextual Bandits, or GLCB, as a fully online contextual bandit algorithm. It builds on Gated Linear Networks, a deep learning architecture whose properties suit online learning. The central design question is how to combine this architecture with an uncertainty estimate useful for the bandit setting.

GLCB uses the network’s data-dependent gating structure to estimate prediction uncertainty. The authors report that this adds effectively zero algorithmic overhead. This matters because the uncertainty mechanism draws on the architecture’s existing structure, allowing the algorithm to remain online without introducing a substantial additional computational procedure for uncertainty estimation.

The evaluation compares GLCB with nine state-of-the-art algorithms using deep neural networks on a standard suite of discrete and continuous contextual bandit problems. GLCB achieves first place on average while being the only online method in that comparison. An additional theoretical study examines its convergence properties. The evidence combines competitive benchmark performance with convergence analysis; the average ranking should be understood as an aggregate result across the evaluated problems.
summary.tldr: GLCB uses Gated Linear Networks for fully online contextual bandits, obtaining inexpensive uncertainty estimates and first-place average benchmark ranking.

title: Online Learning in Contextual Bandits using Gated Linear Networks

abstract: Estimating the probabilities of connections between vertices in a random network using an observed adjacency matrix is an important task for network data analysis. Many existing estimation methods are based on certain assumptions on network structure, which limit their applicability in practice. Without making strong assumptions, we develop an iterative connecting probability estimation method based on neighborhood averaging. Starting at a random initial point or an existing estimate, our method iteratively updates the pairwise vertex distances, the sets of similar vertices, and connecting probabilities to improve the precision of the estimate. We propose a two-stage neighborhood selection procedure to achieve the trade-off between smoothness of the estimate and the ability to discover local structure. The tuning parameters can be selected by cross-validation. We establish desirable theoretical properties for our method, and further justify its superior performance by comparing with existing methods in simulation and real data analysis.

paragraphs: An observed network records which pairs of vertices are connected, but network analysis may require estimating the probabilities behind those observed connections. Many existing estimators impose structural assumptions on the network. This paper develops a neighborhood-averaging approach intended to estimate connection probabilities without making strong assumptions about that structure.

The method starts either from a random initialization or from an existing estimate. It then repeatedly updates distances between vertices, identifies sets of similar vertices, and revises connection probabilities. These quantities are refined together, so the current estimate helps determine which vertices should contribute to the next averaging step.

A two-stage neighborhood-selection procedure balances smooth estimates against the ability to preserve local structure. Cross-validation can select the tuning parameters, making the balance adjustable from data. The authors establish theoretical properties and compare the method with existing approaches in simulations and real-data analyses, reporting superior performance. The contribution combines iterative refinement with an explicit mechanism for managing the tension between averaging and local detail.
summary.tldr: An iterative neighborhood-averaging method estimates network connection probabilities while balancing smoothness and preservation of local structure.

title: Iterative Connecting Probability Estimation for Networks

abstract: The (gradient-based) bilevel programming framework is widely used in hyperparameter optimization and has achieved excellent performance empirically. Previous theoretical work mainly focuses on its optimization properties, while leaving the analysis on generalization largely open. This paper attempts to address the issue by presenting an expectation bound w.r.t. the validation set based on uniform stability. Our results can explain some mysterious behaviours of the bilevel programming in practice, for instance, overfitting to the validation set. We also present an expectation bound for the classical cross-validation algorithm. Our results suggest that gradient-based algorithms can be better than cross-validation under certain conditions in a theoretical perspective. Furthermore, we prove that regularization terms in both the outer and inner levels can relieve the overfitting problem in gradient-based algorithms. In experiments on feature learning and data reweighting for noisy labels, we corroborate our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter optimization often uses a nested learning process: an inner problem trains a model, and an outer problem chooses hyperparameters using validation data. Good optimization performance does not by itself explain how well those choices generalize. This paper investigates that gap for gradient-based bilevel methods, including their tendency to overfit the validation set.

The authors use uniform stability to derive an expectation bound with respect to validation data. They also provide an expectation bound for classical cross-validation, allowing a theoretical comparison. Their results suggest that gradient-based methods can perform better than cross-validation under certain conditions; the comparison is conditional rather than a universal ranking.

The analysis further shows that regularization at both the inner and outer levels can relieve overfitting in gradient-based methods. Experiments on feature learning and reweighting data with noisy labels corroborate the theoretical findings. The contribution links the design of the nested optimization procedure to its generalization behavior, giving theoretical support for regularizing both parts of the process.
summary.tldr: Stability-based bounds explain validation overfitting in bilevel hyperparameter optimization and show how regularization can reduce it.

title: Stability and Generalization of Bilevel Programming in Hyperparameter Optimization

abstract: Recent progress in neural network verification has challenged the notion of a convex barrier, that is, an inherent weakness in the convex relaxation of the output of a neural network. Specifically, there now exists a tight relaxation for verifying the robustness of a neural network to $\ell_\infty$ input perturbations, as well as efficient primal and dual solvers for the relaxation. Buoyed by this success, we consider the problem of developing similar techniques for verifying robustness to input perturbations within the probability simplex. We prove a somewhat surprising result that, in this case, not only can one design a tight relaxation that overcomes the convex barrier, but the size of the relaxation remains linear in the number of neurons, thereby leading to simpler and more efficient algorithms. We establish the scalability of our overall approach via the specification of $\ell_1$ robustness for CIFAR-10 and MNIST classification, where our approach improves the state of the art verified accuracy by up to $14.4\%$. Furthermore, we establish its accuracy on a novel and highly challenging task of verifying the robustness of a multi-modal (text and image) classifier to arbitrary changes in its textual input.

paragraphs: Neural-network verification asks whether a prediction remains robust throughout a specified set of input changes. Convex relaxations make this reasoning more tractable, but their looseness can limit what they certify. This paper examines perturbations within the probability simplex, seeking a tight relaxation suited to that input structure.

The authors prove that a tight relaxation can overcome the stated convex barrier while keeping its size linear in the number of neurons. That combination matters because tightness strengthens verification and linear size supports simpler, more efficient algorithms. The result shows that the structure of the permitted input set can make a substantial difference to verification design.

For l1 robustness on CIFAR-10 and MNIST classification, the approach improves state-of-the-art verified accuracy by up to 14.4%. The authors also evaluate a challenging multimodal classifier task: verifying robustness to arbitrary changes in the textual input. These demonstrations connect the theoretical relaxation to both image-classification guarantees and a setting involving text and images.
summary.tldr: For simplex inputs, a tight convex relaxation with size linear in neuron count enables stronger and more efficient robustness verification.

title: Overcoming the Convex Barrier for Simplex Inputs

abstract: Uncertainty modeling is critical in trajectory-forecasting systems for both interpretation and safety reasons. To better predict the future trajectories of multiple agents, recent works have introduced interaction modules to capture interactions among agents. This approach leads to correlations among the predicted trajectories. However, the uncertainty brought by such correlations is neglected. To fill this gap, we propose a novel concept, collaborative uncertainty (CU), which models the uncertainty resulting from the interaction module. We build a general CU-based framework to make a prediction model learn the future trajectory and the corresponding uncertainty. The CU-based framework is integrated as a plugin module to current state-of-the-art (SOTA) systems and deployed in two special cases based on multivariate Gaussian and Laplace distributions. In each case, we conduct extensive experiments on two synthetic datasets and two public, large-scale benchmarks of trajectory forecasting. The results are promising: 1) The results of synthetic datasets show that CU-based framework allows the model to nicely rebuild the ground-truth distribution. 2) The results of trajectory forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that the CU-based framework steadily helps SOTA systems improve their performances. Specially, the proposed CU-based framework helps VectorNet improve by 57 cm regarding Final Displacement Error on nuScenes dataset. 3) The visualization results of CU illustrate that the value of CU is highly related to the amount of the interactive information among agents.

paragraphs: Trajectory forecasting systems often model interactions among agents because one agent’s future movement depends on others. These interaction modules make predicted trajectories correlated. The paper argues that uncertainty associated with those correlations deserves explicit modeling, and introduces collaborative uncertainty to represent uncertainty arising from the interaction module.

The authors build a framework that learns future trajectories together with their uncertainty. It can be added as a plugin to existing forecasting systems. They develop versions based on multivariate Gaussian and Laplace distributions, providing two ways to represent the joint uncertainty rather than considering only separate trajectory predictions.

Experiments cover two synthetic datasets and two large forecasting benchmarks. On synthetic data, the framework reconstructs the underlying distribution well; on the forecasting benchmarks, it consistently improves the evaluated systems. One reported result is a 57-centimeter improvement in VectorNet’s final displacement error on nuScenes. Visualizations also associate collaborative uncertainty with the amount of interaction information among agents. These findings support treating interaction-related uncertainty as a useful component of joint forecasting.
summary.tldr: Modeling uncertainty caused by interactions among agents improves the evaluated trajectory forecasters and helps represent their joint predictive distributions.

title: Collaborative Uncertainty in Multi-Agent Trajectory Forecasting

abstract: Despite the tremendous success of reinforcement learning (RL) with function approximation, efficient exploration remains a significant challenge, both practically and theoretically. In particular, existing theoretically grounded RL algorithms based on upper confidence bounds (UCBs), such as optimistic least-squares value iteration (LSVI), are often incompatible with practically powerful function approximators, such as neural networks. In this paper, we develop a variant of \underline{boo}tstrapped LS\underline{VI}, namely BooVI, which bridges such a gap between practice and theory. Practically, BooVI drives exploration through (re)sampling, making it compatible with general function approximators. Theoretically, BooVI inherits the worst-case $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{d^3 H^3 T})$-regret of optimistic LSVI in the episodic linear setting. Here $d$ is the feature dimension, $H$ is the episode horizon, and $T$ is the total number of steps.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents must explore to discover rewarding behavior, but exploration methods with strong theoretical guarantees can be difficult to combine with flexible models such as neural networks. This paper focuses on that mismatch in least-squares value iteration, where established optimistic methods use upper confidence bounds to guide exploration.

BooVI is a bootstrapped variant of least-squares value iteration. It drives exploration through sampling and resampling, making the procedure compatible with general function approximators. The methodological contribution is therefore a different way to generate exploratory behavior that can fit a wider range of value-estimation models while retaining a rigorous analysis in a specific setting.

For episodic problems with linear function approximation, BooVI matches the stated worst-case regret bound of optimistic least-squares value iteration: roughly the square root of d³H³T, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Here d is feature dimension, H is episode length, and T is total interaction steps. The distinction matters: compatibility extends to general approximators, while the stated regret guarantee applies to the episodic linear setting.
summary.tldr: BooVI uses resampling to support flexible exploration while matching an established regret guarantee in episodic linear reinforcement learning.

title: BooVI: Provably Efficient Bootstrapped Value Iteration

abstract: Importance Sampling (IS) is a widely used building block for a large variety of off-policy estimation and learning algorithms. However, empirical and theoretical studies have progressively shown that vanilla IS leads to poor estimations whenever the behavioral and target policies are too dissimilar. In this paper, we analyze the theoretical properties of the IS estimator by deriving a novel anticoncentration bound that formalizes the intuition behind its undesired behavior. Then, we propose a new class of IS transformations, based on the notion of power mean. To the best of our knowledge, the resulting estimator is the first to achieve, under certain conditions, two key properties: (i) it displays a subgaussian concentration rate; (ii) it preserves the differentiability in the target distribution. Finally, we provide numerical simulations on both synthetic examples and contextual bandits, in comparison with off-policy evaluation and learning baselines.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation and learning use data from a behavioral policy to reason about a different target policy. Importance sampling is a common tool for this purpose, but ordinary importance sampling can estimate poorly when the two policies are too dissimilar. This paper studies that failure and develops a transformed estimator.

The theoretical analysis introduces an anticoncentration bound that formalizes the undesirable behavior of the ordinary estimator. The proposed alternative uses transformations based on power means. Under certain conditions, the resulting estimator combines subgaussian concentration with differentiability in the target distribution. The first property controls estimation fluctuations, while the second keeps the estimator usable in procedures that optimize the target through derivatives.

The authors describe this combination as a first to their knowledge, with the stated conditions remaining essential to the claim. They also provide numerical simulations on synthetic examples and contextual bandits, comparing against off-policy evaluation and learning baselines. The central contribution is therefore a theoretical route to jointly obtaining concentration and differentiability, accompanied by empirical comparisons in settings relevant to policy evaluation and improvement.
summary.tldr: Power-mean transformations yield importance-sampling estimators that combine subgaussian concentration and target-distribution differentiability under stated conditions.

title: Subgaussian and Differentiable Importance Sampling for Off-Policy Evaluation and Learning

abstract: Despite success in many domains, neural models struggle in settings where train and test examples are drawn from different distributions. In particular, in contrast to humans, conventional sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models fail to generalize systematically, i.e., interpret sentences representing novel combinations of concepts (e.g., text segments) seen in training. Traditional grammar formalisms excel in such settings by implicitly encoding alignments between input and output segments, but are hard to scale and maintain. Instead of engineering a grammar, we directly model segment-to-segment alignments as discrete structured latent variables within a neural seq2seq model. To efficiently explore the large space of alignments, we introduce a reorder-first align-later framework whose central component is a neural reordering module producing separable permutations. We present an efficient dynamic programming algorithm performing exact marginal inference of separable permutations, and, thus, enabling end-to-end differentiable training of our model. The resulting seq2seq model exhibits better systematic generalization than standard models on synthetic problems and NLP tasks (i.e., semantic parsing and machine translation).

paragraphs: Sequence-to-sequence models can struggle with new combinations of concepts that individually appeared during training. This paper addresses that systematic-generalization problem by explicitly modeling alignments between input and output segments. The alignments are discrete hidden structures learned within the neural model, avoiding the need to hand-engineer a grammar.

The proposed framework first reorders segments and then aligns them. Its neural reordering component produces separable permutations, giving structure to a potentially enormous search space. An efficient dynamic-programming algorithm computes exact marginal inference over these permutations, enabling end-to-end differentiable training despite the discrete reordering choices.

The resulting model generalizes more systematically than standard models on synthetic problems and on semantic parsing and machine translation tasks. The contribution links a structured account of how segments correspond with neural learning. Exact inference applies to the specified family of separable permutations, making the reordering component computationally manageable. The empirical findings support explicit latent alignment structure as a way to improve performance when test examples recombine familiar pieces in unfamiliar ways.
summary.tldr: Learning structured segment reorderings and alignments improves systematic generalization in sequence-to-sequence models.

title: Structured Reordering for Modeling Latent Alignments in Sequence Transduction

abstract: This paper presents a new end-to-end semi-supervised framework to learn a dense keypoint detector using unlabeled multiview images. A key challenge lies in ﬁnding the exact correspondences between the dense keypoints in multiple views since the inverse of the keypoint mapping can be neither analytically derived nor differentiated. This limits applying existing multiview supervision approaches used to learn sparse keypoints that rely on the exact correspondences. To address this challenge, we derive a new probabilistic epipolar constraint that encodes the two desired properties. (1) Soft correspondence: we deﬁne a matchability, which measures a likelihood of a point matching to the other image’s corresponding point, thus relaxing the requirement of the exact correspondences. (2) Geometric consistency: every point in the continuous correspondence ﬁelds must satisfy the multiview consistency collectively. We formulate a probabilistic epipolar constraint using a weighted average of epipolar errors through the matchability thereby generalizing the point-to-point geometric error to the ﬁeld-to-ﬁeld geometric error. This generalization facilitates learning a geometrically coherent dense keypoint detection model by utilizing a large number of unlabeled multiview images. Additionally, to prevent degenerative cases, we employ a distillation-based regularization by using a pretrained model. Finally, we design a new neural network architecture, made of twin networks, that effectively minimizes the probabilistic epipolar errors of all possible correspondences between two view images by building afﬁnity matrices. Our method shows superior performance compared to existing methods, including non-differentiable bootstrapping in terms of keypoint accuracy, multiview consistency, and 3D reconstruction accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper learns dense keypoints using a semi-supervised framework that draws on unlabeled images from multiple viewpoints. The central difficulty is finding exact matches between dense keypoints across views. The inverse keypoint mapping cannot be analytically derived or differentiated, preventing straightforward use of multiview supervision methods that depend on exact correspondences.

The authors replace that requirement with a probabilistic epipolar constraint. A matchability score expresses how likely points are to correspond, and these scores weight geometric errors across possible matches. The resulting constraint operates over whole correspondence fields while requiring collective geometric consistency. This provides a training signal even when an individual point's exact match is unavailable.

A twin-network architecture builds affinity matrices to minimize these probabilistic errors across view pairs. Distillation from a pretrained model provides regularization intended to prevent degenerate solutions. The reported comparisons show improvements in keypoint accuracy, consistency across views, and 3D reconstruction accuracy, including over non-differentiable bootstrapping. Together, the results support soft geometric correspondence as useful supervision for dense detection.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic geometric matching enables dense keypoint learning from unlabeled multiview images without requiring exact point correspondences.

title: Dense Keypoints via Multiview Supervision

abstract: In neuroscience, classical Hopfield networks are the standard biologically plausible model of long-term memory, relying on Hebbian plasticity for storage and attractor dynamics for recall. In contrast, memory-augmented neural networks in machine learning commonly use a key-value mechanism to store and read out memories in a single step. Such augmented networks achieve impressive feats of memory compared to traditional variants, yet their biological relevance is unclear. We propose an implementation of basic key-value memory that stores inputs using a combination of biologically plausible three-factor plasticity rules. The same rules are recovered when network parameters are meta-learned. Our network performs on par with classical Hopfield networks on autoassociative memory tasks and can be naturally extended to continual recall, heteroassociative memory, and sequence learning. In contrast, memory-augmented neural networks in machine learning commonly use a key-value mechanism to store and read out memories in a single step. Such augmented networks achieve impressive feats of memory compared to traditional variants, yet their biological relevance is unclear. We propose an implementation of basic key-value memory that stores inputs using a combination of biologically plausible three-factor plasticity rules. The same rules are recovered when network parameters are meta-learned. Our network performs on par with classical Hopfield networks on autoassociative memory tasks and can be naturally extended to continual recall, heteroassociative memory, and sequence learning. Our results suggest a compelling alternative to the classical Hopfield network as a model of biological long-term memory.

paragraphs: Classical Hopfield networks model long-term memory by storing information through Hebbian plasticity and recalling it through attractor dynamics. Memory-augmented neural networks often use a different arrangement: keys identify memories, and associated values can be read out in a single step. These systems perform impressive memory tasks, but their connection to biological learning is less clear.

The authors propose a basic key-value memory network that stores inputs through a combination of biologically plausible three-factor plasticity rules. This supplies a possible biological implementation of the key-value mechanism. When the network’s parameters are meta-learned, the same rules emerge, providing another route to the proposed learning behavior.

On autoassociative memory tasks, the network performs comparably to classical Hopfield networks. It can also be extended to continual recall, associations between different inputs and outputs, and sequence learning. Together, these results suggest an alternative model of biological long-term memory with a broader set of natural extensions. They support the plausibility and usefulness of the mechanism without establishing that biological memory necessarily uses it.
summary.tldr: A biologically plausible key-value memory network matches Hopfield networks on associative recall and extends to other memory tasks.

title: Biological learning in key-value memory networks

abstract: Primal heuristics play a crucial role in exact solvers for Mixed Integer Programming (MIP). While solvers are guaranteed to find optimal solutions given sufficient time, real-world applications typically require finding good solutions early on in the search to enable fast decision-making. While much of MIP research focuses on designing effective heuristics, the question of how to manage multiple MIP heuristics in a solver has not received equal attention. Generally, solvers follow hard-coded rules derived from empirical testing on broad sets of instances. Since the performance of heuristics is problem-dependent, using these general rules for a particular problem might not yield the best performance. In this work, we propose the first data-driven framework for scheduling heuristics in an exact MIP solver. By learning from data describing the performance of primal heuristics, we obtain a problem-specific schedule of heuristics that collectively find many solutions at minimal cost. We formalize the learning task and propose an efficient algorithm for computing such a schedule. Compared to the default settings of a state-of-the-art academic MIP solver, we are able to reduce the average primal integral by up to 49% on two classes of challenging instances.

paragraphs: Exact mixed-integer programming solvers can eventually find optimal solutions, but practical decisions often require good solutions much earlier. Primal heuristics help supply those solutions during search. This paper focuses on how a solver schedules its available heuristics, rather than on designing another individual heuristic.

Solvers commonly manage heuristics through fixed rules developed from broad empirical testing. Because a heuristic's usefulness depends on the problem, those general rules may be a poor fit for a particular problem class. The authors instead learn a problem-specific schedule from data describing heuristic performance, seeking a collection of heuristic executions that finds many solutions at low cost.

The paper formalizes this scheduling task and provides an efficient algorithm for computing a schedule. Against the default configuration of a leading academic solver, the learned schedules reduce average primal integral by up to 49% on two challenging instance classes. This supports using performance data to improve the timing and coordination of existing heuristics. The reported reduction concerns the evaluated classes and metric, rather than a universal solver speedup.
summary.tldr: Learning problem-specific heuristic schedules improves early solution finding in an exact mixed-integer programming solver.

title: Learning to Schedule Heuristics in Branch and Bound

abstract: Recently, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have gained popularity in a variety of real-world scenarios. Despite the great success, the architecture design of GNNs heavily relies on manual labor. Thus, automated graph neural network (AutoGNN) has attracted interest and attention from the research community, which makes significant performance improvements in recent years. However, existing AutoGNN works mainly adopt an implicit way to model and leverage the link information in the graphs, which is not well regularized to the link prediction task on graphs, and limits the performance of AutoGNN for other graph tasks. In this paper, we present a novel AutoGNN work that explicitly models the link information, abbreviated to AutoGEL. In such a way, AutoGEL can handle the link prediction task and improve the performance of AutoGNNs on the node classification and graph classification task. Moreover, AutoGEL proposes a novel search space containing various design dimensions at both intra-layer and inter-layer designs and adopts a more robust differentiable search algorithm to further improve efficiency and effectiveness. Experimental results on benchmark data sets demonstrate the superiority of AutoGEL on several tasks.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks process data whose elements are connected by links, but choosing their architecture often requires substantial manual design. Automated graph neural networks search for suitable architectures. This paper identifies a weakness in existing approaches: their treatment of link information is largely implicit, which limits their suitability for predicting links and can also hinder other graph tasks.

AutoGEL makes link information an explicit part of the model. It also introduces a search space covering design choices both within individual layers and between layers. A differentiable search algorithm is used to explore these choices, with the aim of improving the efficiency and effectiveness of architecture selection.

The authors report superior benchmark performance across several tasks, including link prediction, node classification, and graph classification. The central contribution joins two decisions that affect graph learning: how connections are represented and how the network architecture is selected. Explicitly modeling links supports the prediction of connections while also improving the reported results for classifying nodes and whole graphs.
summary.tldr: AutoGEL combines explicit link modeling with automated architecture search to improve several graph learning tasks.

title: AutoGEL: An Automated Graph Neural Network with Explicit Link Information

abstract: We describe a novel attribution method which is grounded in Sensitivity Analysis and uses Sobol indices. Beyond modeling the individual contributions of image regions, Sobol indices provide an efficient way to capture higher-order interactions between image regions and their contributions to a neural network's prediction through the lens of variance.We describe an approach that makes the computation of these indices efficient for high-dimensional problems by using perturbation masks coupled with efficient estimators to handle the high dimensionality of images.Importantly, we show that the proposed method leads to favorable scores on standard benchmarks for vision (and language models) while drastically reducing the computing time compared to other black-box methods -- even surpassing the accuracy of state-of-the-art white-box methods which require access to internal representations. Our code is freely available:github.com/fel-thomas/Sobol-Attribution-Method.

paragraphs: Attribution methods try to explain which parts of an input contribute to a model’s prediction. This paper approaches attribution through sensitivity analysis, using Sobol indices to examine variation in model outputs. The method considers both individual image regions and interactions among regions, allowing contributions to reflect effects that appear when regions act together.

Computing these quantities directly is challenging for high-dimensional images. The authors combine perturbation masks with efficient estimators to make Sobol-based attribution computationally practical. Because the approach is a black-box method, it can explain predictions without requiring access to the network’s internal representations.

The reported evaluations produce favorable scores on standard vision benchmarks and also include language models. Compared with other black-box methods, the approach substantially reduces computation time. The authors additionally report accuracy exceeding state-of-the-art white-box methods in their evaluations. These findings support variance-based interaction analysis as an efficient explanation strategy, with the performance comparisons grounded in the evaluated benchmarks rather than a universal ranking of explanation methods.
summary.tldr: Sobol-based attribution efficiently captures individual and interacting input contributions, with strong benchmark results and reduced black-box explanation time.

title: Look at the Variance! Efficient Black-box Explanations with Sobol-based Sensitivity Analysis

abstract: Multi-label classification (MLC) has wide practical importance, but the theoretical understanding of its statistical properties is still limited. As an attempt to fill this gap, we thoroughly study upper and lower regret bounds for two canonical MLC performance measures, Hamming loss and Precision@$\kappa$. We consider two different statistical and algorithmic settings, a non-parametric setting tackled by plug-in classifiers \`a la $k$-nearest neighbors, and a parametric one tackled by empirical risk minimization operating on surrogate loss functions. For both, we analyze the interplay between a natural MLC variant of the low noise assumption, widely studied in binary classification, and the label sparsity, the latter being a natural property of large-scale MLC problems. We show that those conditions are crucial in improving the bounds, but the way they are tangled is not obvious, and also different across the two settings.

paragraphs: In multilabel classification, an example can have several correct labels, even when most possible labels do not apply. This paper studies the statistical consequences of that sparsity through upper and lower regret bounds. The measures are Hamming loss, which concerns label-wise mistakes, and Precision at κ, which concerns the selected set of κ labels.

The analysis covers two learning settings. One uses nonparametric plug-in classifiers, including approaches based on nearest neighbors. The other uses parametric models trained by minimizing empirical surrogate losses. Studying both allows the authors to examine how statistical conditions interact with different ways of constructing predictions.

The key conditions are label sparsity and a multilabel version of a low-noise assumption familiar from binary classification. The authors show that these conditions are crucial for improving the bounds, but their interaction differs between the two settings. The contribution clarifies why having few relevant labels can help statistical performance while showing that its benefit depends on the surrounding assumptions and learning approach.
summary.tldr: The paper shows how label sparsity and low-noise assumptions interact differently across two multilabel learning settings to improve regret bounds.

title: Regret Bounds for Multilabel Classification in Sparse Label Regimes

abstract: Few-shot knowledge graph (KG) completion task aims to perform inductive reasoning over the KG: given only a few support triplets of a new relation $\bowtie$ (e.g., (chop,$\bowtie$,kitchen), (read,$\bowtie$,library), the goal is to predict the query triplets of the same unseen relation $\bowtie$, e.g., (sleep,$\bowtie$,?). Current approaches cast the problem in a meta-learning framework, where the model needs to be first jointly trained over many training few-shot tasks, each being defined by its own relation, so that learning/prediction on the target few-shot task can be effective. However, in real-world KGs, curating many training tasks is a challenging ad hoc process. Here we propose Connection Subgraph Reasoner (CSR), which can make predictions for the target few-shot task directly without the need for pre-training on the human curated set of training tasks. The key to CSR is that we explicitly model a shared connection subgraph between support and query triplets, as inspired by the principle of eliminative induction. To adapt to specific KG, we design a corresponding self-supervised pretraining scheme with the objective of reconstructing automatically sampled connection subgraphs. Our pretrained model can then be directly applied to target few-shot tasks on without the need for training few-shot tasks. Extensive experiments on real KGs, including NELL, FB15K-237, and ConceptNet, demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework: we show that even a learning-free implementation of CSR can already perform competitively to existing methods on target few-shot tasks; with pretraining, CSR can achieve significant gains of up to 52% on the more challenging inductive few-shot tasks where the entities are also unseen during (pre)training.

paragraphs: Few-shot knowledge-graph completion asks a model to infer an unfamiliar relation from a handful of example triples. Many approaches first train on numerous relation-specific tasks, but assembling those tasks requires human curation. This paper introduces Connection Subgraph Reasoner, or CSR, to make predictions without that curated collection of training tasks.

CSR explicitly models a connection subgraph shared by the support examples and a candidate query. The underlying idea is to identify connecting structure that can explain the examples and apply it to a new case. To adapt CSR to a particular knowledge graph, the authors pretrain it by reconstructing automatically sampled connection subgraphs, creating supervision from the graph itself.

Experiments on NELL, FB15K-237, and ConceptNet support the approach. Even a learning-free version performs competitively with existing methods. Pretraining yields gains of up to 52% on the harder inductive tasks, where entities as well as relations can be unseen during training. The result suggests that learning reusable graph connections can reduce dependence on manually constructed few-shot training tasks.
summary.tldr: CSR learns reusable connection subgraphs to reason about new knowledge-graph relations without a curated set of few-shot training tasks.

title: Few-shot Relational Reasoning via Connection Subgraph Pretraining

abstract: Precise and accurate predictions over boundary areas are essential for semantic segmentation. However, the commonly used convolutional operators tend to smooth and blur local detail cues, making it difficult for deep models to generate accurate boundary predictions. In this paper, we introduce an operator-level approach to enhance semantic boundary awareness, so as to improve the prediction of the deep semantic segmentation model. Specifically, we formulate the boundary feature enhancement process as an anisotropic diffusion process. We propose a novel learnable approach called semantic diffusion network (SDN) for approximating the diffusion process, which contains a parameterized semantic difference convolution operator followed by a feature fusion module and constructs a differentiable mapping from original backbone features to advanced boundary-aware features. The proposed SDN is an efficient and flexible module that can be plugged into existing encoder-decoder segmentation models. Extensive experiments show that our approach can achieve consistent improvements over several typical state-of-the-art segmentation baseline models on challenging public benchmarks.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation depends on accurate predictions near object boundaries, where small spatial details help separate neighboring regions. Common convolutional operators can smooth those details, making boundary prediction harder. This paper addresses the issue at the operator level by transforming existing features into features that better preserve semantic boundary information.

The authors formulate boundary enhancement as anisotropic diffusion and introduce a learnable semantic diffusion network to approximate that process. The module combines a parameterized semantic difference convolution operator with feature fusion. Its mapping from backbone features to boundary-aware features is differentiable, allowing the enhancement process to be learned within the segmentation model.

SDN is designed as an efficient, flexible module that can be inserted into existing encoder-decoder architectures. Extensive experiments report consistent improvements over several typical state-of-the-art segmentation baselines on challenging public benchmarks. The findings support an approach in which improving how features represent boundaries can strengthen existing segmentation systems, without requiring the contribution to take the form of an entirely new segmentation architecture.
summary.tldr: SDN learns a diffusion-inspired feature transformation that improves boundary awareness in existing semantic segmentation models.

title: Semantic Diffusion Network for Semantic Segmentation

abstract: In general, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are easy to train, but their essential properties, such as generalization error and adversarial robustness, are hard to control. Recent research demonstrated that singular values of convolutional layers significantly affect such elusive properties and offered several methods for controlling them. Nevertheless, these methods present an intractable computational challenge or resort to coarse approximations. In this paper, we offer a principled approach to alleviating constraints of the prior art at the expense of an insignificant reduction in layer expressivity. Our method is based on the tensor-train decomposition; it retains control over the actual singular values of convolutional mappings while providing structurally sparse and hardware-friendly representation. We demonstrate the improved properties of modern CNNs with our method and analyze its impact on the model performance, calibration, and adversarial robustness. The source code is available at: https://github.com/WhiteTeaDragon/practical_svd_conv

paragraphs: Convolutional networks can be straightforward to train while remaining difficult to control in terms of generalization and adversarial robustness. Singular values of convolutional layers influence these properties, making them useful targets for intervention. Existing control methods, however, can be computationally impractical or rely on coarse approximations of the quantities they seek to manage.

This paper proposes a tensor-train-based representation of convolutional layers. It retains control over the actual singular values of the convolutional mappings while introducing structured sparsity and a hardware-friendly form. The authors describe the trade-off as an insignificant reduction in layer expressivity in exchange for easing the computational constraints of previous approaches.

The method is evaluated in modern convolutional networks, with analysis of model performance, calibration, and adversarial robustness. The authors report improved network properties with their construction. The contribution is a practical connection between a mathematically relevant layer property and an implementable representation: singular-value control becomes part of the layer's structure, rather than relying only on expensive computation or coarse estimation.
summary.tldr: A tensor-train representation makes actual convolutional singular values controllable in a hardware-friendly form with a stated small expressivity trade-off.

title: Towards Practical Control of Singular Values of Convolutional Layers

abstract: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are wide-spread machine learning tools for modeling sequential and time series data. They are notoriously hard to train because their loss gradients backpropagated in time tend to saturate or diverge during training. This is known as the exploding and vanishing gradient problem. Previous solutions to this issue either built on rather complicated, purpose-engineered architectures with gated memory buffers, or - more recently - imposed constraints that ensure convergence to a fixed point or restrict (the eigenspectrum of) the recurrence matrix. Such constraints, however, convey severe limitations on the expressivity of the RNN. Essential intrinsic dynamics such as multistability or chaos are disabled. This is inherently at disaccord with the chaotic nature of many, if not most, time series encountered in nature and society. It is particularly problematic in scientific applications where one aims to reconstruct the underlying dynamical system. Here we offer a comprehensive theoretical treatment of this problem by relating the loss gradients during RNN training to the Lyapunov spectrum of RNN-generated orbits. We mathematically prove that RNNs producing stable equilibrium or cyclic behavior have bounded gradients, whereas the gradients of RNNs with chaotic dynamics always diverge. Based on these analyses and insights we suggest ways of how to optimize the training process on chaotic data according to the system's Lyapunov spectrum, regardless of the employed RNN architecture.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks can be difficult to train because gradients propagated through time vanish or explode. Some remedies impose restrictions that stabilize recurrent behavior, but those restrictions can also eliminate multistability or chaos. That creates a problem when the purpose of learning is to reconstruct a dynamical system whose behavior is itself chaotic.

The paper connects training gradients to the Lyapunov spectrum of trajectories generated by the RNN. This spectrum characterizes the stability of the generated dynamics and provides a mathematical link between the behavior being modeled and the optimization difficulty. The authors prove that stable equilibrium or cyclic behavior has bounded gradients, whereas chaotic RNN dynamics have gradients that diverge.

The analysis exposes a tension between suppressing gradient growth and retaining the dynamics needed for chaotic data. Based on this connection, the authors suggest ways to adjust training according to the system's Lyapunov spectrum, independently of the chosen RNN architecture. The contribution is a theoretical explanation of the difficulty together with guidance informed by the dynamics being learned.
summary.tldr: The paper links RNN gradient divergence to chaotic dynamics through Lyapunov spectra and uses that connection to guide training.

title: On the difficulty of learning chaotic dynamics with RNNs

abstract: When we use the wisdom of the crowds, we usually rank the answers according to their popularity, especially when we cannot verify the answers. However, this can be very dangerous when the majority make systematic mistakes. A fundamental question arises: can we build a hierarchy among the answers without any prior where the higher-ranking answers, which may not be supported by the majority, are from more sophisticated people? To address the question, we propose 1) a novel model to describe people's thinking hierarchy; 2) two algorithms to learn the thinking hierarchy without any prior; 3) a novel open-response based crowdsourcing approach based on the above theoretic framework. In addition to theoretic justifications, we conduct four empirical crowdsourcing studies and show that a) the accuracy of the top-ranking answers learned by our approach is much higher than that of plurality voting (In one question, the plurality answer is supported by 74 respondents but the correct answer is only supported by 3 respondents. Our approach ranks the correct answer the highest without any prior); b) our model has a high goodness-of-fit, especially for the questions where our top-ranking answer is correct. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to propose a thinking hierarchy model with empirical validations in the general problem-solving scenarios; and the first to propose a practical open-response-based crowdsourcing approach that beats plurality voting without any prior.

paragraphs: Crowdsourcing commonly ranks answers by popularity when their correctness cannot readily be checked. This can fail when many respondents make the same systematic mistake. The paper asks whether answers can instead be organized by the sophistication of the thinking behind them, allowing a minority answer to rank highly without using a prior.

The authors propose a model of thinking hierarchies, two algorithms for learning such hierarchies, and an open-response crowdsourcing approach built on that framework. The aim is to extract a ranking that reflects more than how frequently each answer appears. The paper provides theoretical justification and evaluates the approach in four empirical crowdsourcing studies.

Across those studies, the highest-ranked answers are much more accurate than plurality voting. In one question, the method ranks the correct answer first despite its having only three supporters, compared with 74 for the plurality answer. The model also fits the observed data well, particularly when its top answer is correct. These findings show that popularity can miss useful structure in crowd responses.
summary.tldr: A learned hierarchy of crowd responses identifies accurate minority answers and outperforms plurality voting in four studies.

title: Eliciting Thinking Hierarchy without a Prior

abstract: Learning safe solutions is an important but challenging problem in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL). Shielded reinforcement learning is one approach for preventing agents from choosing unsafe actions. Current shielded reinforcement learning methods for MARL make strong assumptions about communication and full observability. In this work, we extend the formalization of the shielded reinforcement learning problem to a decentralized multi-agent setting. We then present an algorithm for decomposition of a centralized shield, allowing shields to be used in such decentralized, communication-free environments. Our results show that agents equipped with decentralized shields perform comparably to agents with centralized shields in several tasks, allowing shielding to be used in environments with decentralized training and execution for the first time.

paragraphs: In multi-agent reinforcement learning, agents must learn useful behavior while avoiding unsafe actions. A shield helps enforce safety by preventing an agent from choosing prohibited actions. Existing shielding methods for multiple agents make strong assumptions about communication and full observability, making them difficult to apply when agents must learn and act in a decentralized environment.

The paper extends the formal definition of shielded reinforcement learning to this decentralized setting. It then introduces an algorithm that decomposes a centralized shield into decentralized shields. The purpose is to make shielding usable without communication between agents, connecting a centrally specified protection mechanism with the requirements of distributed decision-making.

Across several tasks, agents using decentralized shields perform comparably to agents using centralized shields. These results support the feasibility of retaining useful task performance while distributing the shielding mechanism. The authors present this as enabling shielding in environments with both decentralized training and decentralized execution, expanding where the approach can be used beyond settings that rely on centralized information or communication.
summary.tldr: A shield-decomposition algorithm enables communication-free multi-agent shielding with performance comparable to centralized shields on several tasks.

title: Shield Decentralization for Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We present a new text-to-SQL dataset for electronic health records (EHRs). The utterances were collected from 222 hospital staff, including physicians, nurses, insurance review and health records teams, and more. To construct the QA dataset on structured EHR data, we conducted a poll at a university hospital and templatized the responses to create seed questions. Then, we manually linked them to two open-source EHR databases—MIMIC-III and eICU—and included them with various time expressions and held-out unanswerable questions in the dataset, which were all collected from the poll. Our dataset poses a unique set of challenges: the model needs to 1) generate SQL queries that reflect a wide range of needs in the hospital, including simple retrieval and complex operations such as calculating survival rate, 2) understand various time expressions to answer time-sensitive questions in healthcare, and 3) distinguish whether a given question is answerable or unanswerable based on the prediction confidence. We believe our dataset, EHRSQL, could serve as a practical benchmark to develop and assess QA models on structured EHR data and take one step further towards bridging the gap between text-to-SQL research and its real-life deployment in healthcare. EHRSQL is available at https://github.com/glee4810/EHRSQL.
