paragraphs: EHRSQL is a benchmark for turning natural-language questions about electronic health records into SQL queries. Its questions originate from a poll of 222 hospital staff, including physicians, nurses, and teams responsible for insurance review and health records. This grounds the dataset in a range of information needs encountered within a hospital.

The researchers converted poll responses into question templates and manually linked them to the open-source MIMIC-III and eICU databases. They incorporated different time expressions and held-out questions that cannot be answered, also drawn from the poll. The resulting task therefore requires more than matching a question to a simple database lookup.

Models must handle requests ranging from basic retrieval to calculations such as survival rates, interpret time-sensitive wording, and use prediction confidence to distinguish answerable from unanswerable questions. The authors position EHRSQL as a practical resource for developing and assessing question-answering systems over structured health records. Its contribution is a benchmark organized around these deployment-relevant challenges, rather than a claim that healthcare deployment has already been solved.
summary.tldr: EHRSQL benchmarks medical text-to-SQL systems using hospital staff questions that require temporal reasoning, complex queries, and recognizing unanswerable requests.

title: EHRSQL: A Practical Text-to-SQL Benchmark for Electronic Health Records

abstract: Large-scale pre-trained language models have achieved impressive results on a wide range of downstream tasks recently. However, fine-tuning an extremely large-scale pre-trained language model on limited target datasets is often plagued by overfitting and representation degradation. In this paper, we propose a Dynamic Parameter Selection (DPS) algorithm for the large-scale pre-trained models during fine-tuning, which adaptively selects a more promising subnetwork to perform staging updates based on gradients of back-propagation. Experiments on the GLUE benchmark show that DPS outperforms previous fine-tuning methods in terms of overall performance and stability, and consistently achieves better results with variable pre-trained language models. In addition, DPS brings a large magnitude of improvement in out-of-domain transferring experiments and low-resource scenarios, which shows that it can maintain stable general contextual features and reduce the representation collapse. We release our code at \url{https://github.com/ZhangHaojie077/DPS}.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a large pretrained language model on a limited dataset can cause overfitting and degrade representations acquired during pretraining. The paper addresses how to adapt the model while preserving useful general contextual features. Its method, Dynamic Parameter Selection, changes which parameters receive updates during fine-tuning.

DPS uses gradients from backpropagation to select a promising subnetwork adaptively and update it in stages. The selection is therefore guided by the ongoing optimization process. This makes the choice of what to update part of fine-tuning itself, allowing adaptation to focus on selected portions of a large pretrained model.

On GLUE, the authors report better overall performance and stability than previous fine-tuning methods, with improvements across different pretrained language models. They also report substantial gains in low-resource settings and transfer outside the training domain. These findings support their interpretation that DPS helps retain general contextual features and reduces representation collapse, connecting selective updates to more stable adaptation when target data are limited.
summary.tldr: Dynamic Parameter Selection uses gradients to adaptively update subnetworks, improving fine-tuning performance and stability in the reported experiments.

title: Fine-Tuning Pre-Trained Language Models Effectively by Optimizing Subnetworks Adaptively

abstract: We propose a geometric scattering-based graph neural network (GNN) for approximating solutions of the NP-hard maximum clique (MC) problem. We construct a loss function with two terms, one which encourages the network to find highly connected nodes and the other which acts as a surrogate for the constraint that the nodes form a clique. We then use this loss to train an efficient GNN architecture that outputs a vector representing the probability for each node to be part of the MC and apply a rule-based decoder to make our final prediction. The incorporation of the scattering transform alleviates the so-called oversmoothing problem that is often encountered in GNNs and would degrade the performance of our proposed setup. Our empirical results demonstrate that our method outperforms representative GNN baselines in terms of solution accuracy and inference speed as well as conventional solvers like Gurobi with limited time budgets. Furthermore, our scattering model is very parameter efficient with only $\sim$ 0.1\% of the number of parameters compared to previous GNN baseline models.

paragraphs: The maximum clique problem asks for the largest group of graph nodes in which every pair is connected. Finding an exact solution is NP-hard, so this paper develops a neural approach for approximating solutions. The model assigns each node a probability of belonging to the maximum clique, then uses a rule-based decoder to produce its final prediction.

Training uses a two-part loss. One part encourages the selection of highly connected nodes, while the other approximates the requirement that the selected nodes form a clique. The architecture incorporates a geometric scattering transform to alleviate oversmoothing, a problem in graph neural networks that would otherwise degrade this approach’s performance.

Empirical results show better solution accuracy and inference speed than representative graph neural network baselines, alongside better results than conventional solvers such as Gurobi under limited time budgets. The model also uses roughly 0.1% as many parameters as previous neural baselines. These findings support an efficient approximation approach; the comparison with conventional solvers specifically concerns restricted computation time.
summary.tldr: A compact geometric scattering network approximates maximum cliques with strong empirical accuracy and speed under the tested conditions.

title: Can Hybrid Geometric Scattering Networks Help Solve the Maximum Clique Problem?

abstract: Data in many applications follows systems of Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs).This paper presents a novel algorithmic and symbolic construction for covariance functions of Gaussian Processes (GPs) with realizations strictly following a system of linear homogeneous ODEs with constant coefficients, which we call LODE-GPs. Introducing this strong inductive bias into a GP improves modelling of such data. Using smith normal form algorithms, a symbolic technique, we overcome two current restrictions in the state of the art: (1) the need for certain uniqueness conditions in the set of solutions, typically assumed in classical ODE solvers and their probabilistic counterparts, and (2) the restriction to controllable systems, typically assumed when encoding differential equations in covariance functions. We show the effectiveness of LODE-GPs in a number of experiments, for example learning physically interpretable parameters by maximizing the likelihood.

paragraphs: When data follows known differential equations, a statistical model can benefit from building those equations into its structure. This paper develops Gaussian processes whose realizations strictly obey a specified system of linear, homogeneous ordinary differential equations with constant coefficients. The equation class is an explicit part of the construction's scope.

The authors construct the covariance functions that define these processes using an algorithmic, symbolic method based on Smith normal form. Their approach removes two restrictions found in existing methods: certain requirements concerning uniqueness of solutions and the requirement that the system be controllable. This extends the systems that can be represented within the stated class of differential equations.

The resulting models, called LODE-GPs, use the equations as a strong inductive bias, improving modeling of data with that structure. Experiments demonstrate their effectiveness, including learning physically interpretable parameters by maximizing likelihood. The contribution connects exact equation compliance with statistical learning, allowing the prescribed dynamics to shape the model while parameters are learned from observations.
summary.tldr: LODE-GPs construct Gaussian-process covariances that enforce linear homogeneous differential equations while removing two restrictions of earlier approaches.

title: Constraining Gaussian Processes to Systems of Linear Ordinary Differential Equations

abstract: Although recent point cloud analysis achieves impressive progress, the paradigm of representation learning from single modality gradually meets its bottleneck. In this work, we take a step towards more discriminative 3D point cloud representation using 2D images, which inherently contain richer appearance information, e.g., texture, color, and shade. Specifically, this paper introduces a simple but effective point cloud cross-modality training (PointCMT) strategy, which utilizes view-images, i.e., rendered or projected 2D images of the 3D object, to boost point cloud classification. In practice, to effectively acquire auxiliary knowledge from view-images, we develop a teacher-student framework and formulate the cross-modal learning as a knowledge distillation problem. Through novel feature and classifier enhancement criteria, PointCMT eliminates the distribution discrepancy between different modalities and avoid potential negative transfer effectively. Note that PointCMT efficiently improves the point-only representation without any architecture modification. Sufficient experiments verify significant gains on various datasets based on several backbones, i.e., equipped with PointCMT, PointNet++ and PointMLP achieve state-of-the-art performance on two benchmarks, i.e., 94.4% and 86.7% accuracy on ModelNet40 and ScanObjectNN, respectively.

paragraphs: Point cloud classification learns about three-dimensional objects from collections of points. This paper supplements that learning with two-dimensional views, which can contain appearance information such as color, texture, and shading. Its PointCMT training strategy uses rendered or projected images of an object to improve the representation learned by a point cloud model.

The approach treats this transfer as knowledge distillation within a teacher-student framework. Feature and classifier enhancement criteria address differences between the image and point cloud modalities and aim to avoid harmful transfer. The resulting improvement is to a point-only representation, and the method does not require changes to the point cloud network's architecture.

Experiments cover multiple datasets and network backbones. The paper reports significant gains and state-of-the-art results with PointCMT-equipped PointNet++ and PointMLP, including 94.4% accuracy on ModelNet40 and 86.7% on ScanObjectNN. The findings show that auxiliary image information during training can improve point cloud classification while preserving the underlying architecture, making cross-modal supervision useful beyond models that directly combine both input types.
summary.tldr: PointCMT distills information from object images into point cloud models, improving classification without modifying their architectures.

title: Let Images Give You More: Point Cloud Cross-Modal Training for Shape Analysis

abstract: We analyze the dynamics of finite width effects in wide but finite feature learning neural networks. Starting from a dynamical mean field theory description of infinite width deep neural network kernel and prediction dynamics, we provide a characterization of the $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{\text{width}})$ fluctuations of the DMFT order parameters over random initializations of the network weights. Our results, while perturbative in width, unlike prior analyses, are non-perturbative in the strength of feature learning. In the lazy limit of network training, all kernels are random but static in time and the prediction variance has a universal form. However, in the rich, feature learning regime, the fluctuations of the kernels and predictions are dynamically coupled with a variance that can be computed self-consistently. In two layer networks, we show how feature learning can dynamically reduce the variance of the final tangent kernel and final network predictions. We also show how initialization variance can slow down online learning in wide but finite networks. In deeper networks, kernel variance can dramatically accumulate through subsequent layers at large feature learning strengths, but feature learning continues to improve the signal-to-noise ratio of the feature kernels. In discrete time, we demonstrate that large learning rate phenomena such as edge of stability effects can be well captured by infinite width dynamics and that initialization variance can decrease dynamically. For CNNs trained on CIFAR-10, we empirically find significant corrections to both the bias and variance of network dynamics due to finite width.

paragraphs: Infinite-width theories simplify neural network training, but actual networks have finite width and differ across random initializations. This paper characterizes fluctuations around infinite-width dynamical mean field predictions at order one over the square root of width. The approximation is perturbative in width, while allowing feature learning to be strong rather than treating it as a small effect.

The analysis distinguishes two training regimes. In the lazy regime, kernels remain fixed during training, and prediction variance follows a universal form. With substantial feature learning, kernel and prediction fluctuations evolve together. For two-layer networks, feature learning can reduce the final variance of both, although initialization variance can also slow online learning.

In deeper networks, strong feature learning can cause kernel variance to accumulate across layers while still improving kernel signal-to-noise ratios. The authors also find that infinite-width dynamics capture large-learning-rate behavior, including edge-of-stability effects. Experiments with convolutional networks on CIFAR-10 show substantial finite-width corrections to both bias and variance, demonstrating why these corrections matter for describing training.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes finite-width training fluctuations and shows how feature learning can reshape initialization variability in kernels and predictions.

title: Dynamics of Finite Width Kernel and Prediction Fluctuations in Mean Field Neural Networks

abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become increasingly integrated into our everyday lives, understanding their ability to comprehend human mental states becomes critical for ensuring effective interactions. However, despite the recent attempts to assess the Theory-of-Mind (ToM) reasoning capabilities of LLMs, the degree to which these models can align with human ToM remains a nuanced topic of exploration. This is primarily due to two distinct challenges: (1) the presence of inconsistent results from previous evaluations, and (2) concerns surrounding the validity of existing evaluation methodologies. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework for procedurally generating evaluations with LLMs by populating causal templates. Using our framework, we create a new social reasoning benchmark (BigToM) for LLMs which consists of 25 controls and 5,000 model-written evaluations. We find that human participants rate the quality of our benchmark higher than previous crowd-sourced evaluations and comparable to expert-written evaluations. Using BigToM, we evaluate the social reasoning capabilities of a variety of LLMs and compare model performances with human performance. Our results suggest that GPT4 has ToM capabilities that mirror human inference patterns, though less reliable, while other LLMs struggle.

paragraphs: Evaluating whether language models reason about human mental states is difficult when earlier tests produce inconsistent results or have questionable validity. This paper introduces a way to generate social-reasoning evaluations by having language models populate causal templates. The approach gives the evaluation process a structured basis while allowing many individual examples to be produced.

The resulting benchmark, BigToM, contains 5,000 model-written evaluations and 25 controls. Human participants rate its quality above earlier crowd-sourced evaluations and comparable to expert-written evaluations. This quality assessment addresses the construction of the benchmark separately from the question of how well language models perform on it.

The authors then compare several language models with human performance. Their results suggest that GPT4 exhibits theory-of-mind inference patterns resembling those of humans, but does so less reliably, while other models struggle. The conclusion concerns observed social reasoning on these evaluations. It preserves a distinction between similarity in inference patterns and consistently matching human performance, which the reported results do not establish.
summary.tldr: BigToM uses causal templates to evaluate social reasoning and finds evidence of human-like but less reliable inference patterns in GPT4.

title: Understanding Social Reasoning in Language Models with Language Models

abstract: Figuring out which Pre-Trained Model (PTM) from a model zoo fits the target task is essential to take advantage of plentiful model resources. With the availability of numerous heterogeneous PTMs from diverse fields, efficiently selecting the most suitable one is challenging due to the time-consuming costs of carrying out forward or backward passes over all PTMs. In this paper, we propose Model Spider, which tokenizes both PTMs and tasks by summarizing their characteristics into vectors to enable efficient PTM selection. By leveraging the approximated performance of PTMs on a separate set of training tasks, Model Spider learns to construct representation and measure the fitness score between a model-task pair via their representation. The ability to rank relevant PTMs higher than others generalizes to new tasks. With the top-ranked PTM candidates, we further learn to enrich task repr. with their PTM-specific semantics to re-rank the PTMs for better selection. Model Spider balances efficiency and selection ability, making PTM selection like a spider preying on a web. Model Spider exhibits promising performance across diverse model zoos, including visual models and Large Language Models (LLMs). Code is available at https://github.com/zhangyikaii/Model-Spider.

paragraphs: Selecting a pretrained model for a new task can be expensive when a model collection contains many different architectures and capabilities. Evaluating every candidate through forward or backward passes adds substantial work. Model Spider addresses this selection problem by learning representations that make it possible to estimate how well a model and task fit together.

The method summarizes both pretrained models and tasks as vectors. Using approximate model performance on a separate collection of training tasks, it learns these representations and a score for each model-task pair. The learned ranking ability transfers to new tasks. It then uses the highest-ranked candidates to enrich the task representation with model-specific information and reranks the candidates.

This staged process balances efficient initial selection with a more informed refinement step. The authors report promising performance across diverse model collections, including visual models and large language models. The contribution is a learned approach to model selection that uses experience from earlier tasks and targeted candidate information to reduce the burden of assessing a large model zoo.
summary.tldr: Model Spider learns vector representations of models and tasks to rank pretrained candidates efficiently, then refines rankings using leading candidates.

title: Model Spider: Learning to Rank Pre-Trained Models Efficiently

abstract: Although supervised image denoising networks have shown remarkable performance on synthesized noisy images, they often fail in practice due to the difference between real and synthesized noise. Since clean-noisy image pairs from the real world are extremely costly to gather, self-supervised learning, which utilizes noisy input itself as a target, has been studied. To prevent a self-supervised denoising model from learning identical mapping, each output pixel should not be influenced by its corresponding input pixel; This requirement is known as J-invariance. Blind-spot networks (BSNs) have been a prevalent choice to ensure J-invariance in self-supervised image denoising. However, constructing variations of BSNs by injecting additional operations such as downsampling can expose blinded information, thereby violating J-invariance. Consequently, convolutions designed specifically for BSNs have been allowed only, limiting architectural flexibility. To overcome this limitation, we propose PUCA, a novel J-invariant U-Net architecture, for self-supervised denoising. PUCA leverages patch-unshuffle/shuffle to dramatically expand receptive fields while maintaining J-invariance and dilated attention blocks (DABs) for global context incorporation. Experimental results demonstrate that PUCA achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming existing methods in self-supervised image denoising.

paragraphs: Real noisy images can differ from synthetic training noise, while collecting matching clean images is expensive. Self-supervised denoising instead learns from noisy images themselves. To prevent simple copying in the approach discussed here, an output pixel must not depend on its corresponding input pixel, a property called J-invariance.

Blind-spot networks enforce that separation, but adding operations such as downsampling can accidentally expose the hidden pixel. This restricts architectural choices and the information a denoiser can gather safely. PUCA proposes a J-invariant U-Net architecture that uses patch-unshuffle and patch-shuffle operations to greatly expand receptive fields while preserving the required separation between corresponding input and output pixels.

The model also uses dilated attention blocks to incorporate global context. Together, these components address how to give the network broader image information without undermining the self-supervised training constraint. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance over existing self-supervised denoising methods. The contribution therefore combines an architectural solution to information leakage with empirical evidence that broader context improves denoising in the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: PUCA expands image context while preserving blind spots, improving reported self-supervised denoising performance.

title: PUCA: Patch-Unshuffle and Channel Attention for Enhanced Self-Supervised Image Denoising

abstract: We propose a foundation model named Brant for modeling intracranial recordings, which learns powerful representations of intracranial neural signals by pre-training, providing a large-scale, off-the-shelf model for medicine. Brant is the largest model in the field of brain signals and is pre-trained on a large corpus of intracranial data collected by us. The design of Brant is to capture long-term temporal dependency and spatial correlation from neural signals, combining the information in both time and frequency domains. As a foundation model, Brant achieves SOTA performance on various downstream tasks (i.e. neural signal forecasting, frequency-phase forecasting, imputation and seizure detection), showing the generalization ability to a broad range of tasks. The low-resource label analysis and representation visualization further illustrate the effectiveness of our pre-training strategy. In addition, we explore the effect of model size to show that a larger model with a higher capacity can lead to performance improvements on our dataset. The source code and pre-trained weights are available at: https://zju-brainnet.github.io/Brant.github.io/.

paragraphs: Brant is a pretrained model for intracranial recordings, designed to provide reusable representations of neural signals. The authors train it on a large collection of intracranial data they gathered and describe it as the largest model in the brain-signal field. The central aim is to make one pretrained model useful across multiple subsequent tasks.

Its design combines information from the time and frequency domains while capturing long-term temporal dependencies and spatial correlations. These perspectives address different aspects of the same recordings: how signals develop over time, how their frequency content behaves, and how signals relate across locations. Bringing them together supports a representation that can serve more than one prediction problem.

The authors report state-of-the-art results for neural-signal forecasting, frequency-phase forecasting, imputation, and seizure detection. Analyses with limited labels and visualizations of the learned representations further support their pretraining strategy. Their model-size investigation also finds that greater capacity can improve performance on their dataset, providing dataset-specific evidence for scaling the approach.
summary.tldr: Brant combines temporal, spatial, and frequency information in a pretrained intracranial-signal model that performs strongly across several downstream tasks.

title: Brant: Foundation Model for Intracranial Neural Signal

abstract: Many real-world experimental design problems (a) evaluate multiple experimental conditions in parallel and (b) replicate each condition multiple times due to large and heteroscedastic observation noise. Given a fixed total budget, this naturally induces a trade-off between evaluating more unique conditions while replicating each of them fewer times vs. evaluating fewer unique conditions and replicating each more times. Moreover, in these problems, practitioners may be risk-averse and hence prefer an input with both good average performance and small variability. To tackle both challenges, we propose the Batch Thompson Sampling for Replicable Experimental Design (BTS-RED) framework, which encompasses three algorithms. Our BTS-RED-Known and BTS-RED-Unknown algorithms, for, respectively, known and unknown noise variance, choose the number of replications adaptively rather than deterministically such that an input with a larger noise variance is replicated more times. As a result, despite the noise heteroscedasticity, both algorithms enjoy a theoretical guarantee and are asymptotically no-regret. Our Mean-Var-BTS-RED algorithm aims at risk-averse optimization and is also asymptotically no-regret. We also show the effectiveness of our algorithms in two practical real-world applications: precision agriculture and AutoML.

paragraphs: When experiments run in parallel, a fixed budget must cover both exploring different conditions and repeating measurements. Repetition is especially valuable when observations are noisy, but spending more on repeats leaves fewer opportunities to explore. This paper addresses that allocation problem when the amount of noise varies across experimental conditions.

The proposed BTS-RED framework contains three algorithms built around batch Thompson sampling. Two handle known and unknown noise variance, respectively. They adapt the number of repetitions to the condition being evaluated, assigning more repeats to noisier inputs. This makes replication part of the optimization decision instead of fixing the same repetition count for every condition.

A third algorithm addresses risk-averse preferences by considering both average performance and variability. The authors establish asymptotic no-regret guarantees for all three algorithms, including the settings with unequal noise levels. These are long-run guarantees rather than promises about each batch. Applications in precision agriculture and automated machine learning demonstrate the framework’s practical effectiveness.
summary.tldr: BTS-RED adaptively balances exploring experimental conditions and repeating noisy measurements, with variants for unknown noise and risk-averse objectives.

title: Batch Bayesian Optimization For Replicable Experimental Design

abstract: We address the problem of designing a sublinear-time spectral clustering oracle for graphs that exhibit strong clusterability. Such graphs contain $k$ latent clusters, each characterized by a large inner conductance (at least $\varphi$) and a small outer conductance (at most $\varepsilon$). Our aim is to preprocess the graph to enable clustering membership queries, with the key requirement that both preprocessing and query answering should be performed in sublinear time, and the resulting partition should be consistent with a $k$-partition that is close to the ground-truth clustering. Previous oracles have relied on either a $\textrm{poly}(k)\log n$ gap between inner and outer conductances or exponential (in $k/\varepsilon$) preprocessing time. Our algorithm relaxes these assumptions, albeit at the cost of a slightly higher misclassification ratio. We also show that our clustering oracle is robust against a few random edge deletions. To validate our theoretical bounds, we conducted experiments on synthetic networks.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to answer graph clustering questions without processing the entire graph for every answer. The goal is an oracle: after an initial preparation stage, it can report which cluster a queried vertex belongs to. Both preparation and answering must take sublinear time, meaning less than time proportional to the graph’s size.

The analysis assumes strong cluster structure. Each hidden cluster has strong internal connectivity, expressed through large inner conductance, and relatively weak connections outward, expressed through small outer conductance. Answers must agree with a single partition that is close to the underlying clustering, so individually fast answers also form a coherent overall assignment.

Earlier approaches required either a demanding separation between internal and external connectivity or preprocessing exponential in relevant clustering parameters. The proposed algorithm relaxes these requirements while accepting a slightly larger misclassification ratio. The authors also establish robustness to a few random edge deletions and test their theoretical bounds on synthetic networks. The contribution is therefore a qualified efficiency improvement for strongly clusterable graphs.
summary.tldr: A spectral clustering oracle reduces preprocessing requirements for strongly clusterable graphs while accepting slightly more misclassification.

title: A Sublinear-Time Spectral Clustering Oracle with Improved Preprocessing Time

abstract: Multi-view clustering (MVC) is a popular technique for improving clustering performance using various data sources. However, existing methods primarily focus on acquiring consistent information while often neglecting the issue of redundancy across multiple views.This study presents a new approach called Sufficient Multi-View Clustering (SUMVC) that examines the multi-view clustering framework from an information-theoretic standpoint. Our proposed method consists of two parts. Firstly, we develop a simple and reliable multi-view clustering method SCMVC (simple consistent multi-view clustering) that employs variational analysis to generate consistent information. Secondly, we propose a sufficient representation lower bound to enhance consistent information and minimise unnecessary information among views. The proposed SUMVC method offers a promising solution to the problem of multi-view clustering and provides a new perspective for analyzing multi-view data. To verify the effectiveness of our model, we conducted a theoretical analysis based on the Bayes Error Rate, and experiments on multiple multi-view datasets demonstrate the superior performance of SUMVC.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering groups examples using several sources of information about them. A central challenge is deciding what to retain from those sources. Methods that emphasize agreement between views can still preserve redundant information. This paper introduces Sufficient Multi-View Clustering, or SUMVC, to address both consistency and unnecessary repetition through an information-theoretic perspective.

The approach has two parts. First, a simpler method called SCMVC uses variational analysis to obtain information that is consistent across views. Second, SUMVC introduces a lower bound for sufficient representations. This component aims to strengthen useful shared information while reducing unnecessary information among the views. The distinction matters because collecting agreement alone does not directly address redundancy.

The authors analyze the method using Bayes Error Rate and report superior clustering performance on multiple multi-view datasets. These theoretical and experimental results support the proposed combination of consistency and information reduction. The contribution is both a clustering method and a way to reason about which information from multiple sources should enter a shared representation.
summary.tldr: SUMVC improves multi-view clustering by combining consistent information across sources while reducing unnecessary information.

title: A Novel Approach for Effective Multi-View Clustering with Information-Theoretic Perspective

abstract: Stein thinning is a promising algorithm proposed by (Riabiz et al., 2022) for post-processing outputs of Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). The main principle is to greedily minimize the kernelized Stein discrepancy (KSD), which only requires the gradient of the log-target distribution, and is thus well-suited for Bayesian inference. The main advantages of Stein thinning are the automatic remove of the burn-in period, the correction of the bias introduced by recent MCMC algorithms, and the asymptotic properties of convergence towards the target distribution. Nevertheless, Stein thinning suffers from several empirical pathologies, which may result in poor approximations, as observed in the literature. In this article, we conduct a theoretical analysis of these pathologies, to clearly identify the mechanisms at stake, and suggest improved strategies. Then, we introduce the regularized Stein thinning algorithm to alleviate the identified pathologies. Finally, theoretical guarantees and extensive experiments show the high efficiency of the proposed algorithm. An implementation of regularized Stein thinning as the kernax library in python and JAX is available at https://gitlab.com/drti/kernax.

paragraphs: Stein thinning post-processes samples produced by Markov chain Monte Carlo to obtain an approximation of a target distribution. It greedily reduces kernelized Stein discrepancy, a criterion requiring only the gradient of the target's log density. This makes the method suitable for Bayesian inference, where the paper highlights its potential to remove burn-in automatically and correct sampling bias.

Despite those advantages and its asymptotic convergence properties, Stein thinning can exhibit practical failure patterns that produce poor approximations. The authors analyze these pathologies theoretically to identify the mechanisms responsible. This distinction matters because a method's long-run guarantees can coexist with problematic behavior in the samples actually selected for use.

The paper then introduces regularized Stein thinning to alleviate the identified problems. The proposed modification is supported by theoretical guarantees and extensive experiments demonstrating its efficiency. The contribution connects an explanation of observed failures to a practical algorithmic adjustment, strengthening the use of discrepancy-based selection for MCMC post-processing.
summary.tldr: The paper explains practical failure patterns in Stein thinning and introduces regularization to alleviate them.

title: Kernel Stein Discrepancy thinning: a theoretical perspective of pathologies and a practical fix with regularization

abstract: Imitation learning uses data for training policies to solve complex tasks. However,when the training data is collected from human demonstrators, it often leadsto multimodal distributions because of the variability in human actions. Mostimitation learning methods rely on a maximum likelihood (ML) objective to learna parameterized policy, but this can result in suboptimal or unsafe behavior dueto the mode-averaging property of the ML objective. In this work, we proposeInformation Maximizing Curriculum, a curriculum-based approach that assignsa weight to each data point and encourages the model to specialize in the data itcan represent, effectively mitigating the mode-averaging problem by allowing themodel to ignore data from modes it cannot represent. To cover all modes and thus,enable versatile behavior, we extend our approach to a mixture of experts (MoE)policy, where each mixture component selects its own subset of the training datafor learning. A novel, maximum entropy-based objective is proposed to achievefull coverage of the dataset, thereby enabling the policy to encompass all modeswithin the data distribution. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach oncomplex simulated control tasks using versatile human demonstrations, achievingsuperior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Human demonstrations can contain several different ways of performing a task. In imitation learning, a policy trained with a maximum-likelihood objective may average these distinct behaviors, potentially producing actions that are ineffective or unsafe. Information Maximizing Curriculum addresses this problem by changing how individual demonstrations contribute to learning.

The method assigns a weight to each data point and encourages a model to specialize in behavior it can represent. It can therefore ignore examples from modes it cannot capture, reducing pressure to average incompatible behaviors. To recover versatility across the dataset, the authors extend this approach to a mixture of experts, with each component selecting its own training subset.

A maximum-entropy-based objective is introduced to encourage full dataset coverage across the mixture. Specialization and coverage thus play complementary roles: individual experts focus, while the overall policy is designed to encompass the different behavior modes. Experiments on complex simulated control tasks with varied human demonstrations report superior performance over state-of-the-art methods, supporting this curriculum-based approach to learning versatile policies.
summary.tldr: Information Maximizing Curriculum combines selective learning and a mixture of experts to reduce behavior averaging in imitation learning.

title: Information Maximizing Curriculum: A Curriculum-Based Approach for Learning Versatile Skills

abstract: Value Iteration (VI) is foundational to the theory and practice of modern reinforcement learning, and it is known to converge at a $\mathcal{O}(\gamma^k)$-rate. Surprisingly, however, the optimal rate for the VI setup was not known, and finding a general acceleration mechanism has been an open problem. In this paper, we present the first accelerated VI for both the Bellman consistency and optimality operators. Our method, called Anc-VI, is based on an \emph{anchoring} mechanism (distinct from Nesterov's acceleration), and it reduces the Bellman error faster than standard VI. In particular, Anc-VI exhibits a $\mathcal{O}(1/k)$-rate for $\gamma\approx 1$ or even $\gamma=1$, while standard VI has rate $\mathcal{O}(1)$ for $\gamma\ge 1-1/k$, where $k$ is the iteration count. We also provide a complexity lower bound matching the upper bound up to a constant factor of $4$, thereby establishing optimality of the accelerated rate of Anc-VI. Finally, we show that the anchoring mechanism provides the same benefit in the approximate VI and Gauss--Seidel VI setups as well.

paragraphs: Value iteration repeatedly applies a Bellman operator to improve value estimates in reinforcement learning. Its familiar convergence rate depends on the discount factor, gamma. When gamma is close to one, the standard guarantee can become weak. This paper asks whether value iteration can be accelerated in a general way and how fast such an accelerated method could possibly be.

The proposed algorithm, Anc-VI, introduces an anchoring mechanism distinct from Nesterov acceleration. It applies to both Bellman consistency and optimality operators and reduces Bellman error faster than standard value iteration. In the regime where gamma is approximately one, including gamma equal to one, the authors establish an O(1/k) rate. They contrast this with an O(1) rate for standard value iteration when gamma is at least 1 − 1/k.

A complexity lower bound matches the accelerated upper bound within a factor of four, establishing the rate's optimality in the studied setup. The authors also extend the acceleration benefit to approximate value iteration and Gauss–Seidel value iteration, showing that anchoring reaches beyond the basic update scheme.
summary.tldr: Anc-VI uses anchoring to accelerate Bellman-error reduction, with an optimal rate up to a constant factor in the studied setting.

title: Accelerating Value Iteration with Anchoring

abstract: Self-supervised methods received tremendous attention thanks to their seemingly heuristic approach to learning representations that respect the semantics of the data without any apparent supervision in the form of labels. A growing body of literature is already being published in an attempt to build a coherent and theoretically grounded understanding of the workings of a zoo of losses used in modern self-supervised representation learning methods. In this paper, we attempt to provide an understanding from the perspective of a Laplace operator and connect the inductive bias stemming from the augmentation process to a low-rank matrix completion problem.To this end, we leverage the results from low-rank matrix completion to provide theoretical analysis on the convergence of modern SSL methods and a key property that affects their downstream performance.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning can produce representations that reflect meaningful structure without explicit labels, yet its many loss functions can seem disconnected or heuristic. This paper develops a theoretical perspective intended to explain how such methods work. It focuses on the role of data augmentation in shaping what a learned representation is encouraged to preserve.

The authors view the problem through a Laplace operator and connect the inductive bias introduced by augmentation to low-rank matrix completion. This creates a bridge between spectral embedding and the problem of recovering a low-rank matrix. Rather than treating augmentation only as a training procedure, the analysis treats it as a source of mathematical structure in the learning problem.

Using results from low-rank matrix completion, the paper analyzes convergence of modern self-supervised methods and a key property affecting their downstream performance. The contribution is an explanatory framework linking augmentation, representation learning, and existing theory. It provides a way to investigate why the learning process converges and what influences the usefulness of the resulting features for later tasks.
summary.tldr: A Laplace-operator perspective connects augmentation-driven self-supervised learning to low-rank matrix completion and its theoretical guarantees.

title: Neural Harmonics: Bridging Spectral Embedding and Matrix Completion in Self-Supervised Learning

abstract: We show that the RandomCoordinateCut algorithm gives the optimal competitive ratio for explainable $k$-medians in $\ell_1$. The problem of explainable $k$-medians was introduced by Dasgupta, Frost, Moshkovitz, and Rashtchian in 2020. Several groups of authors independently proposed a simple polynomial-time randomized algorithm for the problem and showed that this algorithm is $O(\log k \log\log k)$ competitive. We provide a tight analysis of the algorithm and prove that its competitive ratio is upper bounded by $2\ln k+2$. This bound matches the $\Omega(\log k)$ lower bound by Dasgupta et al (2020).

The problem of explainable $k$-medians was introduced by Dasgupta, Frost, Moshkovitz, and Rashtchian in 2020. Several groups of authors independently proposed a simple polynomial-time randomized algorithm for the problem and showed that this algorithm is $O(\log k \log\log k)$ competitive. paragraphs: This paper sharpens the theoretical understanding of an existing randomized algorithm for explainable k-medians clustering under the L1 distance. The algorithm, RandomCoordinateCut, already had polynomial running time and a known performance guarantee. The question addressed here is how much clustering cost its guarantee truly requires as the number of clusters grows.

Previous analyses bounded its competitive ratio by O(log k log log k). The authors provide a tighter analysis showing an upper bound of 2 ln k + 2. This removes the extra log log k factor from the established guarantee without introducing a replacement algorithm. The advance lies in proving stronger performance for the existing procedure.

The improved bound matches a known lower bound of order log k, establishing optimality in its asymptotic dependence on the number of clusters. That does not mean the algorithm always produces an exactly optimal clustering. It means its worst-case competitive behavior has the best possible order for the stated explainable k-medians problem.
summary.tldr: A tighter analysis proves RandomCoordinateCut achieves the optimal asymptotic competitive ratio for explainable L1 k-medians.

title: Random Cuts are Optimal for Explainable k-Medians

abstract: In this paper, we empirically study the optimization dynamics of multi-task learning, particularly focusing on those that govern a collection of tasks with significant data imbalance. We present a simple yet effective method of pre-training on high-resource tasks, followed by fine-tuning on a mixture of high/low-resource tasks. We provide a thorough empirical study and analysis of this method's benefits showing that it achieves consistent improvements relative to the performance trade-off profile of standard static weighting. We analyze under what data regimes this method is applicable and show its improvements empirically in neural machine translation (NMT) and multi-lingual language modeling.

We analyze under what data regimes this method is applicable and show its improvements empirically in neural machine translation (NMT) and multi-lingual language modeling.

paragraphs: Multitask learning can involve tasks with very different amounts of training data. This paper examines how optimization behaves under substantial imbalance, focusing on multilingual learning. The central issue is how the sequence of training affects the performance tradeoffs among tasks, beyond the choice of fixed weights for mixing their data.

The proposed method uses two stages: first pretrain on tasks with abundant data, then fine-tune on a mixture of abundant-data and scarce-data tasks. This changes the composition of training over time. The authors study the method empirically and analyze the data regimes in which this ordering is applicable, connecting its usefulness to the imbalance setting.

Across neural machine translation and multilingual language modeling experiments, the approach consistently improves on the performance tradeoff profile obtained with standard static weighting. The stated result concerns those empirical comparisons rather than a guarantee for every collection of tasks. It shows that training order can be an effective design choice when balancing performance across tasks with unequal data resources.
summary.tldr: Pretraining on high-resource tasks before mixed-task fine-tuning improves evaluated multilingual performance tradeoffs under data imbalance.

title: Order Matters in the Presence of Dataset Imbalance for Multilingual Learning

abstract: Data distillation and coresets have emerged as popular approaches to generate a smaller representative set of samples for downstream learning tasks to handle large-scale datasets. At the same time, machine learning is being increasingly applied to decision-making processes at a societal level, making it imperative for modelers to address inherent biases towards subgroups present in the data. While current approaches focus on creating fair synthetic representative samples by optimizing local properties relative to the original samples, their impact on downstream learning processes has yet to be explored. In this work, we present fair Wasserstein coresets ($\texttt{FWC}$), a novel coreset approach which generates fair synthetic representative samples along with sample-level weights to be used in downstream learning tasks. $\texttt{FWC}$ uses an efficient majority minimization algorithm to minimize the Wasserstein distance between the original dataset and the weighted synthetic samples while enforcing demographic parity. We show that an unconstrained version of $\texttt{FWC}$ is equivalent to Lloyd's algorithm for k-medians and k-means clustering. Experiments conducted on both synthetic and real datasets show that $\texttt{FWC}$: (i) achieves a competitive fairness-performance tradeoff in downstream models compared to existing approaches, (ii) improves downstream fairness when added to the existing training data and (iii) can be used to reduce biases in predictions from large language models (GPT-3.5 and GPT-4).

paragraphs: A coreset is a small collection intended to represent a much larger dataset for subsequent learning. Fair Wasserstein Coresets addresses the additional goal of reducing subgroup bias in models trained with that collection. The paper focuses on downstream effects, asking whether representative synthetic data can improve the fairness of the learning process it supports.

The method generates synthetic samples together with individual sample weights. It minimizes Wasserstein distance between the original data and the weighted synthetic collection while enforcing demographic parity. This couples distributional representativeness with a fairness constraint. The authors also show that an unconstrained version connects directly to Lloyd’s algorithms for k-medians and k-means clustering, relating the approach to established representative-data methods.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show competitive fairness–performance trade-offs in downstream models. Adding the generated samples to existing training data also improves downstream fairness in the reported tests. Further experiments demonstrate reductions in prediction bias for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. These results support weighted synthetic data as a practical intervention whose effects extend beyond the fairness properties of the compressed collection itself.
summary.tldr: Fair Wasserstein Coresets creates weighted synthetic datasets that balance representativeness with fairness and improve downstream fairness in experiments.

title: Fair Wasserstein Coresets

abstract: 3D Gaussian splatting has recently emerged as a promising technique for novel view synthesis from sparse image sets, yet comes at the cost of requiring millions of 3D Gaussian primitives to reconstruct each 3D scene. This largely limits its application to resource-constrained devices and applications.Despite advances in Gaussian pruning techniques that aim to remove individual 3D Gaussian primitives, the significant reduction in primitives often fails to translate into commensurate increases in rendering speed, impeding efficiency and practical deployment. We identify that this discrepancy arises due to the overlooked impact of fragment count per Gaussian (i.e., the number of pixels each Gaussian is projected onto). To bridge this gap and meet the growing demands for efficient on-device 3D Gaussian rendering, we propose fragment pruning, an orthogonal enhancement to existing pruning methods that can significantly accelerate rendering by selectively pruning fragments within each Gaussian. Our pruning framework dynamically optimizes the pruning threshold for each Gaussian, markedly improving rendering speed and quality. Extensive experiments in both static and dynamic scenes validate the effectiveness of our approach. For instance, by integrating our fragment pruning technique with state-of-the-art Gaussian pruning methods, we achieve up to a 1.71$\times$ speedup on an edge GPU device, the Jetson Orin NX, and enhance rendering quality by an average of 0.16 PSNR on the Tanks\&Temples dataset. Our code is available at https://github.com/GATECH-EIC/Fragment-Pruning.

paragraphs: Rendering a scene with 3D Gaussian splatting can require millions of Gaussian primitives. Removing some of these primitives reduces the representation size, but rendering speed does not necessarily improve proportionally. This paper identifies an overlooked reason: each Gaussian can cover many pixels, and those individual contributions, called fragments, also determine the rendering workload.

The proposed method prunes fragments within individual Gaussians. It dynamically optimizes a separate pruning threshold for each Gaussian, allowing the renderer to discard selected pixel contributions. Because this operates within primitives, it can complement methods that remove whole Gaussians. The approach therefore targets a different source of computation from the primitive count alone.

Experiments cover both static and dynamic scenes. Combined with existing Gaussian pruning methods, fragment pruning achieves up to a 1.71-fold rendering speedup on the Jetson Orin NX edge GPU. The authors also report an average improvement of 0.16 PSNR on Tanks&Temples. These results show that reducing fragment work can improve practical rendering efficiency while also improving measured image quality in the reported evaluation.
summary.tldr: Learning which pixel contributions to prune from each Gaussian accelerates rendering and complements methods that remove entire Gaussians.

title: 3D Gaussian Rendering Can Be Sparser: Efficient Rendering via Learned Fragment Pruning

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have been analyzed from multiple perspectives, including the WL-hierarchy, which exposes limits on their expressivity to distinguish graphs. However, characterizing the class of functions that they learn has remained unresolved. We address this fundamental question for message passing GNNs under ReLU activations, i.e., the de-facto choice for most GNNs.We first show that such GNNs learn tropical rational signomial maps or continuous piecewise linear functions, establishing an equivalence with feedforward networks (FNNs). We then elucidate the role of the choice of aggregation and update functions, and derive the first general upper and lower bounds on the geometric complexity (i.e., the number of linear regions), establishing new results for popular architectures such as GraphSAGE and GIN. We also introduce and theoretically analyze several new architectures to illuminate the relative merits of the feedforward and the message passing layers, and the tradeoffs involving depth and number of trainable parameters. Finally, we also characterize the decision boundary for node and graph classification tasks.

title: What do Graph Neural Networks learn? Insights from Tropical Geometry

abstract: Unobserved discrete data are ubiquitous in many scientific disciplines, and how to learn the causal structure of these latent variables is crucial for uncovering data patterns. Most studies focus on the linear latent variable model or impose strict constraints on latent structures, which fail to address cases in discrete data involving non-linear relationships or complex latent structures. To achieve this, we explore a tensor rank condition on contingency tables for an observed variable set $\mathbf{X}_p$, showing that the rank is determined by the minimum support of a specific conditional set (not necessary in $\mathbf{X}_p$) that d-separates all variables in $\mathbf{X}_p$. By this, one can locate the latent variable through probing the rank on different observed variables set, and further identify the latent causal structure under some structure assumptions. We present the corresponding identification algorithm and conduct simulated experiments to verify the effectiveness of our method. In general, our results elegantly extend the identification boundary for causal discovery with discrete latent variables and expand the application scope of causal discovery with latent variables.

Existing approaches often focus on linear models or impose restrictive latent structures. This paper develops a way to extract information about hidden structure from tables describing observed variables.

The key result connects the tensor rank of a contingency table to the minimum support of a particular conditioning set that d-separates the observed variables. That conditioning set need not belong to the observed set being examined. The connection makes rank informative about hidden variables, allowing the method to probe different collections of observations for evidence of latent structure.

Using this result, the authors give an algorithm for identifying latent causal structure under structural assumptions. Simulated experiments support its effectiveness. The contribution expands the kinds of discrete latent-variable models that causal discovery can address. Its identification claim remains conditional on those assumptions: the rank relationship supplies a useful route to discovery, rather than guaranteeing recovery of every possible hidden causal structure from discrete observations.
summary.tldr: Tensor-rank conditions reveal discrete latent variables and enable causal-structure identification under structural assumptions.

title: Learning Discrete Latent Variable Structures with Tensor Rank Conditions

abstract: We introduce a new PAC-Bayes oracle bound for unbounded losses that extends Cramér-Chernoff bounds to the PAC-Bayesian setting. The proof technique relies on controlling the tails of certain random variables involving the Cramér transform of the loss. Our approach naturally leverages properties of Cramér-Chernoff bounds, such as exact optimization of the free parameter in many PAC-Bayes bounds. We highlight several applications of the main theorem. Firstly, we show that our bound recovers and generalizes previous results. Additionally, our approach allows working with richer assumptions that result in more informative and potentially tighter bounds. In this direction, we provide a general bound under a new *model-dependent* assumption from which we obtain bounds based on parameter norms and log-Sobolev inequalities. Notably, many of these bounds can be minimized to obtain distributions beyond the Gibbs posterior and provide novel theoretical coverage to existing regularization techniques.

It extends Cramér–Chernoff bounds into the PAC-Bayesian setting, connecting a way of controlling tail behavior with bounds that apply to distributions over models. summary.tldr: New PAC-Bayes bounds extend Cramér–Chernoff analysis to unbounded losses and support richer assumptions and model distributions.

title: PAC-Bayes-Chernoff bounds for unbounded losses

abstract: Integrating pretrained vision-language foundation models like CLIP into federated learning has attracted significant attention for enhancing generalization across diverse tasks. Typically, federated learning of vision-language models employs prompt learning to reduce communication and computational costs, i.e., prompt-based federated learning. However, there is limited theoretical analysis to understand the performance of prompt-based federated learning. In this work, we construct a theoretical analysis framework for prompt-based federated learning via feature learning theory. Specifically, we monitor the evolution of signal learning and noise memorization in prompt-based federated learning, demonstrating that performance can be assessed by the ratio of task-relevant to task-irrelevant coefficients. Furthermore, we draw an analogy between income and risk in portfolio optimization and the task-relevant and task-irrelevant terms in feature learning. Leveraging inspiration from portfolio optimization that combining two independent assets will maintain the income while reducing the risk, we introduce two prompts: global prompt and local prompt to construct a prompt portfolio to balance the generalization and personalization. Consequently, we showed the performance advantage of the prompt portfolio and derived the optimal mixing coefficient. These theoretical claims have been further supported by empirical experiments.

paragraphs: Federated learning can adapt pretrained vision-language models through prompts, reducing communication and computation. This paper asks why such adaptation succeeds or fails across diverse tasks. It develops a theoretical framework that follows two processes during learning: acquiring useful task signals and memorizing noise.

Within this framework, performance can be assessed through the ratio between coefficients associated with task-relevant and task-irrelevant information. The authors connect this distinction to portfolio optimization, where returns must be balanced against risk. That analogy motivates combining two prompts: a global prompt and a local prompt. The combination is intended to balance generalization with personalization rather than relying on either prompt alone.

The paper analyzes this prompt portfolio, demonstrates a performance advantage in its theoretical setting, and derives an optimal mixing coefficient. Experiments further support the theoretical claims. The contribution connects a practical design choice—how much global and local adaptation to combine—to an analysis of signal learning and noise memorization, providing a principled account of why a mixture can improve federated prompt learning.
summary.tldr: A theory of signal learning and noise memorization motivates combining global and local prompts for better federated vision-language adaptation.

title: Federated Learning from Vision-Language Foundation Models: Theoretical Analysis and Method

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are trained on a deluge of text data with limited quality control. As a result, LLMs can exhibit unintended or even harmful behaviours, such as leaking information, fake news or hate speech. Countermeasures, commonly referred to as preference alignment, include fine-tuning the pretrained LLMs with carefully crafted text examples of desired behaviour. Even then, empirical evidence shows preference aligned LLMs can be enticed to harmful behaviour. This so called jailbreaking of LLMs is typically achieved by adversarially modifying the input prompt to the LLM. Our paper provides theoretical insights into the phenomenon of preference alignment and jailbreaking from a statistical perspective. Under our framework, we first show that pretrained LLMs will mimic harmful behaviour if present in the training corpus. \textbf{Under that same framework, we then introduce a statistical notion of alignment, and lower-bound the jailbreaking probability, showing that it is unpreventable under reasonable assumptions.} Based on our insights, we propose an alteration to the currently prevalent alignment strategy RLHF. Specifically, we introduce a simple modification to the RLHF objective, we call \emph{E-RLHF}, that aims to increase the likelihood of safe responses. \emph{E-RLHF} brings no additional training cost, and is compatible with other methods. Empirically, we demonstrate that \emph{E-RLHF} outperforms RLHF on all alignment problems put forward by the AdvBench \citep{zou2023universal} and HarmBench project \citep{mazeika2024harmbench} without sacrificing model performance as measured by the MT-Bench project \citep{zheng2024judging}.

The paper thus combines a conditional theoretical account of persistent vulnerability with an empirically tested improvement to alignment.
summary.tldr: The paper derives unavoidable jailbreak risk under its statistical assumptions and introduces an RLHF modification that improves evaluated safety without reducing measured model performance.

title: Mission Impossible: A Statistical Perspective on Jailbreaking LLMs

abstract: Existing Video Corpus Moment Retrieval (VCMR) is limited to coarse-grained understanding that hinders precise video moment localization when given fine-grained queries. In this paper, we propose a more challenging fine-grained VCMR benchmark requiring methods to localize the best-matched moment from the corpus with other partially matched candidates. To improve the dataset construction efficiency and guarantee high-quality data annotations, we propose VERIFIED, an automatic \underline{V}id\underline{E}o-text annotation pipeline to generate captions with \underline{R}el\underline{I}able \underline{FI}n\underline{E}-grained statics and \underline{D}ynamics. Specifically, we resort to large language models (LLM) and large multimodal models (LMM) with our proposed Statics and Dynamics Enhanced Captioning modules to generate diverse fine-grained captions for each video. To filter out the inaccurate annotations caused by the LLM hallucination, we propose a Fine-Granularity Aware Noise Evaluator where we fine-tune a video foundation model with disturbed hard-negatives augmented contrastive and matching losses. With VERIFIED, we construct a more challenging fine-grained VCMR benchmark containing Charades-FIG, DiDeMo-FIG, and ActivityNet-FIG which demonstrate a high level of annotation quality. We evaluate several state-of-the-art VCMR models on the proposed dataset, revealing that there is still significant scope for fine-grained video understanding in VCMR.

paragraphs: Finding a video moment becomes harder when several candidates partly match a query and only fine details distinguish the best one. This paper builds a benchmark around that challenge. It asks retrieval systems to identify precisely matching moments across a video collection rather than succeed through coarse understanding alone.

The VERIFIED annotation pipeline uses language and multimodal models to create detailed captions covering both static content and dynamics. Because generated captions can contain hallucinations, a dedicated noise evaluator filters inaccurate annotations. That evaluator is built by fine-tuning a video foundation model with challenging disturbed negatives and contrastive and matching losses.

The pipeline produces Charades-FIG, DiDeMo-FIG, and ActivityNet-FIG, which the authors report have high annotation quality. Evaluations of several state-of-the-art retrieval models reveal substantial room for improvement on these finer distinctions. The contribution combines a scalable annotation process with benchmarks designed to test whether systems understand the particular details needed to distinguish closely competing video moments.
summary.tldr: VERIFIED generates and filters detailed video captions to build benchmarks that expose gaps in fine-grained moment retrieval.

title: VERIFIED: A Video Corpus Moment Retrieval Benchmark for Fine-Grained Video Understanding

abstract: Reconstructing a sequence of sharp images from the blurry input is crucial for enhancing our insights into the captured scene and poses a significant challenge due to the limited temporal features embedded in the image. Spike cameras, sampling at rates up to 40,000 Hz, have proven effective in capturing motion features and beneficial for solving this ill-posed problem. Nonetheless, existing methods fall into the supervised learning paradigm, which suffers from notable performance degradation when applied to real-world scenarios that diverge from the synthetic training data domain. To address these challenges, we propose the first self-supervised framework for the task of spike-guided motion deblurring. Our approach begins with the formulation of a spike-guided deblurring model that explores the theoretical relationships among spike streams, blurry images, and their corresponding sharp sequences. We subsequently develop a self-supervised cascaded framework to alleviate the issues of spike noise and spatial-resolution mismatching encountered in the deblurring model. With knowledge distillation and re-blurring loss, we further design a lightweight deblur network to generate high-quality sequences with brightness and texture consistency with the original input. Quantitative and qualitative experiments conducted on our real-world and synthetic datasets with spikes validate the superior generalization of the proposed framework. Our code, data and trained models are available at \url{https://github.com/chenkang455/S-SDM}.

paragraphs: Recovering several sharp frames from one blurred image is difficult because the image contains limited information about motion over time. Spike cameras provide an additional motion signal through sampling rates of up to 40,000 Hz. SpikeReveal uses these streams to guide reconstruction while addressing the poor real-world transfer of supervised methods trained on synthetic data.

The authors first formulate relationships among spike streams, blurred images, and the underlying sharp sequence. They then build a self-supervised cascade to handle spike noise and mismatched spatial resolution, two obstacles to using that formulation directly. This connects the reconstruction process to both the image and the accompanying temporal measurements.

Knowledge distillation and a re-blurring loss are used to develop a lightweight deblurring network that produces sequences consistent with the input’s brightness and texture. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations on real and synthetic datasets support improved generalization. The contribution is a self-supervised route to spike-guided deblurring that addresses practical sensor discrepancies while reconstructing a sequence, rather than just one sharpened image.
summary.tldr: SpikeReveal combines blurred images with spike-camera streams in a self-supervised framework that reconstructs sharp sequences and improves reported generalization.

title: SpikeReveal: Unlocking Temporal Sequences from Real Blurry Inputs with Spike Streams

abstract: Motion modeling is critical in flow-based Video Frame Interpolation (VFI). Existing paradigms either consider linear combinations of bidirectional flows or directly predict bilateral flows for given timestamps without exploring favorable motion priors, thus lacking the capability of effectively modeling spatiotemporal dynamics in real-world videos. To address this limitation, in this study, we introduce Generalizable Implicit Motion Modeling (GIMM), a novel and effective approach to motion modeling for VFI. Specifically, to enable GIMM as an effective motion modeling paradigm, we design a motion encoding pipeline to model spatiotemporal motion latent from bidirectional flows extracted from pre-trained flow estimators, effectively representing input-specific motion priors. Then, we implicitly predict arbitrary-timestep optical flows within two adjacent input frames via an adaptive coordinate-based neural network, with spatiotemporal coordinates and motion latent as inputs. Our GIMM can be easily integrated with existing flow-based VFI works by supplying accurately modeled motion. We show that GIMM performs better than the current state of the art on standard VFI benchmarks.

paragraphs: Video frame interpolation creates frames between two existing images, making motion modeling central to the task. The authors argue that existing flow-based approaches do not sufficiently exploit useful motion information when combining flows or predicting them for specific times. Their method, Generalizable Implicit Motion Modeling, aims to represent how motion varies across both space and time.

GIMM first takes bidirectional flows from pretrained flow estimators and encodes them into a motion representation tailored to the input frames. An adaptive coordinate-based neural network then receives that representation together with spatial and temporal coordinates. This allows it to predict optical flow at arbitrary intermediate timestamps between the adjacent frames.

The method supplies motion estimates to existing flow-based interpolation systems, so its contribution can be incorporated into those pipelines. The authors report better performance than the current state of the art on standard interpolation benchmarks. The findings support the usefulness of encoding input-specific motion and querying it continuously in time, rather than relying solely on simpler flow combinations or isolated timestamp predictions.
summary.tldr: GIMM encodes motion between adjacent frames and predicts intermediate optical flows through a coordinate-based network, improving benchmark interpolation performance.

title: Generalizable Implicit Motion Modeling for Video Frame Interpolation

abstract: Universal image representations are critical in enabling real-world fine-grained and instance-level recognition applications, where objects and entities from any domain must be identified at large scale.Despite recent advances, existing methods fail to capture important domain-specific knowledge, while also ignoring differences in data distribution across different domains.This leads to a large performance gap between efficient universal solutions and expensive approaches utilising a collection of specialist models, one for each domain.In this work, we make significant strides towards closing this gap, by introducing a new learning technique, dubbed UDON (Universal Dynamic Online distillatioN).UDON employs multi-teacher distillation, where each teacher is specialized in one domain, to transfer detailed domain-specific knowledge into the student universal embedding.UDON's distillation approach is not only effective, but also very efficient, by sharing most model parameters between the student and all teachers, where all models are jointly trained in an online manner.UDON also comprises a sampling technique which adapts the training process to dynamically allocate batches to domains which are learned slower and require more frequent processing.This boosts significantly the learning of complex domains which are characterised by a large number of classes and long-tail distributions.With comprehensive experiments, we validate each component of UDON, and showcase significant improvements over the state of the art in the recent UnED benchmark.Code: https://github.com/nikosips/UDON.

paragraphs: A universal image representation must distinguish objects and instances across many domains. Existing universal approaches can miss specialist knowledge and overlook differences in domain distributions, creating a performance gap relative to maintaining separate specialist models. UDON seeks to narrow that gap while preserving the efficiency advantages of a shared representation.

The method uses several domain-specialist teachers to transfer knowledge into one universal student embedding. Teachers and student share most model parameters and train jointly, making the distillation process efficient. UDON also adjusts sampling during training, assigning more batches to domains that are learning slowly and need additional attention.

This adaptive allocation particularly improves learning for complex domains with many classes and long-tailed distributions. Comprehensive experiments assess the method's components and report significant improvements over leading approaches on UnED. The findings support addressing two problems together: retaining detailed domain knowledge through teachers and allocating training effort according to differences in how quickly domains are learned.
summary.tldr: UDON combines shared-parameter specialist distillation with adaptive domain sampling to improve universal image representations efficiently.

title: UDON: Universal Dynamic Online distillatioN for generic image representations

abstract: This work studies discrete-time discounted Markov decision processes with continuous state and action spaces and addresses the inverse problem of inferring a cost function from observed optimal behavior. We first consider the case in which we have access to the entire expert policy and characterize the set of solutions to the inverse problem by using occupation measures, linear duality, and complementary slackness conditions. To avoid trivial solutions and ill-posedness, we introduce a natural linear normalization constraint. This results in an infinite-dimensional linear feasibility problem, prompting a thorough analysis of its properties. Next, we use linear function approximators and adopt a randomized approach, namely the scenario approach and related probabilistic feasibility guarantees, to derive $\varepsilon$-optimal solutions for the inverse problem. We further discuss the sample complexity for a desired approximation accuracy. Finally, we deal with the more realistic case where we only have access to a finite set of expert demonstrations and a generative model and provide bounds on the error made when working with samples.
