paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning asks which cost function could explain an expert's observed optimal behavior. This paper studies that question for discrete-time, discounted Markov decision processes with continuous states and actions. It first considers access to the entire expert policy, allowing a mathematical characterization of the possible cost functions.

Using occupation measures, linear duality, and complementary slackness, the authors express the inverse problem as an infinite-dimensional linear feasibility problem. They add a linear normalization constraint to avoid trivial solutions and ill-posedness. This step matters because explaining observed behavior requires a meaningful formulation of the admissible costs, rather than merely finding any formally compatible function.

The authors then combine linear function approximators with randomized scenario methods to obtain approximately optimal solutions with probabilistic feasibility guarantees. They analyze the sample complexity needed for a desired approximation accuracy. Finally, they address the more realistic setting of finitely many expert demonstrations plus access to a generative model, providing bounds on the error introduced by using samples.
summary.tldr: The paper develops randomized methods and probabilistic error guarantees for inferring costs from optimal behavior in continuous state and action spaces.

title: Randomized algorithms and PAC bounds for inverse reinforcement learning in continuous spaces

abstract: Dataset condensation, a concept within $\textit{data-centric learning}$, aims to efficiently transfer critical attributes from an original dataset to a synthetic version, meanwhile maintaining both diversity and realism of syntheses. This approach can significantly improve model training efficiency and is also adaptable for multiple application areas. Previous methods in dataset condensation have faced several challenges: some incur high computational costs which limit scalability to larger datasets ($\textit{e.g.,}$ MTT, DREAM, and TESLA), while others are restricted to less optimal design spaces, which could hinder potential improvements, especially in smaller datasets ($\textit{e.g.,}$ SRe$^2$L, G-VBSM, and RDED). To address these limitations, we propose a comprehensive designing-centric framework that includes specific, effective strategies like implementing soft category-aware matching, adjusting the learning rate schedule and applying small batch-size. These strategies are grounded in both empirical evidence and theoretical backing. Our resulting approach, $\textbf{E}$lucidate $\textbf{D}$ataset $\textbf{C}$ondensation ($\textbf{EDC}$), establishes a benchmark for both small and large-scale dataset condensation. In our testing, EDC achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, reaching 48.6% on ImageNet-1k with a ResNet-18 model at an IPC of 10, which corresponds to a compression ratio of 0.78\%. This performance surpasses those of SRe$^2$L, G-VBSM, and RDED by margins of 27.3%, 17.2%, and 6.6%, respectively. Code is available at: https://github.com/shaoshitong/EDC.

They report that this outperforms the compared condensation methods. summary.tldr: EDC improves dataset condensation through coordinated matching and training choices, reporting strong accuracy with heavily compressed synthetic datasets.

title: Elucidating the Design Space of Dataset Condensation

abstract: Domain generalization (DG) methods aim to maintain good performance in an unseen target domain by using training data from multiple source domains. While success on certain occasions are observed, enhancing the baseline across most scenarios remains challenging. This work introduces a simple yet effective framework, dubbed learning from multiple experts (LFME), that aims to make the target model an expert in all source domains to improve DG. Specifically, besides learning the target model used in inference, LFME will also train multiple experts specialized in different domains, whose output probabilities provide professional guidance by simply regularizing the logit of the target model. Delving deep into the framework, we reveal that the introduced logit regularization term implicitly provides effects of enabling the target model to harness more information, and mining hard samples from the experts during training. Extensive experiments on benchmarks from different DG tasks demonstrate that LFME is consistently beneficial to the baseline and can achieve comparable performance to existing arts. Code is available at https://github.com/liangchen527/LFME.

paragraphs: Domain generalization aims to train on several source domains and still perform well on an unseen target domain. Improving on a straightforward baseline across many settings remains difficult. LFME approaches this by training a target model to absorb expertise from all the available source domains, using specialist models to guide its learning.

Alongside the target model, LFME trains experts that specialize in different domains. Their output probabilities regularize the target model's logits, the scores it produces before converting them into probabilities. The target model remains the model used at inference. This arrangement allows domain-specific expertise to influence training through a relatively simple additional objective.

The authors' analysis finds that this regularization helps the target model use more information and implicitly emphasizes difficult samples identified through the experts. Experiments across benchmarks for different domain-generalization tasks show consistent benefits over the baseline and performance comparable to existing methods. The findings support learning broadly useful behavior through coordinated specialist guidance, with the benefit demonstrated across the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: LFME uses domain-specialist predictions to regularize one target model, improving domain-generalization baselines across evaluated tasks.

title: LFME: A Simple Framework for Learning from Multiple Experts in Domain Generalization

abstract: Kernel techniques are among the most influential approaches in data science and statistics. Under mild conditions, the reproducing kernel Hilbert space associated to a kernel is capable of encoding the independence of $M\ge2$ random variables. Probably the most widespread independence measure relying on kernels is the so-called Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion (HSIC; also referred to as distance covariance in the statistics literature). Despite various existing HSIC estimators designed since its introduction close to two decades ago, the fundamental question of the rate at which HSIC can be estimated is still open. In this work, we prove that the minimax optimal rate of HSIC estimation on $\mathbb{R}^d$ for Borel measures containing the Gaussians with continuous bounded translation-invariant characteristic kernels is $\mathcal{O}\left(n^{-1/2}\right)$. Specifically, our result implies the optimality in the minimax sense of many of the most-frequently used estimators (including the U-statistic, the V-statistic, and the Nyström-based one) on $\mathbb{R}^d$.

paragraphs: The Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion, or HSIC, is a kernel-based measure used to study statistical independence. Many estimators already exist, but this paper addresses a more fundamental question: how quickly can any estimator approach the true value as the number of observations grows? Answering this establishes a benchmark for judging existing estimation methods.

The authors prove a minimax optimal estimation rate of order n to the power of minus one-half. The result applies on Euclidean space to classes of Borel probability measures containing Gaussian distributions, using kernels that are continuous, bounded, translation-invariant, and characteristic. These conditions define the scope of the theorem rather than a claim about every possible kernel or distribution class.

Minimax optimality concerns the best achievable worst-case rate over the stated class. The result implies that several frequently used methods, including U-statistic, V-statistic, and Nyström-based estimators, already attain that rate. Its contribution is to establish a fundamental statistical limit and show that familiar estimators meet it under the specified assumptions.
summary.tldr: The paper proves an optimal n⁻¹ᐟ² worst-case rate for HSIC estimation under specified kernel and distribution assumptions, validating several common estimators.

title: The Minimax Rate of HSIC Estimation for Translation-Invariant Kernels

abstract: A primary challenge for visual-based Reinforcement Learning (RL) is to generalize effectively across unseen environments. Although previous studies have explored different auxiliary tasks to enhance generalization, few adopt image reconstruction due to concerns about exacerbating overfitting to task-irrelevant features during training. Perceiving the pre-eminence of image reconstruction in representation learning, we propose SMG (\blue{S}eparated \blue{M}odels for \blue{G}eneralization), a novel approach that exploits image reconstruction for generalization. SMG introduces two model branches to extract task-relevant and task-irrelevant representations separately from visual observations via cooperatively reconstruction. Built upon this architecture, we further emphasize the importance of task-relevant features for generalization. Specifically, SMG incorporates two additional consistency losses to guide the agent's focus toward task-relevant areas across different scenarios, thereby achieving free from overfitting. Extensive experiments in DMC demonstrate the SOTA performance of SMG in generalization, particularly excelling in video-background settings. Evaluations on robotic manipulation tasks further confirm the robustness of SMG in real-world applications. Source code is available at \url{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SMG/}.

paragraphs: An agent learning from images can become attached to visual details that do not help it perform its task. This makes generalization to unfamiliar environments difficult. Image reconstruction could help learn useful representations, but reconstructing an entire observation also encourages attention to irrelevant backgrounds. The paper develops SMG to make reconstruction useful despite that tension.

SMG separates visual processing into two branches intended to capture task-relevant and task-irrelevant information. The branches cooperate to reconstruct the observation, allowing reconstruction to use both kinds of information without requiring a single representation to serve every purpose. Two additional consistency losses encourage the agent to focus on task-relevant regions across different scenarios and reduce overfitting.

Experiments in DMC report state-of-the-art generalization, with particularly strong results when video backgrounds change. Evaluations on robotic manipulation tasks also support the method's robustness in real-world applications. The findings suggest that image reconstruction can support visual control when the representation explicitly separates information needed for action from other information needed to explain the image.
summary.tldr: SMG separates task-relevant and irrelevant visual information so reconstruction training can improve reinforcement learning generalization.

title: Focus On What Matters: Separated Models For Visual-Based RL Generalization

abstract: Causal discovery with time series data remains a challenging yet increasingly important task across many scientific domains. Convergent cross mapping (CCM) and related methods have been proposed to study time series that are generated by dynamical systems, where traditional approaches like Granger causality are unreliable. However, CCM often yields inaccurate results depending upon the quality of the data. We propose the Tangent Space Causal Inference (TSCI) method for detecting causalities in dynamical systems. TSCI works by considering vector fields as explicit representations of the systems' dynamics and checks for the degree of synchronization between the learned vector fields. The TSCI approach is model-agnostic and can be used as a drop-in replacement for CCM and its generalizations. We first present a basic version of the TSCI algorithm, which is shown to be more effective than the basic CCM algorithm with very little additional computation. We additionally present augmented versions of TSCI that leverage the expressive power of latent variable models and deep learning. We validate our theory on standard systems, and we demonstrate improved causal inference performance across a number of benchmark tasks.

paragraphs: Tangent Space Causal Inference, or TSCI, seeks causal relationships in time series generated by dynamical systems. Such settings can make traditional approaches like Granger causality unreliable. Convergent cross mapping is an alternative, but its results can become inaccurate depending on data quality. TSCI introduces a different way to examine the systems' dynamics.

The method learns vector fields that explicitly represent how the systems evolve and checks the degree of synchronization between those fields. This makes the dynamics themselves central to the causal comparison. TSCI is model-agnostic and can replace convergent cross mapping or its generalizations within the intended workflow.

The basic algorithm is more effective than basic convergent cross mapping with very little extra computation. The authors also introduce versions that use latent-variable models and deep learning for greater expressive power. Tests on standard systems validate the theory, and benchmark evaluations show improved causal inference performance. The findings support comparing learned dynamical behavior as a useful approach to causal discovery in these time-series settings.
summary.tldr: TSCI detects causal relationships in dynamical systems by measuring synchronization between learned vector fields.

title: Tangent Space Causal Inference: Leveraging Vector Fields for Causal Discovery in Dynamical Systems

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) traditionally trains agents using interaction data, which limits their capabilities to the scope of the training data. To create more knowledgeable agents, leveraging knowledge from large language models (LLMs) has shown a promising way. Despite various attempts to combine LLMs with RL, there is commonly a semantic gap between action signals and LLM tokens, which hinders their integration. This paper introduces a novel approach, KALM (Knowledgeable Agents from Language Model Rollouts), to learn knowledgeable agents by bridging this gap. KALM extracts knowledge from LLMs in the form of imaginary rollouts, which agents can learn through offline RL. To overcome the limitation that LLMs are inherently text-based and may be incompatible with numerical environmental data, KALM fine-tunes the LLM to perform bidirectional translation between textual goals and rollouts. This process enables the LLM to understand the environment better, facilitating the generation of meaningful rollouts. Experiments on robotic manipulation tasks demonstrate that KALM allows agents to rephrase complex goals and tackle novel tasks requiring new optimal behaviors. KALM achieves a 46% success rate in completing 1400 various novel goals, significantly outperforming the 26% success rate of baseline methods. Project homepage: https://kalmneurips2024.github.io.

paragraphs: KALM aims to transfer knowledge from language models into reinforcement-learning agents through imagined interaction sequences, or rollouts. The obstacle is a mismatch between language tokens and the numerical signals used to describe environments and actions. Without a way to connect these representations, a language model's knowledge is difficult for an agent to learn from.

The method fine-tunes a language model to translate in both directions between textual goals and rollouts. This training helps the model connect task descriptions with environmental behavior and generate meaningful imagined sequences. An agent then learns from those sequences using offline reinforcement learning, turning language-model outputs into training material for action selection.

Experiments in robotic manipulation show agents handling rephrased complex goals and novel tasks that require new optimal behaviors. Across 1,400 novel goals, KALM achieves a 46% success rate compared with 26% for baseline methods. These results support the proposed translation-and-rollout mechanism as a way to expand agent capabilities in the tested setting by drawing on language-model knowledge.
summary.tldr: KALM trains agents offline on language-model-generated rollouts, improving success on novel robotic goals in its reported experiments.

title: KALM: Knowledgeable Agents by Offline Reinforcement Learning from Large Language Model Rollouts

abstract: Image pyramids are commonly used in modern computer vision tasks to obtain multi-scale features for precise understanding of images. However, image pyramids process multiple resolutions of images using the same large-scale model, which requires significant computational cost. To overcome this issue, we propose a novel network architecture known as the Parameter-Inverted Image Pyramid Networks (PIIP). Our core idea is to use models with different parameter sizes to process different resolution levels of the image pyramid, thereby balancing computational efficiency and performance. Specifically, the input to PIIP is a set of multi-scale images, where higher resolution images are processed by smaller networks. We further propose a feature interaction mechanism to allow features of different resolutions to complement each other and effectively integrate information from different spatial scales. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the PIIP achieves superior performance in tasks such as object detection, segmentation, and image classification, compared to traditional image pyramid methods and single-branch networks, while reducing computational cost. Notably, when applying our method on a large-scale vision foundation model InternViT-6B, we improve its performance by 1\%-2\% on detection and segmentation with only 40\%-60\% of the original computation. These results validate the effectiveness of the PIIP approach and provide a new technical direction for future vision computing tasks.

summary.tldr: PIIP pairs higher-resolution images with smaller networks and exchanges features across scales to improve vision performance with less computation.

title: Parameter-Inverted Image Pyramid Networks

abstract: Buildings play a crucial role in human well-being, influencing occupant comfort, health, and safety.Additionally, they contribute significantly to global energy consumption, accounting for one-third of total energy usage, and carbon emissions.Optimizing building performance presents a vital opportunity to combat climate change and promote human flourishing.However, research in building analytics has been hampered by the lack of accessible, available, and comprehensive real-world datasets on multiple building operations.In this paper, we introduce the Building TimeSeries (BTS) dataset.Our dataset covers three buildings over a three-year period, comprising more than ten thousand timeseries data points with hundreds of unique ontologies.Moreover, the metadata is standardized using the Brick schema.To demonstrate the utility of this dataset, we performed benchmarks on two tasks: timeseries ontology classification and zero-shot forecasting.These tasks represent an essential initial step in addressing challenges related to interoperability in building analytics.Access to the dataset and the code used for benchmarking are available here: https://github.com/cruiseresearchgroup/DIEF\_BTS

paragraphs: Building operations affect occupant comfort, health, and safety, while buildings account for roughly one-third of global energy use. Improving their performance therefore has both human and environmental value. Research toward that goal has been constrained by limited access to comprehensive real-world data covering multiple aspects of building operation.

The Building TimeSeries dataset addresses this gap with observations from three buildings over three years. The authors describe more than ten thousand timeseries data points and hundreds of unique ontologies. Metadata follows the Brick schema, giving the data a standardized descriptive structure. This matters for interoperability: building analytics must work with the meanings of measurements as well as their numerical values.

The paper demonstrates the dataset through benchmarks for timeseries ontology classification and zero-shot forecasting. These examine identifying the kinds of recorded series and forecasting in a zero-shot setting. The authors position the benchmarks as an initial step toward resolving interoperability challenges, with the dataset and benchmarking code available to support further building analytics research.
summary.tldr: BTS provides three years of operational data from three buildings, standardized metadata, and benchmarks for classification and zero-shot forecasting.

title: Building Timeseries Dataset: Empowering Large-Scale Building Analytics

abstract: In this paper, we present Language Model as Visual Explainer (\texttt{LVX}), a systematic approach for interpreting the internal workings of vision models using a tree-structured linguistic explanation, without the need for model training. Central to our strategy is the collaboration between vision models and LLM to craft explanations. On one hand, the LLM is harnessed to delineate hierarchical visual attributes, while concurrently, a text-to-image API retrieves images that are most aligned with these textual concepts. By mapping the collected texts and images to the vision model's embedding space, we construct a hierarchy-structured visual embedding tree. This tree is dynamically pruned and grown by querying the LLM using language templates, tailoring the explanation to the model. Such a scheme allows us to seamlessly incorporate new attributes while eliminating undesired concepts based on the model's representations. When applied to testing samples, our method provides human-understandable explanations in the form of attribute-laden trees. Beyond explanation, we retrained the vision model by calibrating it on the generated concept hierarchy, allowing the model to incorporate the refined knowledge of visual attributes. To access the effectiveness of our approach, we introduce new benchmarks and conduct rigorous evaluations, demonstrating its plausibility, faithfulness, and stability.

paragraphs: LVX explains vision models using trees of linguistic attributes. The explanation method does not require model training. It connects language-generated concepts to the vision model's own representations, aiming to produce explanations that people can understand while remaining tied to how the particular model represents visual information.

An LLM proposes hierarchical visual attributes, and a text-to-image API supplies images aligned with those concepts. The collected text and images are mapped into the vision model's embedding space to form a visual embedding tree. Further LLM queries grow or prune that tree, adding useful attributes and removing unwanted concepts according to the model's representations.

For test samples, the resulting explanations take the form of attribute-rich trees. The authors also investigate a separate retraining application, calibrating a vision model on the generated hierarchy so it can incorporate the visual attribute knowledge. New benchmarks and evaluations support the explanations' plausibility, faithfulness, and stability. The training-free explanation process and the additional retraining application serve distinct purposes.
summary.tldr: LVX builds and adapts linguistic attribute trees to explain vision models without training the explanation model.

title: Language Model as Visual Explainer

abstract: Current state-of-the-art synchrony-based models encode object bindings with complex-valued activations and compute with real-valued weights in feedforward architectures. We argue for the computational advantages of a recurrent architecture with complex-valued weights. We propose a fully convolutional autoencoder, SynCx, that performs iterative constraint satisfaction: at each iteration, a hidden layer bottleneck encodes statistically regular configurations of features in particular phase relationships; over iterations, local constraints propagate and the model converges to a globally consistent configuration of phase assignments. Binding is achieved simply by the matrix-vector product operation between complex-valued weights and activations, without the need for additional mechanisms that have been incorporated into current synchrony-based models. SynCx outperforms or is strongly competitive with current models for unsupervised object discovery. SynCx also avoids certain systematic grouping errors of current models, such as the inability to separate similarly colored objects without additional supervision.

paragraphs: Unsupervised object discovery requires a model to group image features into distinct objects without object labels. Synchrony-based approaches represent these groupings through phase relationships in complex-valued activations. SynCx extends this idea by using complex-valued weights and a recurrent architecture, allowing the representation to be revised over multiple iterations.

The model is a fully convolutional autoencoder whose hidden bottleneck captures regular arrangements of features in particular phase relationships. Repeated updates propagate local constraints until the phase assignments form a globally consistent configuration. Object binding happens through multiplication between complex-valued weights and activations, avoiding the additional binding mechanisms used by existing synchrony-based approaches.

The authors report that SynCx outperforms or remains strongly competitive with current models on unsupervised object discovery. It also avoids certain systematic grouping errors, including difficulty separating similarly colored objects without extra supervision. The findings support recurrence and complex-valued computation as useful ingredients for coordinating local feature groupings into coherent object representations.
summary.tldr: SynCx uses recurrent complex-valued computation to discover objects and avoid grouping errors such as merging similarly colored objects.

title: Recurrent Complex-Weighted Autoencoders for Unsupervised Object Discovery

abstract: This paper presents a real-time generative drawing system that interprets and integrates both formal intent—the structural, compositional, and stylistic attributes of a sketch—and contextual intent—the semantic and thematic meaning inferred from its visual content - into a unified transformation process. Unlike conventional text-prompt-based generative systems, which primarily capture high-level contextual descriptions, our approach simultaneously analyzes ground-level intuitive geometric features such as line trajectories, proportions, and spatial arrangement, and high-level semantic cues extracted via vision–language models. These dual intent signals are jointly conditioned in a multi-stage generation pipeline that combines contour-preserving structural control with style and content-aware image synthesis. Implemented with a touchscreen-based interface and distributed inference architecture, the system achieves low-latency, two-stage transformation while supporting multi-user collaboration on shared canvases. The resulting platform enables participants, regardless of artistic expertise, to engage in synchronous, co-authored visual creation, redefining human–AI interaction as a process of co-creation and mutual enhancement.

paragraphs: This drawing system interprets both how a sketch is constructed and what its content means. The paper calls these formal and contextual intent. Formal intent includes structure, composition, and style; contextual intent covers semantic and thematic meaning. Combining them gives the generation process access to more of what participants express through drawing.

The system analyzes line trajectories, proportions, and spatial arrangement alongside semantic cues extracted with vision–language models. A multi-stage pipeline uses both signals, combining structural control that preserves contours with image synthesis sensitive to style and content. The sketch therefore provides geometric guidance as well as information about the intended subject.

A touchscreen interface and distributed inference architecture support a low-latency, two-stage transformation process. Multiple participants can work together on shared canvases, enabling synchronous visual co-creation across levels of artistic expertise. The contribution connects interpretation of the drawing with the practical interaction system, allowing users’ marks and shared participation to guide generated imagery in real time.
summary.tldr: A real-time collaborative drawing system combines sketch geometry and semantic meaning to guide AI transformations on shared canvases.

title: Real-Time Intuitive AI Drawing System for Collaboration: Enhancing Human Creativity through Formal and Contextual Intent Integration

abstract: Human experts employ diverse strategies to complete a task, producing to multi-modal demonstration data. Although traditional Adversarial Imitation Learning (AIL) methods have achieved notable success, they often collapse theses multi-modal behaviors into a single strategy, failing to replicate expert behaviors. To overcome this limitation, we propose DPAIL, an adversarial IL framework that leverages diffusion models as a policy class to enhance expressiveness. Building on the Adversarial Soft Advantage Fitting (ASAF) framework, which removes the need for policy optimization steps, DPAIL trains a diffusion policy using a binary cross-entropy objective to distinguish expert trajectories from generated ones. To enable optimization of the diffusion policy, we introduce a novel, tractable lower bound on the policy's likelihood. Through comprehensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations against various baselines, we demonstrate that our method not only captures diverse behaviors but also remains robust as the number of behavior modes increases.

paragraphs: Expert demonstrations can contain several valid strategies for accomplishing the same task. An imitation learner that compresses these demonstrations into a single behavior loses part of what the experts show. DPAIL addresses this problem by using a diffusion model as its policy, giving the learner a more expressive way to represent multiple behavior modes.

The method builds on Adversarial Soft Advantage Fitting, which removes the need for separate policy optimization steps. DPAIL trains its diffusion policy with a binary cross-entropy objective that distinguishes expert trajectories from generated trajectories. To make this training tractable, the authors derive a lower bound on the policy's likelihood that can be optimized within the framework.

Quantitative and qualitative evaluations show that DPAIL captures diverse behaviors and remains robust as the number of behavior modes increases. The findings support the combination of an expressive diffusion policy with an adversarial training objective that avoids a separate policy optimization stage. The main benefit is preserving the variety present in demonstrations while keeping the learning formulation workable.
summary.tldr: DPAIL learns diverse expert behaviors with a diffusion policy trained adversarially, without requiring separate policy optimization steps.

title: DPAIL: Training Diffusion Policy for Adversarial Imitation Learning without Policy Optimization

abstract: Foundation models for time series analysis (TSA) have attracted significant attention. However, challenges such as training data scarcity and imbalance continue to hinder their development. Inspired by complex dynamic system theories, we design a series-symbol data generation mechanism, enabling the unrestricted creation of high-quality time series data paired with corresponding symbolic expressions. To leverage series-symbol data pairs with strong correlations, we develop SymTime, a pre-trained foundation model for enhancing time series representation using symbolic information. SymTime demonstrates competitive performance across five major TSA tasks when fine-tunes with downstream tasks, rivaling foundation models pre-trained on real-world datasets. This approach underscores the potential of series-symbol data generation and pretraining mechanisms in overcoming data scarcity and enhancing task performance. The code is available at https://github.com/wwhenxuan/SymTime.

paragraphs: Time-series foundation models face shortages and imbalances in training data. This paper addresses those problems by generating synthetic time series together with corresponding symbolic expressions. Inspired by theories of complex dynamical systems, the generation mechanism is designed to produce high-quality paired data without being restricted to an existing collection of recorded series.

The authors build SymTime, a pretrained model that uses the strong relationship between a series and its symbolic counterpart to improve time-series representations. The paired format is central: it supplies symbolic information alongside the numerical sequence during pretraining. The work therefore combines a data-generation mechanism with a model designed to benefit from the resulting pairs.

After fine-tuning on downstream tasks, SymTime achieves competitive performance across five major time-series analysis tasks, rivaling foundation models pretrained on real-world datasets. These findings support synthetic series-symbol pairs as a useful pretraining resource. They suggest that generated data and associated symbolic information can help address data scarcity while supporting performance across multiple downstream analyses.
summary.tldr: SymTime learns from synthetic time series paired with symbolic expressions and rivals real-data-pretrained models across five tasks after fine-tuning.

title: Synthetic Series-Symbol Data Generation for Time Series Foundation Models

abstract: Diffusion models have achieved state-of-the-art performance in generative modeling, yet their sampling procedures remain vulnerable to hallucinations—often stemming from inaccuracies in score approximation. In this work, we reinterpret diffusion sampling through the lens of optimization and introduce RODS (Robust Optimization–inspired Diffusion Sampler), a novel method that detects and corrects high-risk sampling steps using geometric cues from the loss landscape. RODS enforces smoother sampling trajectories and \textit{adaptively} adjusts perturbations, reducing hallucinations without retraining and at minimal additional inference cost. Experiments on AFHQv2, FFHQ, and 11k-hands demonstrate that RODS maintains comparable image quality and preserves generation diversity. More importantly, it improves both sampling fidelity and robustness, detecting over 70\% of hallucinated samples and correcting more than 25\%, all while avoiding the introduction of new artifacts. We release our code at https://github.com/Yiqi-Verna-Tian/RODS.

paragraphs: Diffusion generators can produce hallucinated image content when inaccuracies in their score estimates affect the sampling process. RODS addresses this at generation time by interpreting diffusion sampling as an optimization process. It uses geometric information from the loss landscape to identify steps where the evolving sample is at elevated risk of developing such errors.

The sampler then corrects risky steps by encouraging smoother trajectories and adapting perturbations along the way. Because these changes operate within sampling, the method does not require retraining the generator. The authors also report only a small additional inference cost, making the intervention relevant to models that have already been trained.

Experiments on AFHQv2, FFHQ, and 11k-hands report detection of more than 70% of hallucinated samples and correction of more than 25%. In these evaluations, RODS maintains comparable image quality and generation diversity while improving fidelity and robustness without introducing new artifacts. The findings support using the geometry of the generation process as both a warning signal and a basis for targeted correction.
summary.tldr: RODS uses loss-landscape geometry to detect and correct risky diffusion-sampling steps without retraining the generator.

title: RODS: Robust Optimization Inspired Diffusion Sampling for Detecting and Reducing Hallucination in Generative Models

abstract: Scaling laws for large language models (LLMs) predict model performance based on parameters like size and training data. However, differences in training configurations and data processing across model families lead to significant variations in benchmark performance, making it difficult for a single scaling law to generalize across all LLMs. On the other hand, training family-specific scaling laws requires training models of varying sizes for every family. In this work, we propose Skills Scaling Laws (SSLaws, pronounced as Sloth), a novel scaling law that leverages publicly available benchmark data and assumes LLM performance is driven by low-dimensional latent skills, such as reasoning and instruction following. These latent skills are influenced by computational resources like model size and training tokens, but with varying efficiencies across model families. Sloth exploits correlations across benchmarks to provide more accurate and interpretable predictions while alleviating the need to train multiple LLMs per family. We present both theoretical results on parameter identification and empirical evaluations on 12 prominent benchmarks, from Open LLM Leaderboard v1/v2, demonstrating that Sloth predicts LLM performance accurately and offers insights into scaling behaviors for complex downstream tasks, increased test-time compute, and compute-optimal scaling of skills.

paragraphs: Predicting language model performance from size and training data becomes difficult when model families use different training recipes. A single scaling law may miss these differences, while fitting a separate law for every family can require training several model sizes. Sloth seeks to reduce that burden by using publicly available benchmark results.

The method assumes that benchmark performance reflects a small set of underlying skills, such as reasoning and instruction following. Model size and training tokens influence these skills, but different families develop them with different efficiencies. Correlations among benchmarks help connect observed scores to shared skills, giving predictions a more interpretable structure than treating every benchmark independently.

The authors provide theoretical results on identifying the model’s parameters and evaluate predictions on 12 benchmarks from Open LLM Leaderboard v1 and v2. They report accurate predictions and insights into downstream-task scaling, additional inference-time computation, and compute-efficient skill development. The central contribution is a shared skill-based account of performance that still accommodates differences among model families.
summary.tldr: Sloth predicts performance across language model families by modeling shared latent skills with family-specific scaling efficiencies.

title: Sloth: scaling laws for LLM skills to predict multi-benchmark performance across families

abstract: The molecular large language models have garnered widespread attention due to their promising potential on molecular applications. However, current molecular large language models face significant limitations in understanding molecules due to inadequate textual descriptions and suboptimal molecular representation strategies during pretraining. To address these challenges, we introduce KnowMol-100K, a large-scale dataset with 100K fine-grained molecular annotations across multiple levels, bridging the gap between molecules and textual descriptions. Additionally, we propose chemically-informative molecular representation, effectively addressing limitations in existing molecular representation strategies. Building upon these innovations, we develop KnowMol, a state-of-the-art multi-modal molecular large language model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that KnowMol achieves superior performance across molecular understanding and generation tasks.

paragraphs: KnowMol addresses two weaknesses in molecular language model pretraining: textual descriptions that do not explain molecules adequately, and molecular representations that do not convey chemical information effectively enough. These weaknesses concern both sides of connecting a molecule to language. The paper develops a dataset and a representation approach to strengthen that connection.

KnowMol-100K contains 100,000 fine-grained molecular annotations covering multiple levels of chemical knowledge. The annotations provide richer links between molecules and their textual descriptions. Alongside this dataset, the authors introduce a chemically informative molecular representation designed to address shortcomings in existing representation strategies. The two contributions supply complementary forms of information for building the model.

The resulting multimodal model, KnowMol, combines these developments. The authors report superior performance across molecular understanding and generation tasks in extensive experiments. The findings support the value of improving both chemical descriptions and molecular encoding during model development. The contribution therefore extends beyond a model alone: it includes a resource for molecular annotation and a way to represent molecules for learning.
summary.tldr: KnowMol combines 100,000 detailed molecular annotations with chemically informative representations to improve molecular understanding and generation.

title: KnowMol: Advancing Molecular Large Language Models with Multi-Level Chemical Knowledge

abstract: Interpreting deep neural networks through concept-based explanations offers a bridge between low-level features and high-level human-understandable semantics. However, existing automatic concept discovery methods often fail to align these extracted concepts with the model’s true decision-making process, thereby compromising explanation faithfulness. In this work, we propose FACE (Faithful Automatic Concept Extraction), a novel framework that combines Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) with a Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence regularization term to ensure alignment between the model’s original and concept-based predictions. Unlike prior methods that operate solely on encoder activations, FACE incorporates classifier supervision during concept learning, enforcing predictive consistency and enabling faithful explanations. We provide theoretical guarantees showing that minimizing the KL divergence bounds the deviation in predictive distributions, thereby promoting faithful local linearity in the learned concept space. Systematic evaluations on ImageNet, COCO, and CelebA datasets demonstrate that FACE outperforms existing methods across faithfulness and sparsity metrics.

paragraphs: Concept-based explanations describe a network using higher-level ideas instead of only its low-level features. However, concepts extracted from internal activations may not reflect the decisions the classifier actually makes. FACE addresses this mismatch by making agreement with the original model part of the concept-learning objective.

The method combines non-negative matrix factorization with a Kullback-Leibler divergence regularizer. Factorization provides a concept representation, while the regularizer encourages predictions from that representation to match the model's original predictions. Classifier supervision therefore helps determine which concepts are learned, rather than leaving concept discovery dependent solely on encoder activations. The goal is an explanation whose predictive behavior remains aligned with the system being explained.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees connecting lower KL divergence with bounded differences between predictive distributions, supporting faithful local linearity in concept space. Evaluations on ImageNet, COCO, and CelebA report better faithfulness and sparsity than existing methods. Together, these results support learning compact concept explanations with an explicit predictive-consistency requirement, so that understandable structure remains connected to model behavior.
summary.tldr: FACE learns concept explanations with classifier supervision and predictive-consistency regularization, improving reported faithfulness and sparsity.

title: FACE: Faithful Automatic Concept Extraction

abstract: Algorithmic fairness has emerged as a central issue in ML, and it has become standard practice to adjust ML algorithms so that they will satisfy fairness requirements such as Equal Opportunity. In this paper we consider the effects of adopting such fair classifiers on the overall level of _ecosystem fairness_. Specifically, we introduce the study of fairness with competing firms, and demonstrate the failure of fair classifiers in yielding fair ecosystems. Our results quantify the loss of fairness in systems, under a variety of conditions, based on classifiers' correlation and the level of their data overlap. We show that even if competing classifiers are individually fair, the ecosystem's outcome may be unfair; and that adjusting biased algorithms to improve their individual fairness may lead to an overall decline in ecosystem fairness. In addition to these theoretical results, we also provide supporting experimental evidence. Together, our model and results provide a novel and essential call for action.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether fairness requirements imposed on individual machine-learning classifiers also produce fair outcomes across competing firms. The distinction matters because people experience the combined effects of multiple decision makers. A fairness assessment of one classifier therefore addresses a different question from an assessment of the surrounding ecosystem.

The authors introduce a model of fairness under competition and analyze how ecosystem outcomes depend on relationships between classifiers. Their results quantify fairness losses under various conditions involving classifier correlation and overlap in the data they use. This makes the interaction among firms part of the fairness analysis, rather than evaluating each decision system independently.

The theoretical results show that individually fair classifiers can collectively produce unfair outcomes. They also show that improving an algorithm’s individual fairness can, under the studied conditions, reduce overall ecosystem fairness. Supporting experiments accompany the analysis. The conclusion is conditional rather than a claim that fairness adjustments always backfire: local fairness improvements do not by themselves establish that the combined system has become fairer.
summary.tldr: Individually fair classifiers can produce unfair outcomes across competing firms, and local fairness improvements can sometimes worsen ecosystem fairness.

title: Fairness under Competition

abstract: A major problem of kernel-based methods (e.g., least squares support vector machines, LS-SVMs) for solving linear/nonlinear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) is the prohibitive $O(an^3)$ ($a=1$ for linear ODEs and 27 for nonlinear ODEs) part of their computational complexity with increasing temporal discretization points $n$. We propose a novel Nyström-accelerated LS-SVMs framework that breaks this bottleneck by reformulating ODEs as primal-space constraints. Specifically, we derive for the first time an explicit Nyström-based mapping and its derivatives from one-dimensional temporal discretization points to a higher $m$-dimensional feature space ($1< m\le n$), enabling the learning process to solve linear/nonlinear equation systems with $m$-dependent complexity. Numerical experiments on sixteen benchmark ODEs demonstrate: 1) $10-6000$ times faster computation than classical LS-SVMs and physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), 2) comparable accuracy to LS-SVMs ($<0.13\%$ relative MAE, RMSE, and $\left \| y-\hat{y} \right \| _{\infty } $difference) while maximum surpassing PINNs by 72\% in RMSE, and 3) scalability to $n=10^4$ time steps with $m=50$ features. This work establishes a new paradigm for efficient kernel-based ODEs learning without significantly sacrificing the accuracy of the solution.

paragraphs: Kernel-based methods can learn solutions to ordinary differential equations, but their computational cost becomes prohibitive as the number of time points grows. For the least-squares support vector machine formulation studied here, a major cost term grows cubically with that number. This paper restructures the problem so that the equation systems depend on a chosen feature dimension.

The method derives an explicit Nyström feature mapping and its derivatives, then expresses the differential equations as constraints in primal feature space. The feature count m can be smaller than the number of time points n. This makes it possible to work with many temporal samples while solving systems whose complexity depends on the smaller representation.

Across sixteen benchmark equations, the authors report computation 10–6000 times faster than classical LS-SVMs and physics-informed neural networks, with accuracy comparable to LS-SVMs. They also report improvements over PINNs reaching 72% in RMSE and demonstrate 10,000 time steps using 50 features. These results show a substantial empirical efficiency gain without a significant loss of solution accuracy.
summary.tldr: A Nyström feature-space reformulation accelerates kernel-based ODE learning while retaining accuracy comparable to classical LS-SVMs.

title: Nyström-Accelerated Primal LS-SVMs: Breaking the $O(an^3)$ Complexity Bottleneck for Scalable ODEs Learning

abstract: Modern interactive applications increasingly demand dynamic 3D content, yet the transformation of static 3D models into animated assets constitutes a significant bottleneck in content creation pipelines. While recent advances in generative AI have revolutionized static 3D model creation, rigging and animation continue to depend heavily on expert intervention. We present \textbf{Puppeteer}, a comprehensive framework that addresses both automatic rigging and animation for diverse 3D objects. Our system first predicts plausible skeletal structures via an auto-regressive transformer that introduces a joint-based tokenization strategy for compact representation and a hierarchical ordering methodology with stochastic perturbation that enhances bidirectional learning capabilities. It then infers skinning weights via an attention-based architecture incorporating topology-aware joint attention that explicitly encodes inter-joint relationships based on skeletal graph distances. Finally, we complement these rigging advances with a differentiable optimization-based animation pipeline that generates stable, high-fidelity animations while being computationally more efficient than existing approaches. Extensive evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in both skeletal prediction accuracy and skinning quality. The system robustly processes diverse 3D content, ranging from professionally designed game assets to AI-generated shapes, producing temporally coherent animations that eliminate the jittering issues common in existing methods.

paragraphs: Creating a static 3D object does not automatically make it ready for animation. The object needs a skeleton, a mapping from that skeleton to its surface, and a procedure for generating motion. Puppeteer addresses these stages together, targeting a content-creation bottleneck that still depends heavily on specialist work.

An autoregressive transformer first predicts a plausible skeleton using a compact representation of joints. Its hierarchical ordering includes stochastic perturbations to improve bidirectional learning. An attention-based network then estimates skinning weights, which connect surface movement to the skeleton. This network explicitly represents relationships between joints using distances in the skeletal graph.

A differentiable optimization pipeline completes the system by generating stable animations more efficiently than the compared approaches. Across multiple benchmarks, Puppeteer significantly improves skeletal prediction accuracy and skinning quality over state-of-the-art techniques. It handles both professionally created game assets and AI-generated shapes, producing temporally coherent animation and eliminating the jitter reported for existing methods in the evaluation. The contribution links structural prediction and motion generation in one framework.
summary.tldr: Puppeteer automatically predicts skeletons and skinning weights, then generates efficient, temporally coherent animations for diverse 3D objects.

title: Puppeteer: Rig and Animate Your 3D Models

abstract: The advent of single-cell Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin using sequencing (scATAC-seq) offers an innovative perspective for deciphering regulatory mechanisms by assembling a vast repository of single-cell chromatin accessibility data. While foundation models have achieved significant success in single-cell transcriptomics, there is currently no foundation model for scATAC-seq that supports zero-shot high-quality cell identification and comprehensive multi-omics analysis simultaneously. Key challenges lie in the high dimensionality and sparsity of scATAC-seq data, as well as the lack of a standardized schema for representing open chromatin regions (OCRs). Here, we present ChromFound, a foundation model tailored for scATAC-seq. ChromFound utilizes a hybrid architecture and genome-aware tokenization to effectively capture genome-wide long contexts and regulatory signals from dynamic chromatin landscapes. Pretrained on 1.97 million cells from 30 tissues and 6 disease conditions, ChromFound demonstrates broad applicability across 6 diverse tasks. Notably, it achieves robust zero-shot performance in generating universal cell representations and exhibits excellent transferability in cell type annotation and cross-omics prediction. By uncovering enhancer-gene links undetected by existing computational methods, ChromFound offers a promising framework for understanding disease risk variants in the noncoding genome. The implementation of ChromFound is available via https://github.com/JohnsonKlose/ChromFound.

paragraphs: ChromFound is a foundation model for single-cell chromatin accessibility data, which records accessible regions of the genome. Such data can inform studies of gene regulation, but it is high-dimensional, sparse, and lacks a standardized representation of open chromatin regions. The paper addresses these obstacles while targeting cell identification and analysis across biological data types.

The model combines a hybrid architecture with genome-aware tokenization to capture long genomic contexts and regulatory signals. It is pretrained on 1.97 million cells spanning 30 tissues and six disease conditions. This broad training supports a shared representation intended to transfer across different analysis tasks.

Across six tasks, the authors report robust zero-shot cell representations and strong transfer to cell-type annotation and cross-omics prediction. ChromFound also uncovers enhancer-gene links missed by existing computational methods. These findings suggest that a common model of chromatin accessibility can support both cell-level characterization and investigation of regulatory relationships. The authors present it as a promising route toward understanding disease-associated variants in noncoding genomic regions.
summary.tldr: ChromFound learns transferable representations of single-cell chromatin accessibility for cell identification, cross-omics prediction, and regulatory analysis.

title: ChromFound: Towards A Universal Foundation Model for Single-Cell Chromatin Accessibiltiy Data

abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods have shown promise in adapting large language models, yet existing approaches exhibit counter-intuitive phenomena: integrating either matrix decomposition or mixture-of-experts (MoE) individually decreases performance across tasks, though decomposition improves results on specific domains despite reducing parameters, while MoE increases parameter count without corresponding decrease in training efficiency. Motivated by these observations and the modular nature of PT, we propose PT-MoE, a novel framework that integrates matrix decomposition with MoE routing for efficient PT. Evaluation results across 17 datasets demonstrate that PT-MoE achieves state-of-the-art performance in both question answering (QA) and mathematical problem solving tasks, improving F1 score by 1.49 points over PT and 2.13 points over LoRA in QA tasks, while improving mathematical accuracy by 10.75 points over PT and 0.44 points over LoRA, all while using 25% fewer parameters than LoRA. Our analysis reveals that while PT methods generally excel in QA tasks and LoRA-based methods in math datasets, the integration of matrix decomposition and MoE in PT-MoE yields complementary benefits: decomposition enables efficient parameter sharing across experts while MoE provides dynamic adaptation, collectively enabling PT-MoE to demonstrate cross-task consistency and generalization abilities. These findings, along with ablation studies on routing mechanisms and architectural components, provide insights for future PEFT methods.

title: PT-MoE: An Efficient Finetuning Framework for Integrating Mixture-of-Experts into Prompt Tuning

abstract: In non-clairvoyant scheduling, the goal is to minimize the total job completion time without prior knowledge of individual job processing times. This classical online optimization problem has recently gained attention through the framework of learning-augmented algorithms. We introduce a natural setting in which the scheduler receives continuous feedback in the form of progress bars—estimates of the fraction of each job completed over time. We design new algorithms for both adversarial and stochastic progress bars and prove strong competitive bounds. Our results in the adversarial case surprisingly induce improved guarantees for learning-augmented scheduling with job size predictions. We also introduce a general method for combining scheduling algorithms, yielding further insights in scheduling with predictions. Finally, we propose a stochastic model of progress bars as a more optimistic alternative to conventional worst-case models, and present an asymptotically optimal scheduling algorithm in this setting.

paragraphs: A scheduler may need to decide which jobs to run without knowing how long each will take. The objective here is to minimize the sum of job completion times. This paper adds a natural source of information to that setting: continuously updated progress bars that estimate the fraction of each job already completed.

The authors design algorithms for two ways of modeling that feedback. In the adversarial setting, progress information is treated through a worst-case perspective, and the algorithms receive competitive guarantees. These results also yield improved guarantees for learning-augmented scheduling based on job-size predictions. The paper additionally develops a general method for combining scheduling algorithms, contributing another tool for using predictive information.

A stochastic progress-bar model provides a more optimistic alternative to the worst-case setting. Within that model, the authors present an asymptotically optimal scheduling algorithm. The distinction between the two settings matters: the optimality claim belongs to the proposed stochastic model. Overall, the work formalizes how ongoing estimates of completion can improve scheduling even when processing times are initially unknown.
summary.tldr: The paper develops scheduling algorithms with guarantees that use continuous progress estimates despite unknown job processing times.

title: Non-Clairvoyant Scheduling with Progress Bars

abstract: When do diffusion models reproduce their training data, and when are they able to generate samples beyond it? A practically relevant theoretical understanding of this interplay between memorization and generalization may significantly impact real-world deployments of diffusion models with respect to issues such as copyright infringement and data privacy. In this paper, we propose a scientific and mathematical “laboratory” for investigating memorization and generalization in diffusion models trained on fully synthetic or natural image-like structured data. Within this setting, we theoretically characterize a crossover point wherein the weighted training loss of a fully generalizing model becomes greater than that of an underparameterized memorizing model at a critical value of model (under)parameterization. We then demonstrate via carefully-designed experiments that the location of this crossover predicts a phase transition in diffusion models trained via gradient descent, as our theory enables us to analytically predict the model size at which memorization becomes predominant. Our work provides an analytically tractable and practically meaningful setting for future theoretical and empirical investigations. Code for our experiments is available at https://github.com/DruvPai/diffusion_mem_gen.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate samples beyond their training set, but they can also reproduce training examples. This paper creates a mathematically tractable setting for studying the boundary between those behaviors. Its experimental and theoretical laboratory uses fully synthetic data or structured data resembling natural images.

Within that setting, the authors compare the weighted training loss of a fully generalizing model with that of an underparameterized model that memorizes. They characterize a critical level of model parameterization where the generalizing model's loss becomes larger. This crossover provides a concrete theoretical quantity for investigating when training may favor memorization.

Carefully designed experiments show that the predicted crossover locates a transition in diffusion models trained by gradient descent. The theory analytically predicts the model size at which memorization becomes predominant in the studied setting. The contribution is a controlled way to connect a loss-based mathematical comparison with observed training behavior, creating a foundation for further investigations into memorization and generalization relevant to privacy and copyright concerns.
summary.tldr: A controlled theoretical and experimental framework predicts when memorization becomes predominant as diffusion-model size changes.

title: On the Edge of Memorization in Diffusion Models

abstract: Foundation Vision Encoders have become indispensable across a wide range of dense vision tasks. However, their operation at low spatial feature resolutions necessitates subsequent feature decompression to enable full-resolution processing. To address this limitation, we introduce JAFAR, a lightweight and flexible feature upsampler designed to enhance the spatial resolution of visual features from any Foundation Vision Encoder to any target resolution. JAFAR features an attention-based upsampling module that aligns the spatial representations of high-resolution queries with semantically enriched low-resolution keys via Spatial Feature Transform modulation. Despite the absence of high-resolution feature ground truth; we find that learning at low upsampling ratios and resolutions generalizes surprisingly well to much higher scales. Extensive experiments demonstrate that JAFAR recovers intricate pixel-level details and consistently outperforms existing feature upsampling techniques across a diverse set of dense downstream applications.

paragraphs: Foundation vision encoders produce useful representations, but their feature maps often have low spatial resolution. Tasks that need detailed outputs across an image therefore require a way to expand those features. JAFAR is a lightweight feature upsampler designed to work with different foundation encoders and requested output resolutions.

Its attention-based module connects high-resolution queries with low-resolution keys carrying semantic information. Spatial Feature Transform modulation helps align the spatial representations involved. This arrangement aims to retain the encoder's useful semantic content while recovering the fine spatial detail needed for dense downstream processing.

The authors find that learning at relatively low resolutions and small upsampling ratios generalizes well to substantially higher scales. Across the evaluated dense vision applications, JAFAR recovers intricate pixel-level detail and consistently outperforms existing feature upsampling methods. These findings make modest-scale training relevant to higher-resolution use, while supporting a reusable component for expanding the spatial usefulness of foundation-model features.
summary.tldr: JAFAR expands low-resolution vision features into detailed spatial representations, with training at small scales generalizing to larger ones.

title: JAFAR: Jack up Any Feature at Any Resolution

abstract: Recent progress in Sign Language Translation has focussed primarily on improving the representational capacity of large language models to incorporate sign-language features. This work explores an alternative direction: enhancing the geometric properties of skeletal representations themselves. We propose Geo-Sign, a method that leverages the properties of hyperbolic geometry to model the hierarchical structure inherent in sign language kinematics. By projecting skeletal features derived from Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks (ST-GCNs) into the Poincaré ball model, we aim to create more discriminative embeddings, particularly for fine-grained motions like finger articulations. We introduce a hyperbolic projection layer, a weighted Fréchet mean aggregation scheme, and a geometric contrastive loss operating directly in hyperbolic space. These components are integrated into an end-to-end translation framework as a regularisation function, to enhance the representations within the language model. This work demonstrates the potential of hyperbolic geometry to improve skeletal representations for Sign Language Translation, improving on SOTA RGB methods while preserving privacy and improving computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Sign language translation depends on representing movement precisely, including small finger articulations. Geo-Sign focuses on the geometry of skeletal movement representations. Its motivation is that the hierarchical organization of sign-language motion may be represented effectively in hyperbolic space, giving the translation model features that better distinguish subtle movements.

The method first obtains skeletal features from spatio-temporal graph convolutional networks, which process relationships across body joints and time. These components act as regularization within an end-to-end translation framework, guiding the representations used by the language model. The authors report improvements over state-of-the-art RGB methods alongside privacy and computational-efficiency benefits. The findings support the potential of improving skeletal representation geometry as a route to better translation, complementing efforts centered on the language model's capacity.
summary.tldr: Geo-Sign uses hyperbolic geometry to structure skeletal motion features and improve sign language translation.

title: Geo-Sign: Hyperbolic Contrastive Regularisation for Geometrically Aware Sign Language Translation

abstract: Adaptive cooperation in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) requires policies to express homogeneous, specialised, or mixed behaviours, yet achieving this adaptivity remains a critical challenge. While parameter sharing (PS) is standard for efficient learning, it notoriously suppresses the behavioural diversity required for specialisation. This failure is largely due to cross-agent gradient interference, a problem we find is surprisingly exacerbated by the common practice of *coupling agent IDs with observations*. Existing remedies typically add complexity through altered objectives, manual preset diversity levels, or sequential updates -- raising a fundamental question: *can shared policies adapt without these intricacies?* We propose a solution built on a key insight: an agent-conditioned hypernetwork can generate agent-specific parameters and *decouple* observation- and agent-conditioned gradients, directly countering the interference from coupling agent IDs with observations. Our resulting method, **HyperMARL**, avoids the complexities of prior work and empirically reduces policy gradient variance. Across diverse MARL benchmarks (22 scenarios, up to 30 agents), HyperMARL achieves performance competitive with six key baselines while preserving behavioural diversity comparable to non-parameter sharing methods, establishing it as a versatile and principled approach for adaptive MARL. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/KaleabTessera/HyperMARL.

paragraphs: Cooperating agents sometimes need similar behavior and sometimes need specialized roles. These findings suggest that a shared parameter-generating mechanism can support differentiated agent policies, allowing efficient learning and specialization to coexist in the tested cooperative settings.
summary.tldr: HyperMARL generates agent-specific policy parameters with a shared hypernetwork to reduce gradient interference and preserve behavioral diversity.

title: HyperMARL: Adaptive Hypernetworks for Multi-Agent RL

abstract: Top-$k$ decoding is a widely used method for sampling from LLMs: at each token, only the largest $k$ next-token-probabilities are kept, and the next token is sampled after re-normalizing them to sum to unity. Top-$k$ and other sampling methods are motivated by the intuition that true next-token distributions are sparse, and the noisy LLM probabilities need to be truncated. However, to our knowledge, a precise theoretical motivation for the use of top-$k$ decoding is missing. In this work, we develop a theoretical framework that both explains and generalizes top-$k$ decoding. We view decoding at a fixed token as the recovery of a sparse probability distribution. We introduce *Bregman decoders* obtained by minimizing a separable Bregman divergence (for both the *primal* and *dual* cases) with a sparsity-inducing $\ell_0$-regularization; in particular, these decoders are *adaptive* in the sense that the sparsity parameter $k$ is chosen depending on the underlying token distribution. Despite the combinatorial nature of the sparse Bregman objective, we show how to optimize it efficiently for a large class of divergences. We prove that (i) the optimal decoding strategies are greedy, and further that (ii) the objective is discretely convex in $k$, such that the optimal $k$ can be identified in logarithmic time. We note that standard top-$k$ decoding arises as a special case for the KL divergence, and construct new decoding strategies with substantially different behaviors (e.g., non-linearly up-weighting larger probabilities after re-normalization).

paragraphs: Top-k decoding samples a language model's next token after retaining only its k most probable options and rescaling their probabilities. It is often motivated by the idea that model probabilities contain noise and the desired distribution has relatively few plausible tokens. This paper gives that intuition a mathematical formulation based on recovering a sparse probability distribution.

The authors introduce Bregman decoders, which balance a divergence-based measure of distribution mismatch against a penalty for keeping more tokens. They study both primal and dual formulations. These decoders can adapt the number of retained tokens to the current distribution, giving an optimization-based way to choose k instead of fixing it across all token predictions.

For a large class of divergences, the authors prove that greedy strategies solve the selection problem and that the objective is discretely convex in k, enabling logarithmic-time identification of the optimal k. Standard top-k emerges from the KL-divergence case. Other choices produce different behavior, including nonlinear increases in the weight assigned to larger probabilities, broadening the available decoding strategies.
summary.tldr: A sparse-distribution optimization framework explains top-k decoding and yields efficient alternatives that adapt how many tokens they retain.

title: Foundations of Top-$k$ Decoding for Language Models

abstract: The task of Knowlegde-Based Visual Question Answering (KB-VQA) requires the model to understand visual features and retrieve external knowledge. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) have been employed to address this problem through knowledge base querying. However, existing work demonstrate two limitations: insufficient interactivity during knowledge retrieval and ineffective organization of retrieved information for Visual-Language Model (VLM). To address these challenges, we propose a three-stage visual language model with Process, Retrieve and Filter (VLM-PRF) framework. For interactive retrieval, VLM-PRF uses reinforcement learning (RL) to guide the model to strategically process information via tool-driven operations. For knowledge filtering, our method trains the VLM to transform the raw retrieved information into into task-specific knowledge. With a dual reward as supervisory signals, VLM-PRF successfully enable model to optimize retrieval strategies and answer generation capabilities simultaneously. Experiments on two datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework.

paragraphs: Some questions about images require knowledge that the image itself does not contain. A model must understand what it sees, retrieve relevant external information, and use that information to answer. This paper identifies two weaknesses in existing retrieval-augmented approaches: retrieval is insufficiently interactive, and retrieved material is not effectively organized for the vision-language model.

VLM-PRF addresses those weaknesses with stages for processing, retrieval, and filtering. Reinforcement learning guides the model's tool-driven information processing, allowing it to learn retrieval strategies. A separate filtering capability trains the model to transform raw retrieved material into knowledge tailored to the question. The framework therefore addresses both how information is obtained and how it is prepared for answering.

Two reward signals supervise the system so that retrieval strategy and answer generation can improve together. Experiments on two datasets demonstrate the framework's effectiveness. The stated contribution is an integrated way to learn information gathering and task-specific filtering, treating retrieval as part of the model's decision process rather than a fixed preliminary step.
summary.tldr: VLM-PRF jointly improves tool-guided retrieval and answer generation while filtering external information into question-specific knowledge.

title: Knowledge-based Visual Question Answer with Multimodal Processing, Retrieval and Filtering

abstract: Hands are essential to human interaction, and exploring contact between hands and the world can promote comprehensive understanding of their function. Recently, there have been growing number of hand interaction datasets that cover interaction with object, other hand, scene, and body. Despite the significance of the task and increasing high-quality data, how to effectively learn dense hand contact estimation remains largely underexplored. There are two major challenges for learning dense hand contact estimation. First, there exists class imbalance issue from hand contact datasets where majority of regions are not in contact. Second, hand contact datasets contain spatial imbalance issue with most of hand contact exhibited in finger tips, resulting in challenges for generalization towards contacts in other hand regions. To tackle these issues, we present a framework that learns dense HAnd COntact estimation (HACO) from imbalanced data. To resolve the class imbalance issue, we introduce balanced contact sampling, which builds and samples from multiple sampling groups that fairly represent diverse contact statistics for both contact and non-contact vertices. Moreover, to address the spatial imbalance issue, we propose vertex-level class-balanced (VCB) loss, which incorporates spatially varying contact distribution by separately reweighting loss contribution of each vertex based on its contact frequency across dataset. As a result, we effectively learn to predict dense hand contact estimation with large-scale hand contact data without suffering from class and spatial imbalance issue. The codes are available at https://github.com/dqj5182/HACO_RELEASE.
