We estimate the Stein discrepancy between the data density p(x) and the model density q(x) based on a vector function of the data. We parameterize this function with a neural network and fit its parameters to maximize this discrepancy. This yields a novel goodness-of-fit test which outperforms existing methods on high dimensional data. Furthermore, optimizing q(x) to minimize this discrepancy produces a novel method for training unnormalized models. This training method can fit large unnormalized models faster than existing approaches. The ability to both learn and compare models is a unique feature of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Unnormalized density models describe relative density without requiring an explicitly normalized probability expression. This paper develops a shared method for evaluating and training such models using only the gradient of the model’s unnormalized log-density. It uses a learned Stein discrepancy to measure disagreement between the observed data distribution and the model.

The discrepancy depends on a vector-valued function evaluated on the data. The authors represent this function with a neural network and optimize it to make the discrepancy large. This learned function provides a way to expose differences between data and model, yielding a goodness-of-fit test that outperforms existing methods on high-dimensional data.

Training reverses the objective for the density model: its parameters are adjusted to reduce the discrepancy. The authors report that this procedure can fit large unnormalized models faster than existing approaches. The same discrepancy thus supports both comparison and learning, giving a common framework for detecting a model’s mismatch and then optimizing the model to reduce it.
summary.tldr: A neural-network estimate of Stein discrepancy supports both goodness-of-fit testing and faster training of large unnormalized density models.

title: Learning the Stein Discrepancy for Training and Evaluating Energy-Based Models without Sampling

abstract: We propose new multi-input shape constraints across four intuitive categories: complements, diminishers, dominance, and unimodality constraints. We show these shape constraints can be checked and even enforced when training machine-learned models for linear models, generalized additive models, and the nonlinear function class of multi-layer lattice models. Real-world experiments illustrate how the different shape constraints can be used to increase explainability and improve regularization, especially for non-IID train-test distribution shift.

Real-world experiments illustrate how the different shape constraints can be used to increase explainability and improve regularization, especially for non-IID train-test distribution shift.

Such constraints describe the shape of the model's input-output relationship and provide a way to express desired behavior during learning. The authors introduce four categories, called complements, diminishers, dominance, and unimodality, to organize these multi-input restrictions.

The contribution includes ways to check whether models satisfy the proposed constraints and to enforce them during training. The treatment covers linear models, generalized additive models, and multilayer lattice models, a nonlinear function class. This makes the constraints usable within several modeling approaches and connects descriptions of desired behavior to procedures that can maintain that behavior while fitting data.

Real-world experiments illustrate benefits for explainability and regularization, particularly when training and test data do not follow the same distribution. The results suggest that constraining relationships across inputs can help guide model behavior when the deployment distribution differs. The evidence establishes practical examples of these benefits rather than a universal improvement for every constrained model.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces enforceable multi-input shape constraints that improve explainability and regularization in evaluated applications, especially under distribution shift.

title: Multidimensional Shape Constraints

abstract: Joint filtering is a fundamental problem in computer vision with applications in many different areas. Most existing algorithms solve this problem with a weighted averaging process to aggregate input pixels. However, the weight matrix of this process is often empirically designed and not robust to complex input. In this work, we propose to learn the weight matrix for joint image filtering. This is a challenging problem, as directly learning a large weight matrix is computationally intractable. To address this issue, we introduce the correlation of deep features to approximate the aggregation weights. However, this strategy only uses inner product for the weight matrix estimation, which limits the performance of the proposed algorithm. Therefore, we further propose to learn a nonlinear function to predict sparse residuals of the feature correlation matrix. Note that the proposed method essentially factorizes the weight matrix into a low-rank and a sparse matrix and then learn both of them simultaneously with deep neural networks. Extensive experiments show that the proposed algorithm compares favorably against the state-of-the-art approaches on a wide variety of joint filtering tasks.

The choice of weights determines how information is aggregated, but hand-designed weights can struggle with complex inputs. This paper proposes learning those weights with neural networks while addressing the computational difficulty of directly predicting the full, very large weight matrix.

The first component estimates aggregation weights from correlations between learned deep features. This supplies a low-rank representation of the matrix, but relies on inner products and therefore restricts what the weights can express. The second component learns a nonlinear function that predicts sparse residual corrections to the correlation matrix. Both components are learned together.

The resulting design combines a compact low-rank component with a sparse component that adds corrections beyond feature similarity alone. This makes learning the aggregation process more tractable while addressing a limitation of the initial approximation. Across a broad collection of joint-filtering tasks, the experiments report favorable comparisons with state-of-the-art approaches, supporting the usefulness of learning both components simultaneously.
summary.tldr: The method learns joint-filtering weights through low-rank deep-feature correlations plus sparse nonlinear corrections.

title: Learning Factorized Weight Matrix for Joint Filtering

abstract: Single-objective black box optimization (also known as zeroth-order optimization) is the process of minimizing a scalar objective $f(x)$, given evaluations at adaptively chosen inputs $x$. In this paper, we consider multi-objective optimization, where $f(x)$ outputs a vector of possibly competing objectives and the goal is to converge to the Pareto frontier. Quantitatively, we wish to maximize the standard \emph{hypervolume indicator} metric, which measures the dominated hypervolume of the entire set of chosen inputs. In this paper, we introduce a novel scalarization function, which we term the \emph{hypervolume scalarization}, and show that drawing random scalarizations from an appropriately chosen distribution can be used to efficiently approximate the \emph{hypervolume indicator} metric. We utilize this connection to show that Bayesian optimization with our scalarization via common acquisition functions, such as Thompson Sampling or Upper Confidence Bound, provably converges to the whole Pareto frontier by deriving tight \emph{hypervolume regret} bounds on the order of $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$. Furthermore, we highlight the general utility of our scalarization framework by showing that any provably convergent single-objective optimization process can be converted to a multi-objective optimization process with provable convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Multi-objective black-box optimization seeks useful tradeoffs among competing objectives using only evaluations at selected inputs. Its target is the Pareto frontier, rather than a single best scalar value. This paper measures progress through the hypervolume indicator, which assesses the dominated volume covered by the full collection of selected solutions.

The authors introduce a hypervolume scalarization that converts multiple objectives into a scalar quantity. Drawing these scalarizations from an appropriately chosen distribution allows efficient approximation of the hypervolume indicator. This relationship gives a principled connection between optimizing individual scalar objectives and improving coverage of the multi-objective solution set.

It also shows how any single-objective optimization procedure with proven convergence can be converted into a multi-objective procedure with convergence guarantees, broadening the framework beyond those particular acquisition rules.
summary.tldr: Random hypervolume scalarizations turn convergent single-objective optimization into multi-objective optimization with provable Pareto-frontier convergence.

title: Random Hypervolume Scalarizations for Provable Multi-Objective Black Box Optimization

abstract: We consider the problem of learning Markov Random Fields (including the prototypical example, the Ising model) under the constraint of differential privacy. Our learning goals include both \emph{structure learning}, where we try to estimate the underlying graph structure of the model, as well as the harder goal of \emph{parameter learning}, in which we additionally estimate the parameter on each edge. We provide algorithms and lower bounds for both problems under a variety of privacy constraints – namely pure, concentrated, and approximate differential privacy. While non-privately, both learning goals enjoy roughly the same complexity, we show that this is not the case under differential privacy. In particular, only structure learning under approximate differential privacy maintains the non-private logarithmic dependence on the dimensionality of the data, while a change in either the learning goal or the privacy notion would necessitate a polynomial dependence. As a result, we show that the privacy constraint imposes a strong separation between these two learning problems in the high-dimensional data regime.

paragraphs: Learning a Markov random field can mean identifying which variables are connected or also estimating the parameters on those connections. This paper studies both goals under differential privacy, including models such as the Ising model. Its central question is how privacy changes the difficulty of recovering a model’s structure versus its numerical parameters.

The authors provide algorithms and lower bounds for pure, concentrated, and approximate differential privacy. Without privacy, structure learning and parameter learning have roughly comparable complexity. Under privacy, their dimensional dependence separates sharply: only structure learning with approximate differential privacy retains the logarithmic dependence available without privacy.

Changing either that learning goal or that privacy notion requires polynomial dependence on dimensionality in the studied setting. The distinction matters especially for high-dimensional data, where logarithmic and polynomial growth lead to very different scaling. By combining achievable algorithms with lower bounds, the paper shows that the separation reflects a fundamental privacy cost rather than merely a weakness of a particular algorithm.
summary.tldr: Differential privacy sharply separates structure and parameter learning for Markov random fields, with favorable dimensional scaling only in one studied setting.

title: Privately Learning Markov Random Fields

abstract: It is well-known that, for separable data, the regularised two-class logistic regression or support vector machine re-normalised estimate converges to the maximal margin classifier as the regularisation hyper-parameter $\lambda$ goes to 0. The fact that different loss functions may lead to the same solution is of theoretical and practical relevance as margin maximisation allows more straightforward considerations in terms of generalisation and geometric interpretation. We investigate the case where this convergence property is not guaranteed to hold and show that it can be fully characterised by the distribution of error terms in the latent variable interpretation of linear classifiers. In particular, if errors follow a regularly varying distribution, then the regularised and re-normalised estimate does not converge to the maximal margin classifier. This shows that classification with fat tails has a qualitatively different behaviour, which should be taken into account when considering real-life data.

paragraphs: For separable data, regularized logistic regression and support vector machines have a familiar limiting behavior: after renormalization, their estimates approach the maximum-margin classifier as regularization vanishes. This links different learning objectives through a shared geometric solution and helps organize reasoning about generalization.

The paper investigates when that convergence does not hold. It characterizes the behavior through the error distribution in a latent-variable interpretation of linear classifiers. This shifts attention from the apparent similarity of classification methods to the assumptions encoded by their underlying error terms.

In particular, the authors show that regularly varying error distributions prevent the regularized, renormalized estimate from converging to the maximum-margin classifier. This class of heavy-tailed errors therefore produces qualitatively different limiting behavior. The result means that maximum-margin intuition cannot automatically be carried over to such classifiers. The relevant distinction is the modeled error distribution, and the paper argues that this distinction deserves attention when choosing interpretations and methods for real data.
summary.tldr: Regularly varying latent errors break the usual convergence of regularized linear classifiers to the maximum-margin solution.

title: Narrow Margins: Classification, Margins and Fat Tails

abstract: A black-box spectral method is introduced for evaluating the adversarial robustness of a given machine learning (ML) model. Our approach, named SPADE, exploits bijective distance mapping between the input/output graphs constructed for approximating the manifolds corresponding to the input/output data. By leveraging the generalized Courant-Fischer theorem, we propose a SPADE score for evaluating the adversarial robustness of a given model, which is proved to be an upper bound of the best Lipschitz constant under the manifold setting. To reveal the most non-robust data samples highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks, we develop a spectral graph embedding procedure leveraging dominant generalized eigenvectors. This embedding step allows assigning each data point a robustness score that can be further harnessed for more effective adversarial training of ML models. Our experiments show promising empirical results for neural networks trained with the MNIST and CIFAR-10 data sets.

paragraphs: SPADE evaluates a model’s adversarial robustness through a black-box analysis of its inputs and outputs. It constructs graphs that approximate the corresponding data manifolds and studies a bijective distance mapping between them. The aim is to characterize how the model changes relationships among data points, connecting that geometry to sensitivity under perturbations.

Using the generalized Courant–Fischer theorem, the authors define a model-level SPADE score. Under the manifold setting, they prove that this score upper-bounds the best Lipschitz constant. This provides a theoretical connection between a quantity computed through spectral analysis and a measure of how strongly output changes can respond to input changes.

The method also uses dominant generalized eigenvectors to embed the graph and assign robustness scores to individual data points. These scores are intended to reveal especially vulnerable samples and can guide adversarial training. Experiments with neural networks trained on MNIST and CIFAR-10 produce promising results. The contribution therefore includes both a global robustness assessment and a way to identify where vulnerability is concentrated.
summary.tldr: SPADE uses spectral analysis of input and output graphs to score model robustness and identify samples vulnerable to adversarial attacks.

title: SPADE: A Spectral Method for Black-Box Adversarial Robustness Evaluation

abstract: Deep neural networks have emerged as very successful tools for image restoration and reconstruction tasks. These networks are often trained end-to-end to directly reconstruct an image from a noisy or corrupted measurement of that image. To achieve state-of-the-art performance, training on large and diverse sets of images is considered critical. However, it is often difficult and/or expensive to collect large amounts of training images. Inspired by the success of Data Augmentation (DA) for classification problems, in this paper, we propose a pipeline for data augmentation for accelerated MRI reconstruction and study its effectiveness at reducing the required training data in a variety of settings. Our DA pipeline, MRAugment, is specifically designed to utilize the invariances present in medical imaging measurements as naive DA strategies that neglect the physics of the problem fail. Through extensive studies on multiple datasets we demonstrate that in the low-data regime DA prevents overfitting and can match or even surpass the state of the art while using significantly fewer training data, whereas in the high-data regime it has diminishing returns. Furthermore, our findings show that DA improves the robustness of the model against various shifts in the test distribution.

paragraphs: Neural networks can reconstruct images from corrupted measurements, but strong results often require large, varied training collections. For MRI, obtaining those collections can be difficult or expensive. This paper asks whether data augmentation can reduce the amount of training data needed for accelerated MRI reconstruction while preserving reconstruction performance.

The proposed pipeline, MRAugment, is built around invariances in medical imaging measurements. This design matters because a reconstruction example links an image to the physical process that produced its measurements. The authors report that naive augmentation strategies fail when they ignore that physics. MRAugment therefore adapts augmentation to the measurement problem rather than simply transferring classification-oriented strategies.

Across multiple datasets, augmentation prevents overfitting in the low-data setting and can match or exceed leading performance with substantially less training data. Its gains diminish when plentiful data is already available. The experiments also show improved robustness to several shifts in the test distribution, suggesting that the pipeline helps both data efficiency and performance under the tested changes.
summary.tldr: MRAugment uses measurement-aware augmentation to improve MRI reconstruction with limited training data and increase robustness to tested distribution shifts.

title: Data augmentation for deep learning based accelerated MRI reconstruction with limited data

abstract: We prove new upper and lower bounds for sample complexity of finding an $\epsilon$-optimal policy of an infinite-horizon average-reward Markov decision process (MDP) given access to a generative model. When the mixing time of the probability transition matrix of all policies is at most $t_\mathrm{mix}$, we provide an algorithm that solves the problem using $\widetilde{O}(t_\mathrm{mix} \epsilon^{-3})$ (oblivious) samples per state-action pair. Further, we provide a lower bound showing that a linear dependence on $t_\mathrm{mix}$ is necessary in the worst case for any algorithm which computes oblivious samples. We obtain our results by establishing connections between infinite-horizon average-reward MDPs and discounted MDPs of possible further utility.

paragraphs: The paper studies how much data is needed to find a nearly optimal policy for an infinite-horizon Markov decision process evaluated by average reward. The learner has access to a generative model that supplies samples. The analysis concerns sample complexity, connecting the required data to accuracy and how quickly the system mixes.

The main assumption is that every policy's transition matrix has mixing time at most t_mix. Under this condition, the authors provide an algorithm using roughly t_mix times epsilon to the power of minus three samples per state-action pair, with logarithmic factors suppressed. The sampling is oblivious, using the sampling framework specified in the result.

A lower bound shows that linear dependence on mixing time is unavoidable in the worst case for algorithms using oblivious samples. This establishes tightness of that particular dependence, without claiming that every factor in the upper bound is matched. The proofs connect average-reward problems to discounted MDPs, providing a relationship the authors suggest may have further theoretical uses.
summary.tldr: New average-reward MDP bounds establish linear mixing-time dependence as sufficient and worst-case necessary for oblivious sampling under the stated assumptions.

title: Towards Tight Bounds on the Sample Complexity of Average-reward MDPs

abstract: Generative adversarial networks (GAN) are a widely used class of deep generative models, but their minimax training dynamics are not understood very well. In this work, we show that GANs with a 2-layer infinite-width generator and a 2-layer finite-width discriminator trained with stochastic gradient ascent-descent have no spurious stationary points. We then show that when the width of the generator is finite but wide, there are no spurious stationary points within a ball whose radius becomes arbitrarily large (to cover the entire parameter space) as the width goes to infinity.

We then show that when the width of the generator is finite but wide, there are no spurious stationary points within a ball whose radius becomes arbitrarily large (to cover the entire parameter space) as the width goes to infinity.

paragraphs: Generative adversarial training involves competing objectives, making its optimization behavior difficult to understand. This paper studies stationary points in a particular WGAN setting. The generator has two layers and infinite width, while the discriminator has two layers and finite width; training uses stochastic gradient ascent-descent.

For that setting, the authors prove that there are no spurious stationary points. The result concerns the structure of the training problem under the specified architecture and width assumptions. It identifies a favorable property of stationary points in an infinite-width generator model, providing a precise theoretical statement about this adversarial setup.

The authors then consider generators that are finite but wide. Here, the absence of spurious stationary points is established within a ball in parameter space. The radius of that ball grows arbitrarily large as generator width tends to infinity, eventually covering the entire parameter space in the limit. This connects a regional finite-width guarantee with the global infinite-width result.
summary.tldr: The studied two-layer WGAN has no spurious stationary points at infinite generator width, with expanding regional guarantees for finite wide generators.

title: WGAN with an Infinitely Wide Generator Has No Spurious Stationary Points

abstract: We investigate the problem of hierarchically clustering data streams containing metric data in R^d. We introduce a desirable invariance property for such algorithms, describe a general family of hyperplane-based methods enjoying this property, and analyze two scalable instances of this general family against recently popularized similarity/dissimilarity-based metrics for hierarchical clustering. We prove a number of new results related to the approximation ratios of these algorithms, improving in various ways over the literature on this subject. Finally, since our algorithms are principled but also very practical, we carry out an experimental comparison on both synthetic and real-world datasets showing competitive results against known baselines.

We prove a number of new results related to the approximation ratios of these algorithms, improving in various ways over the literature on this subject. paragraphs: Hierarchical clustering organizes data into nested groups rather than producing only one flat partition. This paper studies that problem for streams of metric data represented in a multidimensional space. The streaming setting motivates algorithms that can scale while still supporting a principled analysis of the hierarchies they produce.

The authors introduce an invariance property they consider desirable and describe a general family of hyperplane-based algorithms that satisfy it. They then focus on two scalable members of that family. Their analysis evaluates these algorithms using similarity-based and dissimilarity-based criteria for hierarchical clustering, connecting the construction procedure to explicit measures of clustering quality.

The theoretical results improve approximation-ratio guarantees in several ways over prior work. Such guarantees characterize how an algorithm's result compares with the objective used to judge it. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets also show competitive performance against known baselines. The paper therefore combines a shared structural principle, scalable algorithm instances, and both theoretical and empirical assessments of the resulting hierarchies.
summary.tldr: Hyperplane-based algorithms provide scalable hierarchical clustering of data streams with improved approximation guarantees and competitive experimental results.

title: Hierarchical Clustering of Data Streams: Scalable Algorithms and Approximation Guarantees

abstract: Electrocardiogram (ECG) is a widely used non-invasive diagnostic tool for heart diseases. Many studies have devised ECG analysis models (e.g., classifiers) to assist diagnosis. As an upstream task, researches have built generative models to synthesize ECG data, which are beneficial to providing training samples, privacy protection, and annotation reduction. However, previous generative methods for ECG often neither synthesized multi-view data, nor dealt with heart disease conditions. In this paper, we propose a novel disease-aware generative adversarial network for multi-view ECG synthesis called ME-GAN, which attains panoptic electrocardio representations conditioned on heart diseases and projects the representations onto multiple standard views to yield ECG signals. Since ECG manifestations of heart diseases are often localized in specific waveforms, we propose a new "mixup normalization" to inject disease information precisely into suitable locations. In addition, we propose a "view discriminator" to revert disordered ECG views into a pre-determined order, supervising the generator to obtain ECG representing correct view characteristics. Besides, a new metric, rFID, is presented to assess the quality of the synthesized ECG signals. Comprehensive experiments verify that our ME-GAN performs well on multi-view ECG signal synthesis with trusty morbid manifestations.

paragraphs: ECG generation can provide synthetic signals for downstream analysis, but the paper identifies two gaps in previous methods: producing multiple views and conditioning the output on heart disease. ME-GAN addresses both by learning a shared electrocardio representation conditioned on disease and projecting it into multiple standard ECG views.

The architecture includes two specialized mechanisms. Mixup normalization injects disease information into suitable waveform locations, reflecting the observation that disease manifestations can be localized. A view discriminator learns to restore disordered ECG views to a predetermined order. This supplies supervision intended to make each generated view exhibit its appropriate characteristics.

The authors also introduce rFID as a metric for assessing generated ECG quality. Their experiments report effective multi-view synthesis with credible disease manifestations. The contribution combines a common representation across views with explicit guidance about where disease features should appear and how views should differ. The stated findings concern the quality and disease-related characteristics of synthesized signals, supporting the paper's goal of more controlled ECG generation.
summary.tldr: ME-GAN generates multiple ECG views conditioned on heart disease, with mechanisms for localized disease features and correct view characteristics.

title: ME-GAN: Learning Panoptic Electrocardio Representations for Multi-view ECG Synthesis Conditioned on Heart Diseases

abstract: We consider the infinitely many-armed bandit problem with rotting rewards, where the mean reward of an arm decreases at each pull of the arm according to an arbitrary trend with maximum rotting rate $\varrho=o(1)$. We show that this learning problem has an $\Omega(\max\{\varrho^{1/3}T, \sqrt{T}\})$ worst-case regret lower bound where $T$ is the time horizon. We show that a matching upper bound $\tilde{O}(\max\{\varrho^{1/3}T, \sqrt{T}\})$, up to a poly-logarithmic factor, can be achieved by an algorithm that uses a UCB index for each arm and a threshold value to decide whether to continue pulling an arm or remove the arm from further consideration, when the algorithm knows the value of the maximum rotting rate $\varrho$. We also show that an $\tilde{O}(\max\{\varrho^{1/3}T, T^{3/4}\})$ regret upper bound can be achieved by an algorithm that does not know the value of $\varrho$, by using an adaptive UCB index along with an adaptive threshold value.

We show that a matching upper bound $\tilde{O}(\max\{\varrho^{1/3}T, \sqrt{T}\})$, up to a poly-logarithmic factor, can be achieved by an algorithm that uses a UCB index for each arm and a threshold value to decide whether to continue pulling an arm or remove the arm from further consideration, when the algorithm knows the value of the maximum rotting rate $\varrho$. We also show that an $\tilde{O}(\max\{\varrho^{1/3}T, T^{3/4}\})$ regret upper bound can be achieved by an algorithm that does not know the value of $\varrho$, by using an adaptive UCB index along with an adaptive threshold value.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential choice among infinitely many options whose expected rewards deteriorate whenever they are selected. The deterioration can follow an arbitrary trend, subject to a maximum rate ρ that is o(1). The learner must decide when an option remains worthwhile and when to abandon it.

The authors establish a worst-case regret lower bound of order max{ρ^(1/3)T, √T}, where T is the number of rounds. When the maximum deterioration rate is known, their algorithm matches this bound up to polylogarithmic factors. It combines an upper-confidence-bound index for each option with a threshold that determines whether to keep selecting it or remove it from consideration.

When the rate is unknown, the authors adapt both the confidence index and the threshold. This gives a regret upper bound of order max{ρ^(1/3)T, T^(3/4)}, again with polylogarithmic factors suppressed. The results distinguish the guarantees available with and without knowledge of deterioration, while showing how confidence-based selection can be combined with explicit abandonment decisions.
summary.tldr: Confidence-based selection and abandonment thresholds achieve near-optimal regret for infinitely many deteriorating options when the maximum deterioration rate is known.

title: Rotting Infinitely Many-Armed Bandits

abstract: In this paper, we study the finite-sum convex optimization problem focusing on the general convex case. Recently, the study of variance reduced (VR) methods and their accelerated variants has made exciting progress. However, the step size used in the existing VR algorithms typically depends on the smoothness parameter, which is often unknown and requires tuning in practice. To address this problem, we propose two novel adaptive VR algorithms: Adaptive Variance Reduced Accelerated Extra-Gradient (AdaVRAE) and Adaptive Variance Reduced Accelerated Gradient (AdaVRAG). Our algorithms do not require knowledge of the smoothness parameter. AdaVRAE uses $\mathcal{O}\left(n\log\log n+\sqrt{\frac{n\beta}{\epsilon}}\right)$ and AdaVRAG uses $\mathcal{O}\left(n\log\log n+\sqrt{\frac{n\beta\log\beta}{\epsilon}}\right)$ gradient evaluations to attain an $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon)$-suboptimal solution, where $n$ is the number of functions in the finite sum and $\beta$ is the smoothness parameter. This result matches the best-known convergence rate of non-adaptive VR methods and it improves upon the convergence of the state of the art adaptive VR method, AdaSVRG. We demonstrate the superior performance of our algorithms compared with previous methods in experiments on real-world datasets.

paragraphs: The paper studies convex optimization objectives formed by adding together many component functions. Variance reduction and acceleration can make these problems cheaper to solve, but their step sizes often depend on a smoothness parameter describing how quickly gradients change. When that parameter is unknown, choosing an effective step size becomes a practical tuning problem.

The authors introduce two adaptive algorithms, AdaVRAE and AdaVRAG, that combine variance reduction with accelerated updates without requiring advance knowledge of smoothness. AdaVRAE uses an extra-gradient approach, while AdaVRAG uses a gradient approach. Their guarantees still reflect the problem's smoothness; adaptation removes the need to supply its value to the algorithm, rather than removing its influence on difficulty.

For target error epsilon, AdaVRAE requires on the order of n log log n plus the square root of n times smoothness divided by epsilon gradient evaluations. AdaVRAG has an additional logarithmic smoothness factor inside the square root. The authors report improved guarantees over AdaSVRG and stronger experimental performance than previous methods on real datasets.
summary.tldr: AdaVRAE and AdaVRAG combine acceleration and variance reduction while adapting their updates without prior knowledge of the smoothness parameter.

title: Adaptive Accelerated (Extra-)Gradient Methods with Variance Reduction

abstract: Models that generate extractive rationales (i.e., subsets of features) or natural language explanations (NLEs) for their predictions are important for explainable AI. While an extractive rationale provides a quick view of the features most responsible for a prediction, an NLE allows for a comprehensive description of the decision-making process behind a prediction. However, current models that generate the best extractive rationales or NLEs often fall behind the state-of-the-art (SOTA) in terms of task performance. In this work, we bridge this gap by introducing RExC, a self-rationalizing framework that grounds its predictions and two complementary types of explanations (NLEs and extractive rationales) in background knowledge. Our framework improves over previous methods by: (i) reaching SOTA task performance while also providing explanations, (ii) providing two types of explanations, while existing models usually provide only one type, and (iii) beating by a large margin the previous SOTA in terms of quality of both types of explanations. Furthermore, a perturbation analysis in RExC shows a high degree of association between explanations and predictions, a necessary property of faithful explanations.

paragraphs: Models can explain predictions by selecting relevant input features or by producing a natural-language account. These formats serve complementary purposes: selected features offer a compact view of supporting material, while text can give a fuller explanation. The paper addresses a gap in which models producing strong explanations often trail the best models on the underlying prediction task.

RExC is a self-rationalizing framework that grounds predictions and both explanation formats in background knowledge. It combines extractive rationales with natural-language explanations within the same framework. The authors report state-of-the-art task performance alongside explanations, as well as large improvements over previous state-of-the-art results in the quality of both explanation types.

The paper also uses perturbation analysis to examine how explanations relate to predictions. It finds a strong association between them, supplying evidence for a necessary property of faithful explanations. That result supports a connection between what the model says and what it predicts, but association alone does not establish complete faithfulness. The overall contribution combines predictive performance, complementary explanation formats, and evidence about their relationship.
summary.tldr: RExC grounds predictions and two complementary explanation types in background knowledge, reporting strong task performance and improved explanation quality.

title: Knowledge-Grounded Self-Rationalization via Extractive and Natural Language Explanations

abstract: Recent studies show that Vision Transformers (ViTs) exhibit strong robustness against various corruptions. Although this property is partly attributed to the self-attention mechanism, there is still a lack of an explanatory framework towards a more systematic understanding. In this paper, we examine the role of self-attention in learning robust representations. Our study is motivated by the intriguing properties of self-attention in visual grouping which indicate that self-attention could promote improved mid-level representation and robustness. We thus propose a family of fully attentional networks (FANs) that incorporate self-attention in both token mixing and channel processing. We validate the design comprehensively on various hierarchical backbones. Our model with a DeiT architecture achieves a state-of-the-art 47.6% mCE on ImageNet-C with 29M parameters. We also demonstrate significantly improved robustness in two downstream tasks: semantic segmentation and object detection

paragraphs: Vision Transformers have shown strong resistance to various image corruptions, with self-attention considered part of the explanation. This paper investigates how self-attention contributes to robust representations. Its motivation comes from visual grouping properties suggesting that attention could improve intermediate visual representations and, through them, robustness.

The authors propose fully attentional networks, a family of architectures that uses self-attention for both token mixing and channel processing. This extends attention across two kinds of representation processing. They evaluate the design across different hierarchical backbones, connecting their investigation of attention with a concrete architectural proposal.

A model using a DeiT architecture achieves a reported state-of-the-art mean corruption error of 47.6% on ImageNet-C with 29 million parameters. The authors also demonstrate significantly improved robustness in semantic segmentation and object detection. These findings support the proposed attention design across classification and downstream vision tasks, while the suggested role of visual grouping remains the motivating explanation for the architectural changes.
summary.tldr: Fully attentional networks apply self-attention to token and channel processing, improving measured robustness across several vision tasks.

title: Understanding The Robustness in Vision Transformers

abstract: Source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) is compelling because it allows adapting an off-the-shelf model to a new domain using only unlabelled data. In this work, we apply existing SFDA techniques to a challenging set of naturally-occurring distribution shifts in bioacoustics, which are very different from the ones commonly studied in computer vision. We find existing methods perform differently relative to each other than observed in vision benchmarks, and sometimes perform worse than no adaptation at all. We propose a new simple method which outperforms the existing methods on our new shifts while exhibiting strong performance on a range of vision datasets. Our findings suggest that existing SFDA methods are not as generalizable as previously thought and that considering diverse modalities can be a useful avenue for designing more robust models.

paragraphs: Source-free domain adaptation adjusts an existing model to a new domain using only unlabelled data. This is appealing when the original training data are unavailable. The paper examines whether methods developed and assessed largely through computer-vision benchmarks transfer successfully to naturally occurring distribution changes in bioacoustics.

The findings challenge that expectation. On the bioacoustic shifts studied, existing methods change their relative ordering compared with vision evaluations. Some even perform worse than leaving the original model unadapted. This means that success on familiar adaptation benchmarks does not reliably establish usefulness across different kinds of data and distribution change.

The authors propose a simple new method that outperforms the existing methods on their bioacoustic shifts while also performing strongly across several vision datasets. These results support the usefulness of evaluating adaptation across diverse modalities. The broader contribution is both an improved method for the tested settings and evidence that benchmark diversity can expose weaknesses hidden by a narrower evaluation. The findings suggest a route toward more generalisable adaptation without establishing universal success.
summary.tldr: Bioacoustic distribution shifts expose failures in existing source-free adaptation methods, motivating a simple alternative that also performs strongly on vision datasets.

title: In Search for a Generalizable Method for Source Free Domain Adaptation

abstract: Pretraining on a large-scale corpus has become a standard method to build general language models (LMs). Adapting a model to new data distributions targeting different downstream tasks poses significant challenges. Naive fine-tuning may incur catastrophic forgetting when the over-parameterized LMs overfit the new data but fail to preserve the pretrained features. Lifelong learning (LLL) aims to enable information systems to learn from a continuous data stream across time. However, most prior work modifies the training recipe assuming a static fixed network architecture. We find that additional model capacity and proper regularization are key elements to achieving strong LLL performance. Thus, we propose Lifelong-MoE, an extensible MoE (Mixture-of-Experts) architecture that dynamically adds model capacity via adding experts with regularized pretaining. Our results show that by only introducing a limited number of extra experts while keeping the computation cost constant, our model can steadily adapt to data distribution shifts while preserving the previous knowledge. Compared to existing lifelong learning approaches, Lifelong-MoE achieves better few-shot performance on NLP tasks. More impressively, Lifelong-MoE surpasses multi-task learning on 19 downstream NLU tasks.

paragraphs: A language model that keeps learning from new data must adapt without losing useful knowledge from earlier training. Ordinary fine-tuning can overfit the latest distribution and cause catastrophic forgetting. This paper studies lifelong pretraining as a problem involving both training procedures and the capacity available to the model.

The authors identify additional capacity and appropriate regularization as key ingredients. Their Lifelong-MoE architecture grows by adding experts, with regularized pretraining accompanying that expansion. This gives the system new capacity as distributions change, extending approaches that keep the network architecture fixed throughout lifelong learning.

The reported results show that a limited number of additional experts enables continuing adaptation while retaining previous knowledge and keeping computation cost constant. Lifelong-MoE achieves better few-shot performance than existing lifelong-learning approaches and surpasses multitask learning on 19 downstream language-understanding tasks. These findings support expanding model capacity selectively: the model can gain parameters for new distributions without a corresponding increase in the reported computation cost.
summary.tldr: Lifelong-MoE adds regularized experts to adapt language models to changing data while preserving earlier knowledge at constant computation cost.

title: Lifelong Language Pretraining with Distribution-Specialized Experts

abstract: We introduce in this paper the mechanism of graph random features (GRFs). GRFs can be used to construct unbiased randomized estimators of several important kernels defined on graphs’ nodes, in particular the regularized Laplacian kernel. As regular RFs for non-graph kernels, they provide means to scale up kernel methods defined on graphs to larger networks. Importantly, they give substantial computational gains also for smaller graphs, while applied in downstream applications. Consequently, GRFs address the notoriously difficult problem of cubic (in the number of the nodes of the graph) time complexity of graph kernels algorithms. We provide a detailed theoretical analysis of GRFs and an extensive empirical evaluation: from speed tests, through Frobenius relative error analysis to kmeans graph-clustering with graph kernels. We show that the computation of GRFs admits an embarrassingly simple distributed algorithm that can be applied if the graph under consideration needs to be split across several machines. We also introduce a (still unbiased) quasi Monte Carlo variant of GRFs, q-GRFs, relying on the so-called reinforced random walks that might be used to optimize the variance of GRFs. As a byproduct, we obtain a novel approach to solve certain classes of linear equations with positive and symmetric matrices.

paragraphs: Graph kernels describe relationships between nodes, but kernel algorithms can incur computation that grows cubically with the number of nodes. This paper introduces graph random features to approximate several important node kernels, including the regularized Laplacian kernel. The resulting randomized estimators are unbiased, providing a way to scale graph kernel methods to larger networks.

The authors combine theoretical analysis with empirical evaluation of speed, approximation error, and kernel-based graph clustering. They report substantial computational gains in downstream applications even for smaller graphs. They also show that feature computation supports a simple distributed algorithm, making the approach applicable when a graph is split across multiple machines.

A further variant, q-GRFs, uses reinforced random walks in a quasi Monte Carlo construction while retaining unbiasedness. The authors identify this as a possible way to optimize estimator variance. The work also yields an approach for solving certain linear systems with positive, symmetric matrices. Together, these contributions connect randomized graph representations to practical kernel computation, distributed processing, and a related class of numerical problems.
summary.tldr: Graph random features provide unbiased kernel approximations with computational gains and a simple route to distributed computation.

title: Taming graph kernels with random features

abstract: In recent years, increasing attention has been directed to leveraging pre-trained vision models for motor control. While existing works mainly emphasize the importance of this pre-training phase, the arguably equally important role played by downstream policy learning during control-specific fine-tuning is often neglected. It thus remains unclear if pre-trained vision models are consistent in their effectiveness under different control policies. To bridge this gap in understanding, we conduct a comprehensive study on 14 pre-trained vision models using 3 distinct classes of policy learning methods, including reinforcement learning (RL), imitation learning through behavior cloning (BC), and imitation learning with a visual reward function (VRF). Our study yields a series of intriguing results, including the discovery that the effectiveness of pre-training is highly dependent on the choice of the downstream policy learning algorithm. We show that conventionally accepted evaluation based on RL methods is highly variable and therefore unreliable, and further advocate for using more robust methods like VRF and BC. To facilitate more universal evaluations of pre-trained models and their policy learning methods in the future, we also release a benchmark of 21 tasks across 3 different environments alongside our work.

paragraphs: Pretrained vision models are increasingly used to help agents learn motor control, but their value depends on what happens after visual pretraining. This paper examines the downstream policy-learning stage: the process that turns visual information into actions. It asks whether a vision model's apparent effectiveness remains consistent across different ways of learning control policies.

The study evaluates 14 pretrained vision models using three classes of methods: reinforcement learning, behavior cloning, and imitation learning with a visual reward function. This comparison treats the policy-learning algorithm as a central experimental variable. The authors find that the effectiveness of pretraining depends strongly on which downstream method is used.

In the study, evaluations based on reinforcement learning are highly variable, leading the authors to question their reliability and advocate more robust alternatives such as behavior cloning and visual-reward methods. They also release a benchmark containing 21 tasks across three environments. The findings suggest that assessments of pretrained vision for control should account for the policy-learning procedure used to measure its usefulness.
summary.tldr: A study of 14 pretrained vision models finds that their usefulness for motor control depends strongly on the downstream policy-learning method.

title: For Pre-Trained Vision Models in Motor Control, Not All Policy Learning Methods are Created Equal

abstract: Symmetry-based neural networks often constrain the architecture in order to achieve invariance or equivariance to a group of transformations. In this paper, we propose an alternative that avoids this architectural constraint by learning to produce canonical representations of the data. These canonicalization functions can readily be plugged into non-equivariant backbone architectures. We offer explicit ways to implement them for some groups of interest. We show that this approach enjoys universality while providing interpretable insights. Our main hypothesis, supported by our empirical results, is that learning a small neural network to perform canonicalization is better than using predefined heuristics. Our experiments show that learning the canonicalization function is competitive with existing techniques for learning equivariant functions across many tasks, including image classification, $N$-body dynamics prediction, point cloud classification and part segmentation, while being faster across the board.

paragraphs: Neural networks that respect symmetries often achieve this by restricting their internal architecture. Depending on the task, an output should either remain unchanged under a transformation or change in a corresponding way. This paper proposes learning a canonical representation of the input as another route to obtaining those symmetry properties.

A learned canonicalization function can be attached to a backbone that is not itself equivariant. The authors give explicit constructions for several transformation groups and show that the approach has universal approximation capabilities. This arrangement makes the learned choice of canonical representation an interpretable component of the system, while allowing flexibility in the backbone architecture.

The central hypothesis is that a small network can learn canonicalization more effectively than predefined heuristics; experiments support that claim. Across image classification, N-body dynamics prediction, point cloud classification, and part segmentation, the method is competitive with existing equivariant approaches and faster throughout the reported comparisons. These results support learned canonicalization as a practical way to introduce symmetry handling across several kinds of tasks.
summary.tldr: Learned canonicalization adds symmetry handling to ordinary neural backbones and achieves competitive performance with faster execution in the reported experiments.

title: Equivariance with Learned Canonicalization Functions

abstract: Being able to provide explanations for a model’s decision has become a central requirement for the development, deployment, and adoption of machine learning models. However, we are yet to understand what explanation methods can and cannot do. How do upstream factors such as data, model prediction, hyperparameters, and random initialization influence downstream explanations? While previous work raised concerns that explanations (E) may have little relationship with the prediction (Y), there is a lack of conclusive study to quantify this relationship. Our work borrows tools from causal inference to systematically assay this relationship. More specifically, we study the relationship between E and Y by measuring the treatment effect when intervening on their causal ancestors, i.e., on hyperparameters and inputs used to generate saliency-based Es or Ys. Our results suggest that the relationships between E and Y is far from ideal. In fact, the gap between ’ideal’ case only increase in higher-performing models — models that are likely to be deployed. Our work is a promising first step towards providing a quantitative measure of the relationship between E and Y, which could also inform the future development of methods for E with a quantitative metric.

paragraphs: An explanation of a model's decision is useful only insofar as its relationship to that decision is understood. This paper investigates that relationship for saliency-based explanations. It asks how factors upstream of both predictions and explanations affect the two, moving the discussion toward a quantitative assessment of their connection.

The authors use tools from causal inference and intervene on shared causal ancestors, including hyperparameters and inputs. They measure the resulting treatment effects on explanations and predictions. This approach examines how the two respond when their generating conditions change, providing a systematic way to assess whether their relationship matches the desired ideal.

The results suggest a substantial gap from that ideal, with a larger gap in higher-performing models in the study. Better predictive performance therefore does not, in these findings, imply a closer relationship between saliency explanations and predictions. The authors present the work as an initial step toward a quantitative measure that could also guide development of explanation methods. The evidence concerns the examined saliency-based explanations and interventions.
summary.tldr: Causal interventions reveal a less-than-ideal relationship between saliency explanations and predictions, especially in higher-performing models studied.

title: On the Relationship Between Explanation and Prediction: A Causal View

abstract: We study a synthetic corpus based approach for language models (LMs) to acquire logical deductive reasoning ability. The previous studies generated deduction examples using specific sets of deduction rules. However, these rules were limited or otherwise arbitrary. This can limit the generalizability of acquired deductive reasoning ability. We rethink this and adopt a well-grounded set of deduction rules based on formal logic theory, which can derive any other deduction rules when combined in a multistep way. We empirically verify that LMs trained on the proposed corpora, which we name $\textbf{FLD}$ ($\textbf{F}$ormal $\textbf{L}$ogic $\textbf{D}$eduction), acquire more generalizable deductive reasoning ability. Furthermore, we identify the aspects of deductive reasoning ability on which deduction corpora can enhance LMs and those on which they cannot. Finally, on the basis of these results, we discuss the future directions for applying deduction corpora or other approaches for each aspect. We release the code, data, and models.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether synthetic training examples can teach language models more generalizable deductive reasoning. Earlier approaches generated examples from selected deduction rules, but limited or arbitrary rule choices can restrict what a model learns. The authors instead build their training corpus around a rule set grounded in formal logic.

The resulting corpus is called FLD, for Formal Logic Deduction. Its rules can be combined through multiple steps to derive other deduction rules. This gives the example-generation process a principled foundation for covering deductions beyond a narrow list of templates. The logical capability of the rule system motivates the corpus; the model’s learned ability is assessed empirically.

Experiments show that language models trained on these corpora acquire more generalizable deductive reasoning. The study also distinguishes aspects of reasoning that deduction corpora improve from aspects they do not improve. That makes the contribution both a training resource and an investigation of its reach. The authors use these findings to discuss future approaches and release their code, data, and models.
summary.tldr: FLD uses formally grounded deduction rules to generate synthetic training data that empirically improves language models’ reasoning generalization.

title: Learning Deductive Reasoning from Synthetic Corpus based on Formal Logic

abstract: The effectiveness of neural processes (NPs) in modelling posterior prediction maps—the mapping from data to posterior predictive distributions—has significantly improved since their inception. This improvement can be attributed to two principal factors: (1) advancements in the architecture of permutation invariant set functions, which are intrinsic to all NPs; and (2) leveraging symmetries present in the true posterior predictive map, which are problem dependent. Transformers are a notable development in permutation invariant set functions, and their utility within NPs has been demonstrated through the family of models we refer to as TNPs. Despite significant interest in TNPs, little attention has been given to incorporating symmetries. Notably, the posterior prediction maps for data that are stationary—a common assumption in spatio-temporal modelling—exhibit translation equivariance. In this paper, we introduce of a new family of translation equivariant TNPs that incorporate translation equivariance. Through an extensive range of experiments on synthetic and real-world spatio-temporal data, we demonstrate the effectiveness of TE-TNPs relative to their non-translation-equivariant counterparts and other NP baselines.
originalAbstract: The effectiveness of neural processes (NPs) in modelling posterior prediction maps—the mapping from data to posterior predictive distributions—has significantly improved since their inception. This improvement can be attributed to two principal factors: (1) advancements in the architecture of permutation invariant set functions, which are intrinsic to all NPs; and (2) leveraging symmetries present in the true posterior predictive map, which are problem dependent. Transformers are a notable development in permutation invariant set functions, and their utility within NPs has been demonstrated through the family of models we refer to as TNPs. Despite significant interest in TNPs, little attention has been given to incorporating symmetries. Notably, the posterior prediction maps for data that are stationary—a common assumption in spatio-temporal modelling—exhibit translation equivariance. In this paper, we introduce of a new family of translation equivariant TNPs that incorporate translation equivariance. Through an extensive range of experiments on synthetic and real-world spatio-temporal data, we demonstrate the effectiveness of TE-TNPs relative to their non-translation-equivariant counterparts and other NP baselines.

paragraphs: Neural processes learn mappings from observed data to predictive distributions. Their effectiveness depends partly on how they handle sets of observations and partly on whether they reflect symmetries of the prediction problem. Transformer neural processes address set modeling, but this paper focuses on incorporating a symmetry that has received less attention.

For stationary data, the posterior prediction map is translation equivariant. Intuitively, shifting the input locations should shift the prediction in the corresponding way. The authors introduce translation-equivariant transformer neural processes that build this behavior into the model. The symmetry is motivated by stationarity, a common assumption in spatial and temporal modeling.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world spatio-temporal data demonstrate effectiveness relative to transformer neural processes without translation equivariance and other neural-process baselines. The contribution combines transformer-based set modeling with a structural property of the target predictive map. Its significance is that improving the architecture need not rely only on more expressive set functions: incorporating a symmetry appropriate to the problem can also improve predictive modeling.
summary.tldr: Translation-equivariant transformer neural processes incorporate a symmetry of stationary prediction problems and perform well on spatio-temporal evaluations.

title: Translation Equivariant Transformer Neural Processes

abstract: Diffusion models have made significant contributions to computer vision, sparking a growing interest in the community recently regarding the application of it to graph generation. The existing discrete graph diffusion models exhibit heightened computational complexity and diminished training efficiency. A preferable and natural way is to directly diffuse the graph within the latent space. However, due to the non-Euclidean structure of graphs is not isotropic in the latent space, the existing latent diffusion models effectively make it difficult to capture and preserve the topological information of graphs. To address the above challenges, we propose a novel geometrically latent diffusion framework HypDiff. Specifically, we first establish a geometrically latent space with interpretability measures based on hyperbolic geometry, to define anisotropic latent diffusion processes for graphs. Then, we propose a geometrically latent diffusion process that is constrained by both radial and angular geometric properties, thereby ensuring the preservation of the original topological properties in the generative graphs. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the superior effectiveness of HypDiff for graph generation with various topologies.

The contribution is a latent diffusion framework that explicitly incorporates geometric structure into graph generation, alongside empirical evidence that this design handles a variety of graph organizations effectively.
summary.tldr: HypDiff uses radially and angularly constrained diffusion in a hyperbolic latent space to preserve topology during graph generation.

title: Hyperbolic Geometric Latent Diffusion Model for Graph Generation

abstract: Mixed linear regression is a well-studied problem in parametric statistics and machine learning. Given a set of samples, tuples of covariates and labels, the task of mixed linear regression is to find a small list of linear relationships that best fit the samples. Usually it is assumed that the label is generated stochastically by randomly selecting one of two or more linear functions, applying this chosen function to the covariates, and potentially introducing noise to the result. In that situation, the objective is to estimate the ground-truth linear functions up to some parameter error. The popular expectation maximization (EM) and alternating minimization (AM) algorithms have been previously analyzed for this. In this paper, we consider the more general problem of agnostic learning of mixed linear regression from samples, without such generative models. In particular, we show that the AM and EM algorithms, under standard conditions of separability and good initialization, lead to agnostic learning in mixed linear regression by converging to the population loss minimizers, for suitably defined loss functions. In some sense, this shows the strength of AM and EM algorithms that converges to “optimal solutions” even in the absence of realizable generative models.

paragraphs: Mixed linear regression fits a small collection of linear relationships to observations. Conventional analyses assume that each label was generated by randomly choosing one of several underlying linear functions, possibly adding noise. Success then means recovering those generating functions accurately. This paper asks what familiar algorithms can achieve when that account of the data is unavailable.

The authors study expectation maximization and alternating minimization in an agnostic setting, where the observations need not come from an assumed mixture-generating process. They show that these algorithms converge to population loss minimizers for suitably chosen losses. The guarantee still requires standard separation conditions and a good initialization.

This changes what the algorithms are justified as finding: a best fit according to the specified population objective, even when there are no true generating linear functions to recover. The result therefore extends their theoretical usefulness beyond correctly specified mixture models. Separation and initialization remain substantive conditions; removing the generative assumption does not make convergence unconditional.
summary.tldr: With separation and good initialization, EM and alternating minimization can learn mixed linear regressions without assuming a mixture-generating model.

title: Agnostic Learning of Mixed Linear Regressions with EM and AM Algorithms

abstract: Graph transformers typically lack third-order interactions, limiting their geometric understanding which is crucial for tasks like molecular geometry prediction. We propose the Triplet Graph Transformer (TGT) that enables direct communication between pairs within a 3-tuple of nodes via novel triplet attention and aggregation mechanisms. TGT is applied to molecular property prediction by first predicting interatomic distances from 2D graphs and then using these distances for downstream tasks. A novel three-stage training procedure and stochastic inference further improve training efficiency and model performance. Our model achieves new state-of-the-art (SOTA) results on open challenge benchmarks PCQM4Mv2 and OC20 IS2RE. We also obtain SOTA results on QM9, MOLPCBA, and LIT-PCBA molecular property prediction benchmarks via transfer learning. We also demonstrate the generality of TGT with SOTA results on the traveling salesman problem (TSP).

The paper argues that graph transformers typically lack third-order interactions, limiting their geometric understanding. Its Triplet Graph Transformer, or TGT, adds direct communication between pairs belonging to a shared group of three nodes.

Novel triplet-attention and aggregation mechanisms implement this communication. They also demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on the traveling salesman problem. Together, these evaluations support the usefulness of triplet interactions for molecular learning and show that the architecture's reported benefits extend to an additional graph-based problem beyond molecular property prediction.
summary.tldr: TGT adds interactions among node triplets to improve molecular geometry and property learning, with strong results on several benchmarks.

title: Triplet Interaction Improves Graph Transformers: Accurate Molecular Graph Learning with Triplet Graph Transformers

abstract: Textural Inversion, a prompt learning method, learns a singular text embedding for a new "word" to represent image style and appearance, allowing it to be integrated into natural language sentences to generate novel synthesised images. However, identifying multiple unknown object-level concepts within one scene remains a complex challenge. While recent methods have resorted to cropping or masking individual images to learn multiple concepts, these techniques often require prior knowledge of new concepts and are labour-intensive. To address this challenge, we introduce Multi-Concept Prompt Learning (MCPL), where multiple unknown "words" are simultaneously learned from a single sentence-image pair, without any imagery annotations. To enhance the accuracy of word-concept correlation and refine attention mask boundaries, we propose three regularisation techniques: Attention Masking, Prompts Contrastive Loss, and Bind Adjective. Extensive quantitative comparisons with both real-world categories and biomedical images demonstrate that our method can learn new semantically disentangled concepts. Our approach emphasises learning solely from textual embeddings, using less than 10% of the storage space compared to others. The project page, code, and data are available at https://astrazeneca.github.io/mcpl.github.io.

paragraphs: Prompt learning can represent a new visual concept through a learned text embedding that functions like a new word. A harder problem is separating several unfamiliar objects within one scene. Existing approaches that crop or mask objects can require prior knowledge of the concepts and substantial manual effort.

Multi-Concept Prompt Learning learns several unknown words together from a single sentence-image pair, without image annotations. Its central challenge is associating each learned word with the appropriate visual concept. The method introduces three regularizers—Attention Masking, Prompts Contrastive Loss, and Bind Adjective—to strengthen those associations and refine attention boundaries.

Quantitative comparisons involving real-world categories and biomedical images show that the method can learn concepts with distinct semantic meanings. This matters because representing multiple objects separately makes the learned words more informative than an undivided representation of a scene. The approach learns only textual embeddings and uses less than 10% of the storage required by the compared methods, combining concept separation with a compact learned representation.
summary.tldr: MCPL learns multiple distinct object concepts from one sentence-image pair without image annotations, using compact textual embeddings.

title: An Image is Worth Multiple Words: Discovering Object Level Concepts using Multi-Concept Prompt Learning

abstract: Effective action abstraction is crucial in tackling challenges associated with large action spaces in Imperfect Information Extensive-Form Games (IIEFGs). However, due to the vast state space and computational complexity in IIEFGs, existing methods often rely on fixed abstractions, resulting in sub-optimal performance. In response, we introduce RL-CFR, a novel reinforcement learning (RL) approach for dynamic action abstraction. RL-CFR builds upon our innovative Markov Decision Process (MDP) formulation, with states corresponding to public information and actions represented as feature vectors indicating specific action abstractions. The reward is defined as the expected payoff difference between the selected and default action abstractions. RL-CFR constructs a game tree with RL-guided action abstractions and utilizes counterfactual regret minimization (CFR) for strategy derivation. Impressively, it can be trained from scratch, achieving higher expected payoff without increased CFR solving time. In experiments on Heads-up No-limit Texas Hold’em, RL-CFR outperforms ReBeL’s replication and Slumbot, demonstrating significant win-rate margins of $64\pm 11$ and $84\pm 17$ mbb/hand, respectively.

paragraphs: Large games with hidden information can have too many actions to consider directly, making action abstraction a crucial part of solving them. Fixed abstractions simplify computation but may limit performance. RL-CFR learns to choose abstractions dynamically, allowing the simplified game representation to respond to public information.

The authors formulate abstraction selection as a Markov decision process. States represent public information, actions encode particular abstractions as feature vectors, and rewards measure expected payoff differences from a default abstraction. Reinforcement learning guides construction of the game tree, after which counterfactual regret minimization derives a strategy. This separates learning which actions to retain from solving the resulting game.

These results support dynamic abstraction as a way to improve the usefulness of the game tree being solved.
summary.tldr: RL-CFR learns dynamic action abstractions that improve poker performance without increasing counterfactual regret minimization solving time.

title: RL-CFR: Improving Action Abstraction for Imperfect Information Extensive-Form Games with Reinforcement Learning

abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of preserving privacy in Federated Learning (FL) within centralized systems, focusing on both trusted and untrusted server scenarios. We analyze this setting within the Stochastic Convex Optimization (SCO) framework, and devise methods that ensure Differential Privacy (DP) while maintaining optimal convergence rates for homogeneous and heterogeneous data distributions. Our approach, based on a recent stochastic optimization technique, offers linear computational complexity, comparable to non-private FL methods, and reduced gradient obfuscation. This work enhances the practicality of DP in FL, balancing privacy, efficiency, and robustness in a variety of server trust environments.

paragraphs: Privacy-preserving federated learning must account for both how data are distributed and whether the coordinating server can be trusted. This paper studies those issues within stochastic convex optimization. It addresses centralized federated systems under both trusted and untrusted server scenarios, placing privacy and optimization efficiency within the same analysis.

The authors devise methods that provide differential privacy while maintaining optimal convergence rates for homogeneous and heterogeneous data distributions. The distinction matters because their stated results cover both similar and differing distributions across participants. The optimization framework also defines the scope of the contribution: these guarantees are developed for the stochastic convex setting considered in the paper.

The approach builds on a recent stochastic optimization technique and has linear computational complexity comparable to non-private federated learning methods. It also reduces gradient obfuscation. Taken together, the stated results address the practical cost of adding privacy: the methods combine privacy guarantees, convergence performance, and computational efficiency across different server trust environments and participant data distributions.
summary.tldr: The paper develops differentially private federated convex optimization methods with optimal convergence and linear computational complexity across server trust settings.

title: Private and Federated Stochastic Convex Optimization: Efficient Strategies for Centralized Systems

abstract: Multi-modal foundation models like OpenFlamingo, LLaVA, and GPT-4 are increasingly used for various real-world tasks. Prior work has shown that these models are highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks on the vision modality. These attacks can be leveraged to spread fake information or defraud users, and thus pose a significant risk, which makes the robustness of large multi-modal foundation models a pressing problem. The CLIP model, or one of its variants, is used as a frozen vision encoder in many large vision-language models (LVLMs), e.g. LLaVA and OpenFlamingo. We propose an unsupervised adversarial fine-tuning scheme to obtain a robust CLIP vision encoder, which yields robustness on all vision down-stream tasks (LVLMs, zero-shot classification) that rely on CLIP. In particular, we show that stealth-attacks on users of LVLMs by a malicious third party providing manipulated images are no longer possible once one replaces the original CLIP model with our robust one. No retraining or fine-tuning of the down-stream LVLMs is required. The code and robust models are available on GitHub.

Many use CLIP or a related model as a frozen visual encoder, making that shared component an important place to address the vulnerability. This paper proposes strengthening the image representation before it reaches the downstream model.

The authors use unsupervised adversarial fine-tuning to obtain a robust CLIP vision encoder. summary.tldr: Unsupervised adversarial fine-tuning produces a robust CLIP encoder that improves downstream robustness without retraining the vision-language models.

title: Robust CLIP: Unsupervised Adversarial Fine-Tuning of Vision Embeddings for Robust Large Vision-Language Models

abstract: Recent advances in diffusion models attempt to handle conditional generative tasks by utilizing a differentiable loss function for guidance without the need for additional training. While these methods achieved certain success, they often compromise on sample quality and require small guidance step sizes, leading to longer sampling processes. This paper reveals that the fundamental issue lies in the manifold deviation during the sampling process when loss guidance is employed. We theoretically show the existence of manifold deviation by establishing a certain lower bound for the estimation error of the loss guidance. To mitigate this problem, we propose Diffusion with Spherical Gaussian constraint (DSG), drawing inspiration from the concentration phenomenon in high-dimensional Gaussian distributions. DSG effectively constrains the guidance step within the intermediate data manifold through optimization and enables the use of larger guidance steps. Furthermore, we present a closed-form solution for DSG denoising with the Spherical Gaussian constraint. Notably, DSG can seamlessly integrate as a plugin module within existing training-free conditional diffusion methods. Implementing DSG merely involves a few lines of additional code with almost no extra computational overhead, yet it leads to significant performance improvements. Comprehensive experimental results in various conditional generation tasks validate the superiority and adaptability of DSG in terms of both sample quality and time efficiency.
