paragraphs: Multimodal reasoning can accumulate long sequences of textual and visual intermediate steps, increasing computation and memory demands. SpecFlow replaces an expanding collection of visual thoughts with a fixed-size workspace represented in discrete cosine space. This representation concentrates information so that global layout and relationships can be retained while finer spatial details are introduced when needed.

Autoregressive textual thoughts steer flow-based updates of the visual workspace through classifier-free guidance. Each visual update depends on the current visual state and the accumulated textual trace, rather than adding more visual tokens to the context. The design therefore preserves a bounded visual workspace while allowing its contents to evolve with the reasoning process.

The paper reports stable latency and memory usage independent of reasoning depth for its framework, alongside competitive or superior reasoning performance in experiments. Computation and memory costs fall by up to a factor of 2.1. The findings support progressively refining a compact visual representation as a way to sustain longer multimodal reasoning without continually expanding its visual workspace.
summary.tldr: SpecFlow progressively updates a fixed-size visual reasoning workspace, reducing computation and memory costs by up to 2.1 times.

title: Spectral-Progressive Thought Flow for Lightweight Multimodal Reasoning

abstract: The integration of external tools has substantially expanded the capabilities of large language model (LLM) agents, but it also introduces new attack surfaces beyond prompt injection. In particular, cross-tool description poisoning can manipulate planner-visible tool metadata to steer an agent’s trajectory, even if the poisoned tool itself is never chosen. To understand the effectiveness of existing defenses against this emerging threat, we first evaluate several prompt-injection defenses and find that they transfer poorly to cross-tool description poisoning. A key observation is that poisoned descriptions persist in the planning context across steps, enabling continuous influence over subsequent tool choices. Building on this insight, we propose Tool-Guard, a novel system-level defense based on a new concept called isolated planning, in which tool invocations that are detected as misaligned or suspicious cause the corresponding tool to be placed in a quarantined list (the influenced list), breaking further influence from poisoned descriptions. With this influence isolated, the tool can continue to be used to support the task, enabling a robust defense that preserves legitimate tool utility. Experiments on the AgentDojo and ASB benchmarks show that Tool-Guard substantially reduces attack success while maintaining high task utility. Our code is available at https://github.com/shishishi123/Tool-Guard.

paragraphs: An agent can be manipulated through a tool’s description even when it never calls that tool. The description is visible during planning and can steer choices involving other tools. This paper studies that cross-tool poisoning threat and finds that several existing prompt-injection defenses transfer poorly to it.

The key observation is persistence: poisoned descriptions remain in the planning context across multiple steps, giving them repeated opportunities to influence the agent. Tool-Guard addresses this through isolated planning. When a proposed invocation is detected as suspicious or misaligned, the corresponding tool enters a quarantined influenced list, interrupting further influence from poisoned descriptions.

The design preserves the ability to use the tool for legitimate task support while isolating the harmful planning influence. This makes management of the planning context central to the defense. Experiments on AgentDojo and ASB substantially reduce attack success while maintaining high task utility, providing evidence that isolating persistent influence can improve security without simply sacrificing useful tool access.
summary.tldr: Tool-Guard isolates suspicious tools’ influence on planning to reduce description-poisoning attacks while preserving legitimate tool use.

title: Think Twice Before You Act: Protecting LLM Agents Against Tool Description Poisoning via Isolated Planning

abstract: Modern imaging techniques heavily rely on Bayesian statistical models to address difficult image reconstruction and restoration tasks. This paper addresses the objective evaluation of such models in settings where ground truth is unavailable, with a focus on model selection and misspecification diagnosis. Existing unsupervised model evaluation methods are often unsuitable for computational imaging due to their high computational cost and incompatibility with modern image priors defined implicitly via machine learning models. We herein propose a general methodology for unsupervised model selection and misspecification detection in Bayesian imaging sciences, based on a novel combination of Bayesian cross-validation and data fission, a randomized measurement splitting technique. The approach is compatible with any Bayesian imaging sampler, including diffusion and plug-and-play samplers. We demonstrate the methodology through experiments involving various scoring rules and types of model misspecification, where we achieve excellent selection and detection accuracy with a low computational cost.

paragraphs: Image reconstruction often starts with incomplete, noisy measurements rather than a known correct image. Bayesian models help recover an image, but evaluating those models is difficult when ground truth is unavailable. This paper tackles both choosing among candidate models and detecting misspecification, meaning a mismatch between the model and the process behind the measurements.

The proposed approach combines Bayesian cross-validation with data fission, a randomized way to split measurements. That combination supports unsupervised evaluation using the available observations. It is designed to work with any Bayesian imaging sampler, including diffusion and plug-and-play samplers, addressing the incompatibility that some existing evaluation methods have with image priors represented implicitly by learned models.

Experiments examine different scoring rules and different kinds of model misspecification. The authors report strong model-selection and misspecification-detection accuracy at low computational cost. The practical significance is that evaluating a reconstruction model need not depend on access to a clean reference image. The same measurement-based framework supports both comparing alternatives and diagnosing whether an assumed model fits the observations.
summary.tldr: Combining Bayesian cross-validation with randomized measurement splitting enables imaging-model selection and misspecification detection without ground-truth images.

title: Bayesian model selection and misspecification testing in imaging inverse problems only from noisy and partial measurements

abstract: RL training of multi-turn LLM agents is unstable, and reasoning quality drives task performance. Entropy, the standard reasoning-stability monitor, only measures within-input diversity and misses whether reasoning depends on the input. We identify template collapse: stable entropy alongside input-agnostic boilerplate, invisible to entropy and existing metrics. We diagnose it via a mutual-information (MI) proxy that scores cross-input distinguishability online; across tasks, MI correlates with final performance far more strongly than entropy. We then explain collapse via a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) mechanism: low within-input reward variance weakens task gradients, letting input-agnostic regularization dominate and erase cross-input differences. We mitigate this with SNR-Aware Filtering, prioritizing high-variance prompts each iteration. Across planning, math reasoning, web navigation, and code execution, the method consistently improves input dependence and task performance.

paragraphs: During reinforcement learning, a multi-turn language-model agent can retain diverse outputs while losing sensitivity to the actual task input. RAGEN-2 calls this template collapse: reasoning becomes generic boilerplate even though entropy remains stable. Entropy misses the problem because it measures variation for a given input, rather than differences in reasoning across inputs.

The authors introduce an online mutual-information proxy that measures cross-input distinguishability. Across tasks, this signal correlates with final performance much more strongly than entropy. They explain collapse through a signal-to-noise mechanism: when rewards vary little among responses to the same input, task-specific gradients weaken, allowing input-independent regularization to dominate and erase distinctions between tasks.

Their remedy, SNR-Aware Filtering, prioritizes prompts with high within-input reward variance at each training iteration. Across planning, mathematical reasoning, web navigation, and code execution, it consistently improves both input dependence and task performance. The findings distinguish two kinds of diversity that can otherwise be confused: generating varied text and generating reasoning that meaningfully changes with the problem being solved.
summary.tldr: RAGEN-2 detects input-insensitive reasoning that entropy misses and mitigates it by prioritizing prompts with stronger reward variation.

title: RAGEN-2: Reasoning Collapse in Agentic RL

abstract: Source-Free Domain Adaptation (SFDA) enables model adaptation under distribution shifts without access to source data, providing a practical solution for privacy-sensitive applications and having shown substantial progress in classification. In contrast, regression involves ordered and continuous target variables, posing unique challenges for representation adaptation and pseudo-label refinement in the SFDA setting. To address this gap, we propose a novel algorithm for continuous label prediction in SFDA that leverages instance-dependent, discretized density–informed supervisory signals to refine pseudo-labels within an uncertainty-aware paradigm. By incorporating auxiliary discretized distribution learning, our method also promotes more compact and structured feature representations, mitigating the inherent difficulties of adapting regression models under distribution shift. We theoretically demonstrate that the resulting density structure is robust to potential perturbations, supporting reliable SFDA for regression. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

paragraphs: Source-free domain adaptation adjusts an existing model to a changed data distribution without revisiting its original training data. This paper studies regression, where predictions lie on an ordered, continuous scale. That structure makes adapting representations and refining model-generated training targets different from the corresponding problems in classification.

The proposed algorithm uses discretized density information to guide the refinement of pseudo-labels. Its supervisory signals depend on individual examples and account for uncertainty, rather than treating every predicted target as equally dependable. An auxiliary task learns a discretized distribution and encourages the model’s internal features to become more compact and structured.

The authors theoretically show that the resulting density structure is robust to potential perturbations and report effective adaptation across multiple benchmarks. The approach connects two parts of the problem: improving the provisional labels used for adaptation and organizing the representations that produce them. Its source-free setting is particularly relevant when access to the original data is restricted for privacy reasons.
summary.tldr: The method adapts regression models without source data by using uncertainty-aware, discretized density signals to refine pseudo-labels and representations.

title: Discretized Density-Guided Source-Free Domain Adaptation for Regression

abstract: Most Vision Language Models (VLMs) directly map outputs from ViT encoders to the LLM via a lightweight projector. While effective, recent analysis suggests this architecture suffers from an alignment challenge: visual features remain distant from the text space in the initial layers of the LLM, forcing the model to waste critical depth on superficial modality alignment rather than deep understanding and complex reasoning. In this work, we propose Deep Pre-Alignment (DPA), a novel architecture that replaces the standard ViT encoder with a small VLM as perceiver, ensuring visual features are deeply aligned with the text space of the target large language model. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of DPA. On the 4B parameter scale, DPA outperforms baselines by 1.9 points across 8 multimodal benchmarks, with gains widening to 3.0 points at the 32B scale. Moreover, by offloading alignment to the perceiver, DPA achieves a 32.9% reduction in language capability forgetting over 3 text benchmarks. We further demonstrate that these gains are consistent across different LLM families including Qwen3 and LLaMA 3.2, highlighting the generality of our approach. Beyond performance, DPA also offers a seamless upgrade path for current VLM development, requiring only a modular replacement for the visual encoder with marginal computation overhead.

paragraphs: Many vision-language models connect a vision transformer to a language model through a lightweight projector. The paper starts from analysis suggesting that this leaves visual features poorly aligned with text representations in the language model's early layers. Those layers consequently spend capacity on basic modality alignment that could otherwise support deeper understanding and reasoning.

Deep Pre-Alignment replaces the standard visual encoder with a small vision-language model acting as a perceiver. This component prepares visual features that are already deeply aligned with the target language model's text space. The architectural change moves alignment work into the perceiver and provides a modular upgrade with marginal additional computation.

Across eight multimodal benchmarks, DPA improves on baselines by 1.9 points at the 4B parameter scale and 3.0 points at 32B. It also reduces language capability forgetting by 32.9% across three text benchmarks. Consistent gains with Qwen3 and LLaMA 3.2 support the approach across the tested model families, connecting better visual preparation with both multimodal performance and preservation of language abilities.
summary.tldr: Deep Pre-Alignment uses a small vision-language perceiver to prepare visual features, improving multimodal performance while reducing language capability forgetting.

title: Deep Pre-Alignment for VLMs

abstract: Accurate precipitation nowcasting is vital for disaster mitigation, but deep learning methods face a key trade-off: regression models produce over-smoothed, spectrally decaying predictions that blur convective details and violate turbulence power laws; diffusion models generate realistic yet unanchored hallucinations lacking physical grounding. We propose Spectral-Decoupled Iterative Refinement (SDIR), a deterministic framework that reformulates nowcasting as progressive frequency-decoupled refinement. SDIR first extracts a stable low-frequency synoptic skeleton, then iteratively refines high-frequency textures under physical constraints, eliminating both blurring and hallucinations. It features a dual-path design: the Synoptic Frequency-Guided Former (SFG-Former) with Scale-Adaptive Transformers for global structure, and the Fourier Residual Refiner (FR-Refiner) with Scale-Conditioned Fourier Neural Operators for fine residuals. A Physically Consistent Power Spectral Density (PCPSD) loss with dynamic masking enforces a turbulence-consistent spectral distribution. Experiments on three benchmarks show SDIR significantly outperforms SOTA methods in spatial accuracy while achieving spectral fidelity competitive with diffusion-based methods, enabling reliable high-resolution operational nowcasting. Code link: https://github.com/RuntimeWarning/SDIR.

paragraphs: Short-term precipitation forecasting must preserve both broad weather patterns and fine convective detail. The paper identifies a trade-off: regression models blur small-scale structure, while diffusion models can generate realistic-looking details that lack physical grounding. Spectral-Decoupled Iterative Refinement, or SDIR, approaches forecasting as deterministic refinement across different spatial-frequency scales.

SDIR first extracts a stable low-frequency representation of the large-scale weather structure. It then iteratively refines high-frequency detail under physical constraints. A global-structure path uses scale-adaptive Transformers, while a residual-refinement path uses scale-conditioned Fourier neural operators. A power-spectral-density loss with dynamic masking encourages the distribution of detail across frequencies to remain consistent with turbulence.

On three benchmarks, the authors report significantly better spatial accuracy than state-of-the-art methods and spectral fidelity competitive with diffusion-based approaches. This combination matters because a prediction should put precipitation in the right places while also preserving plausible structure across scales. The findings support separating large-scale organization from fine-detail refinement as an approach to reliable, high-resolution nowcasting.
summary.tldr: SDIR refines precipitation forecasts across spatial frequencies, improving spatial accuracy while maintaining competitive spectral realism on three benchmarks.

title: Learning to Refine: Spectral-Decoupled Iterative Refinement Framework for Precipitation Nowcasting

abstract: MLLMs frequently hallucinate objects inconsistent with visual inputs. This issue is typically attributed to the over-reliance on language priors, which can override the visual context. Recent training-free decoding strategies address this by penalizing language priors. However, these methods overlook the dual nature of language priors, where they can be both helpful and harmful depending on the alignment with visual evidence. In particular, blindly suppressing language priors often disrupts the model’s semantic manifold, leading to performance degradation, a phenomenon we term Manifold Departure. To address this, we propose Manifold-Guided Adaptive Projection (MGAP), a geometry-aware, training-free decoding method that mitigates hallucinations while preserving representation structure. MGAP first constructs a language-prior subspace from blind hidden states via SVD. During decoding, MGAP projects each multimodal hidden state onto this subspace and applies a consistency-aware gate to adaptively attenuate only the projected prior component, yielding a subspace-selective update that largely preserves the orthogonal semantic components. Extensive experiments on POPE and CHAIR show that MGAP outperforms prior decoding baselines, achieving stronger hallucination suppression without sacrificing coherence.

paragraphs: Language priors help a multimodal model produce meaningful text, but they can also cause it to describe objects unsupported by an image. The paper argues that indiscriminately suppressing those priors can damage the structure of the model’s representations and reduce performance. It calls this disruption Manifold Departure and proposes a more selective decoding intervention.

Manifold-Guided Adaptive Projection, or MGAP, first uses singular value decomposition on blind hidden states to identify a language-prior subspace. During multimodal generation, it projects each hidden state onto that subspace. A consistency-aware gate then adaptively weakens only the projected prior component, largely preserving semantic components orthogonal to it.

This training-free design makes both the location and strength of the correction selective. It addresses potentially harmful prior information while retaining representation structure that supports coherent language. Experiments on POPE and CHAIR report stronger hallucination suppression than previous decoding baselines without sacrificing coherence. The stated findings support treating language priors according to their consistency with visual evidence, rather than assuming they are uniformly harmful.
summary.tldr: MGAP selectively attenuates language-prior components during multimodal decoding, reducing hallucinations while preserving coherent representation structure.

title: Mitigating Manifold Departure: Uncertainty-Aware Subspace Rectification for Trustworthy MLLM Decoding

An adaptation of Relief for attribute estimation in regression

abstract: Markov networks are extensively used to model complex sequential, patial, andrelational interactions in fields as diverse as image processing, naturallanguage analysis, and bioinformatics. However, inference and learning ingeneral Markov networks is intractable. In this paper, we focus on learning alarge subclass of such models (which we call associative Markov networks) thatare tractable or closely approximable. This subclass contains networks ofdiscrete variables with K labels each and clique potentials that favor thesame labels for all variables in the clique. Such networks capture the``guilt by association'' pattern of reasoning present in many domains, inwhich connected (``associated'') variables tend to have the same label. Ourapproach exploits a linear programming relaxation for the task of finding thebest joint assignment in such networks, which provides an approximatequadratic program (QP) for the problem of learning a margin-maximizing Markov network. We show that forassociative Markov network over binary-valued variables, this approximate QPis guaranteed to return an optimal parameterization for Markov networks ofarbitrary topology. For the non-binary case, optimality is not guaranteed,but the relaxation produces good solutions in practice. Experimental resultswith hypertext and newswire classification show significant advantages overstandard approaches.

paragraphs: General Markov networks can represent complex interactions, but learning and inference are intractable in general. This paper focuses on associative networks: discrete-variable models whose clique potentials favor assigning the same label to associated variables. The restriction captures situations where connections provide evidence that variables should share a classification.

The learning method uses a linear-programming relaxation for finding a best joint assignment. That relaxation leads to an approximate quadratic program for learning a margin-maximizing Markov network. The approach connects a structured prediction problem to an optimization procedure that exploits the model's preference for agreement, making the associative subclass central to its computational properties.

For binary-valued variables, the approximate quadratic program is guaranteed to return an optimal parameterization even for arbitrary network topology. For more than two labels, the authors do not guarantee optimality, although they report good practical solutions. Experiments on hypertext and newswire classification show significant advantages over standard approaches. The theoretical guarantee and empirical findings therefore apply at different levels of generality.
summary.tldr: Associative Markov networks enable margin-based learning with guaranteed optimal parameterization for binary variables and promising empirical results for broader settings.

title: Learning associative Markov networks

abstract: Reinforcement learning algorithms can become unstable when combined with linear function approximation. Algorithms that minimize the mean-square Bellman error are guaranteed to converge, but often do so slowly or are computationally expensive. In this paper, we propose to improve the convergence speed of piecewise linear function approximation by tracking the dynamics of the value function with the Kalman filter using a random-walk model. We cast this as a general framework in which we implement the TD, Q-Learning and MAXQ algorithms for different domains, and report empirical results demonstrating improved learning speed over previous methods.
originalAbstract: Reinforcement learning algorithms can become unstable when combined with linear function approximation. Algorithms that minimize the mean-square Bellman error are guaranteed to converge, but often do so slowly or are computationally expensive. In this paper, we propose to improve the convergence speed of piecewise linear function approximation by tracking the dynamics of the value function with the Kalman filter using a random-walk model. We cast this as a general framework in which we implement the TD, Q-Learning and MAXQ algorithms for different domains, and report empirical results demonstrating improved learning speed over previous methods.

paragraphs: The paper addresses learning speed when reinforcement learning uses piecewise linear value-function approximation. It starts from a broader difficulty: combining reinforcement learning with linear approximation can cause instability. Methods that minimize mean-square Bellman error offer convergence guarantees, but may learn slowly or require expensive computation.

The proposed approach tracks changes in the value function using a Kalman filter and a random-walk model. This treats the evolving value function as something to estimate dynamically during learning. The random-walk model is the stated modeling choice underlying that tracking procedure, and the intended benefit is faster convergence of the approximation.

The authors present the approach as a general framework and implement TD, Q-learning, and MAXQ within it for different domains. Their empirical results demonstrate improved learning speed over previous methods. These findings support value-function tracking as a way to accelerate the evaluated algorithms; the abstract's convergence guarantees concern the Bellman-error-minimizing methods discussed as background, rather than establishing a new universal guarantee for the proposed framework.
summary.tldr: Kalman-filter tracking of value-function dynamics improves learning speed for piecewise linear TD, Q-learning, and MAXQ implementations in reported experiments.

title: Tracking value function dynamics to improve reinforcement learning with piecewise linear function approximation

abstract: Errors in map-making tasks using computer vision are sparse. We demonstrate this by considering the construction of digital elevation models that employ stereo matching algorithms to triangulate real-world points. This sparsity, coupled with a geometric theory of errors recently developed by the authors, allows for autonomous agents to calculate their own precision independently of ground truth. We connect these developments with recent advances in the mathematics of sparse signal reconstruction or compressed sensing. The theory presented here extends the autonomy of 3-D model reconstructions discovered in the 1990s to their errors.

We connect these developments with recent advances in the mathematics of sparse signal reconstruction or compressed sensing. paragraphs: The paper examines how a vision system can estimate the precision of the maps it constructs. Its example is the creation of digital elevation models through stereo matching, where corresponding image information is used to triangulate real-world points. The authors demonstrate that errors in these map-making tasks have a sparse structure.

They combine that sparsity with a geometric theory of errors they had developed. Together, these ingredients allow autonomous agents to calculate their own precision without relying on ground truth. This addresses the problem of assessing a reconstruction when an independently known correct version is unavailable for direct comparison.

The authors connect the approach to sparse signal reconstruction and compressed sensing. The key connection is the usefulness of sparse error structure for recovering information about uncertainty in the reconstruction. Their theoretical contribution extends the autonomy previously established for three-dimensional reconstruction to the errors of those reconstructions. The claimed self-assessment depends on the sparse structure and geometric theory developed in this setting.
summary.tldr: Sparse errors and geometric error theory let vision agents estimate reconstruction precision independently of ground truth.

title: Autonomous geometric precision error estimation in low-level computer vision tasks

abstract: The development of mechanisms to understand and model the expected behaviour of multiagent learners is becoming increasingly important as the area rapidly find application in a variety of domains. In this paper we present a framework to model the behaviour of Q-learning agents using the e-greedy exploration mechanism. For this, we analyse a continuous-time version of the Q-learning update rule and study how the presence of other agents and the e-greedy mechanism affect it. We then model the problem as a system of difference equations which is used to theoretically analyse the expected behaviour of the agents. The applicability of the framework is tested through experiments in typical games selected from the literature.

paragraphs: When several agents learn at once, understanding their behavior requires accounting for their interactions as well as their individual learning rules. This paper develops a framework for studying Q-learning agents that use epsilon-greedy exploration. The focus is on modeling their expected behavior, including the effects of exploration and the presence of other learners.

The authors begin by analyzing a continuous-time version of the Q-learning update. This provides a way to examine how the update is affected by the multiagent setting and the exploration mechanism. They then express the problem as a system of difference equations, which becomes the basis for theoretical analysis of the agents' expected behavior.

The framework is tested experimentally in representative games drawn from the literature. These experiments assess its applicability to interacting learners. The contribution is an analytical description of learning dynamics: it connects the agents' update rules to equations that can be studied, rather than presenting a new exploration strategy or asserting that all such learners reach the same outcome.
summary.tldr: A dynamical framework analyzes the expected behavior of interacting Q-learning agents using epsilon-greedy exploration.

title: Dynamic analysis of multiagent Q-learning with ε-greedy exploration

abstract: Previous studies on multi-instance learning typically treated instances in the \textit{bags} as independently and identically distributed. The instances in a bag, however, are rarely independent in real tasks, and a better performance can be expected if the instances are treated in an non-i.i.d. way that exploits relations among instances. In this paper, we propose two simple yet effective methods. In the first method, we explicitly map every bag to an undirected graph and design a graph kernel for distinguishing the positive and negative bags. In the second method, we implicitly construct graphs by deriving affinity matrices and propose an efficient graph kernel considering the clique information. The effectiveness of the proposed methods are validated by experiments.
originalAbstract: Previous studies on multi-instance learning typically treated instances in the \textit{bags} as independently and identically distributed. The instances in a bag, however, are rarely independent in real tasks, and a better performance can be expected if the instances are treated in an non-i.i.d. way that exploits relations among instances. In this paper, we propose two simple yet effective methods. In the first method, we explicitly map every bag to an undirected graph and design a graph kernel for distinguishing the positive and negative bags. In the second method, we implicitly construct graphs by deriving affinity matrices and propose an efficient graph kernel considering the clique information. The effectiveness of the proposed methods are validated by experiments.

paragraphs: Multi-instance learning organizes examples into bags, and this paper challenges the common treatment of instances inside a bag as independent and identically distributed. The authors argue that real tasks often contain relationships among those instances. Their aim is to use those relationships when distinguishing positive bags from negative ones.

The first proposed method explicitly represents every bag as an undirected graph and builds a graph kernel for classification. The second represents graph structure implicitly through affinity matrices and develops an efficient kernel that incorporates clique information. Both approaches make within-bag relationships part of the representation used to compare bags, although they construct that representation differently.

Experiments validate the effectiveness of the two methods. The findings support the paper's expectation that exploiting relationships can help multi-instance learning in practice. The central contribution is the move from treating a bag as a collection of independent samples to representing its internal connections, with explicit and implicit graph constructions offering two ways to put that idea into a classifier.
summary.tldr: Two graph-kernel methods improve multi-instance modeling by representing relationships among instances within each bag.

title: Multi-instance learning by treating instances as non-I.I.D. samples

abstract: Supervised topic models utilize document's side information for discovering predictive low dimensional representations of documents; and existing models apply likelihood-based estimation. In this paper, we present a max-margin supervised topic model for both continuous and categorical response variables. Our approach, the maximum entropy discrimination latent Dirichlet allocation (MedLDA), utilizes the max-margin principle to train supervised topic models and estimate predictive topic representations that are arguably more suitable for prediction. We develop efficient variational methods for posterior inference and demonstrate qualitatively and quantitatively the advantages of MedLDA over likelihood-based topic models on movie review and 20 Newsgroups data sets.

In this paper, we present a max-margin supervised topic model for both continuous and categorical response variables. Our approach, the maximum entropy discrimination latent Dirichlet allocation (MedLDA), utilizes the max-margin principle to train supervised topic models and estimate predictive topic representations that are arguably more suitable for prediction. We develop efficient variational methods for posterior inference and demonstrate qualitatively and quantitatively the advantages of MedLDA over likelihood-based topic models on movie review and 20 Newsgroups data sets.

paragraphs: Supervised topic models use information associated with documents to learn compact representations that help predict a response. The paper observes that existing models use likelihood-based estimation. It proposes MedLDA, a supervised topic model that instead brings the maximum-margin principle into training for both continuous responses and categorical labels.

The objective is to make the learned topic representation useful for prediction as part of the modeling process. Continuous and categorical responses connect the same approach to regression and classification. The authors argue that a maximum-margin training principle can produce topic representations better suited to prediction, rather than treating predictive usefulness as a consequence of likelihood-based fitting alone.

The paper develops efficient variational methods for posterior inference. It evaluates MedLDA on movie reviews and the 20 Newsgroups datasets, reporting both qualitative and quantitative advantages over likelihood-based topic models. Those findings support the proposed training principle in the evaluated settings. The broader claim that the representations are more suitable for prediction is presented as an argument supported by these demonstrations.
summary.tldr: MedLDA uses maximum-margin training to learn predictive topic representations for regression and classification, with reported advantages over likelihood-based models.

title: MedLDA: maximum margin supervised topic models for regression and classification

abstract: Classical dynamic Bayesian networks (DBNs) are based on the homogeneous Markov assumption and cannot deal with heterogeneity and non-stationarity in temporal processes. Various approaches to relax the homogeneity assumption have recently been proposed. The present paper aims to improve the shortcomings of three recent versions of heterogeneous DBNs along the following lines:(i) avoiding the need for data discretization,(ii) increasing the flexibility over a time-invariant network structure,(iii) avoiding over-flexibility and over fitting by introducing a regularization scheme based in inter-time segment information sharing. The improved method is evaluated on synthetic data and compared with alternative published methods on gene expression time series from Drosophila melanogaster.

Various approaches to relax the homogeneity assumption have recently been proposed. The present paper aims to improve the shortcomings of three recent versions of heterogeneous DBNs along the following lines:(i) avoiding the need for data discretization,(ii) increasing the flexibility over a time-invariant network structure,(iii) avoiding over-flexibility and over fitting by introducing a regularization scheme based in inter-time segment information sharing. The improved method is evaluated on synthetic data and compared with alternative published methods on gene expression time series from Drosophila melanogaster.

paragraphs: Classical dynamic Bayesian networks assume homogeneous temporal behavior, which limits their ability to represent processes that change over time. This paper develops a heterogeneous model intended to address shortcomings in three recent approaches. It focuses on combining support for continuous data, greater structural flexibility, and control over excessive model flexibility.

The method avoids requiring data discretization and relaxes restrictions associated with a network structure that stays fixed over time. At the same time, it introduces regularization through information sharing between time segments. These choices address a central modeling tension: allowing relationships to vary while preventing that freedom from producing overfitting.

The method is evaluated on synthetic data and compared with published alternatives using gene-expression time series from Drosophila melanogaster. The contribution is the combination of these modeling improvements within a heterogeneous dynamic Bayesian network. Its information-sharing mechanism is especially relevant to the stated goal because it connects flexible temporal structure with a means of constraining that flexibility across segments.
summary.tldr: A heterogeneous dynamic Bayesian network combines continuous data modeling and flexible structure with regularization through information sharing across time segments.

title: Heterogeneous Continuous Dynamic Bayesian Networks with Flexible Structure and Inter-Time Segment Information Sharing

abstract: We investigate the sparse eigenvalue problem which arises in various fields such as machine learning and statistics. Unlike standard approaches relying on approximation of the $l_{0}$-norm, we work with an equivalent reformulation of the problem at hand as a DC program. Our starting point is the eigenvalue problem to which a constraint for sparsity requirement is added. The obtained problem is first formulated as a mixed integer program, and exact penalty techniques are used to equivalently transform the resulting problem into a DC program, whose solution is assumed by a customized DCA. Computational results for sparse principal component analysis are reported, which show the usefulness of our approach that compares favorably with some related standard methods using approximation of the $l_{0}$-norm.
originalAbstract: We investigate the sparse eigenvalue problem which arises in various fields such as machine learning and statistics. Unlike standard approaches relying on approximation of the $l_{0}$-norm, we work with an equivalent reformulation of the problem at hand as a DC program. Our starting point is the eigenvalue problem to which a constraint for sparsity requirement is added. The obtained problem is first formulated as a mixed integer program, and exact penalty techniques are used to equivalently transform the resulting problem into a DC program, whose solution is assumed by a customized DCA. Computational results for sparse principal component analysis are reported, which show the usefulness of our approach that compares favorably with some related standard methods using approximation of the $l_{0}$-norm.

paragraphs: The paper studies an eigenvalue problem with an added sparsity requirement: the solution must use only a limited set of coordinates. This connects eigenvalue calculations to applications such as sparse principal component analysis, where selecting a small number of participating variables is part of the learning problem.

The authors begin by expressing the sparsity-constrained problem as a mixed integer program. They then use exact penalty techniques to transform it into an equivalent difference-of-convex, or DC, program. The distinction is that their formulation preserves the original problem rather than replacing the count of nonzero entries with an approximation. A customized DC algorithm is used to tackle the resulting formulation.

Computational results on sparse principal component analysis compare the approach favorably with some established methods that approximate the sparsity count. These results support the usefulness of the reformulation in that application. The equivalence concerns the optimization formulations; the abstract does not turn the computational comparison into a claim that every run finds a globally best sparse solution.
summary.tldr: An exact DC reformulation offers an alternative to approximating sparsity in eigenvalue problems, with favorable sparse PCA results.

title: A DC Programming Approach for Sparse Eigenvalue Problem
